99 
 
The saint was martyred in 302 AD. 
 [Butler: February 23] 
SERENUS; SAINTS BY THAT NAME 
More than one martyr carried the name Serenus: 
1- Serenus and Serenus : two martyrs among the students  of Origen (184 -
253 AD), who happen to carry the same name . They were tortured during 
the persecution stirred up by Emperor Severus (222-235 AD). They were 
martyred along with a third martyr by the name Plutarch . The Western 
Church celebrates them on the 28th of June. 
2- Father Serenus of the desert of Nitria : who was a climax in asceticism 
and had many virtues . He was visited by Father John Cassian (360 -435 
AD) in the year 395 AD . They discussed two subjects . In the first one, 
father Serenus talked to him abo ut the Nature of the Spirit, the rapid 
movement of the thoughts, the influence of the evil spirits upon them, and 
the importance of fixing the desire on God. In the following discussion, he 
talked to him about the nature of the evil spirits, their fall, su bordination, 
and occupation. 
 [A Dictionary of Christian Biography, Vol. IV, pp. 615-616] 
 
SERGIUS OF ATRIPE AND HIS COMPANIONS 
(The martyrs) 
This saint was born in the city of Atripe, by a good father called Tadros and 
a pious mother called Mary. When he reached 20 years of age, he decided to 
die in the Name of the Lord Christ. He went to Cyprian , the governor, and 
before him, he confessed the name of the Lord. 
A Night Vision in Prison: 
After torturing him by several kinds of tools, he was cast in prison. In a 
night vision, he saw himself in heaven, where he saw the dwelling places of 
the saints, which brought comfort to his soul; and the Lord Christ healed his 
wounds. 
Martyrdom of Fr. Mansoon: 
On hearing about the strife of Sergius, a priest called  Fr. Mansoon went to 
Atripe accompanied by two deacons . They confessed the Lord Christ before 
the governor, who ordered beating them with ferocity. There, a great multitude 
gathered around the priest, sympathizing with him; and he addressed them and 
counseled them to hold fast to the Upright faith in the Lord Christ, he prayed

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Volume 4, p. 89
passages.text:
89 
 
to the church. 
His Prophecy about Ariana: 
Before the boat started to sail from Alexandria, St. Serabamon told the 
governor Ariana: “Ariana! The Lord Christ is going to call upon you to go to 
His wedding. And, when He does , hasten without slothfulness to respond to 
his invitation. You will strive, you will overcome Diocletian by your 
perseverance and will receive the crown of martyrdom.”  The governor 
naturally mocked that prophecy, counting it as fantasy; until the time came 
when Ariana received the Christian faith and persisted on being martyred. 
Pope of Alexandria Alexandros I wrote: 
* O Saint Serabamon! Who would be wise enough and prudent to 
describe the loftiness of your virtues?! 
* Who is eloquent enough to narrate your miracles, O wearer of God! 
* Who is the researcher who could show the extent of your strife, O the 
utterer of Divinities, the perfect in every goodness; who strove for the sake of 
the flocks of the Lord Christ; and suffered to guide the multitudes, and lea d 
them away from vanity; following the lead of Paul the Apostle, who guided 
multitudes to the sure way of the Truth. 
 [Manuscript# 214 in the Library of the Syrian Monastery; published by Fr. 
Serabamon St. Anthony] 
 
SERABAMON, THE HEGOMEN, ST. 
Hegomen of the Monastery of Abu-Yeĥness: 
This St. Serabamon , the hermit , became the hegomen (abbot) of the 
monastery of Abu-Yeĥness. He was a monk in that monastery from an early 
age. He remained in his worship and in serving the older monks for 32 years 
until he was ordained as a hegomen on the monastery to supervise its affairs . 
Since then, he increased his devotion and asceticism. Although, he used to fast 
the whole day, from the day he became a monk until the day he reposed. 
After 20 years in this fellowship, he cl osed on himself in a room in one of 
the churches and was not seen for almost ten years, during which he broke his 
fast only on Saturdays and Sundays.  
A Cross of Fire: 
When it was time for him to depart from this world, an angel of the Lord 
appeared to him in a night vision. The angel handed him a Cross of fire, saying: 
“Take this in your hand.” He said to the angel: “How could I hold fire with my 
hand?” The angel answered him: “Do not be afraid, for the Lord Christ will

91 
 
they would assume that the saint has seen a vision. St. Anthony used to tell St. 
Serapion about these visions. It was also said that St. Anthony while sitting on 
the mountain, he often saw what was going on in Egy pt. The second time , 
when he knew that his departure was near, he requested that his clothes be 
distributed, giving one of sheepskin to Pope Athanasius and the one he has 
gotten new from bishop Serapion to be given back to him worn out, to keep. 
Heading a Monastic Congregation: 
According to the historian Sozomen, before St. Serapion was ordained as a 
bishop, he was the abbot of a monastic congregation in Upper Egypt, and that 
he was well known for his fantastic sanctity and eloquence. His close friend, 
Pope Athanasius, also mentioned in his letter to Dracontius, that he was the 
abbot of a significant number of monks. 
His Support of Pope Athanasius: 
St. Serapion supported the Pope in his strife against the Arianism . Being 
like his right hand , the pope used hi m as his deputy during his frequent 
absences from the throne. In the year 340 AD, the pope let him declare the date 
of the Passover; and it is believed that he let him write the Passover papal 
messages during the two years 341 and 342 AD. 
His Exile and Departure: 
On the 18 th of May 353 AD, Pope Athanasius sent a delegation of five 
bishops and three priests, headed by bishop Serapion, to Emperor Constantius 
II after his conquests and reigning over both the East and the West. The papal 
delegation was carrying to the emperor a document signed by 80 bishops from 
Egypt in support of Pope Athanasius and refuting the evil reports presented by 
the Arians against him.  However, the emperor 's response was to send St. 
Serapion to exile, for the sake of his Upright faith ; and hence was called the 
Confessor. This saint was chosen based on his ability to defend the Upright 
faith, and his firm stands in encountering the emperor and opposing the Arian 
pressure. It was said that St. Serapion reposed in his exile around the year 370 
AD, even though the exact date is not certain. 
Letters of St. Athanasius to Him: 
St. Athanasius the Apostolic sent him five dogmatic letters: 
1- A letter sent in 339 AD, while in exile, concerning the death of Arius, in 
which St. Athanasius denied that Arius changed his views or that he 
reconciled with the Church before he died. 
2- Four very important letters about the Holy Spirit, which the pope wrote in 
response to a request from St. Serapion , who was complaining that the

passages.text:
94 
 
 [Baring-Gould: October 30] 
 
SERAPION, THE ABBOT, ST. 
This St. Serapion was a priest and one of the most famous Fathers. He was 
mentioned in the book: On Illustrious Men written by St. Jerome, as follows: 
“We saw him in the region of Arsinoe (Fayyum) , an elder father in charge 
of many monasteries that embraced about 10,000 monks , and he cared for all 
their needs. Those who harvested the fields used to bring to him 12 bushels of 
wheat, to give to those in need in the area. He used to distribute these needs by 
his own hands, and to send to those in Alexandria their portions as well. 
The Fathers of the wilderness used to do that regularly, always taking care 
of the poor in Alexandria . But, because of being occupied with the life of 
spiritual strife, they used to just fill boats with food and clothes and send them 
every year to the capital; on account of that, the poor around them in the desert 
were not that many. 
We also saw in the region of Babylon (Old Cairo) and Memphis (El -
Badrashin) so many great Fathers, who were adorned with good deeds, blessed 
and well accepted by God .” The name of St. Serapion was also mentioned in 
the biography of the Libyan recluse Marcus Atheniensis, who cared to bury his 
body. 
 [A Dictionary of Christian Biography, Vol. IV, p. 613] 
 
SERAPION, THE CORINTHIAN MARTYR 
This St. Serapion was originally from Corinth in Greece. He was martyred 
in Egypt, along with Niceporus, under the rule of Emperor Numerian (283-284 
AD) in the year 284 AD. 
 [A Dictionary of Christian Biography, Vol. IV, p. 613] 
 
SERAPION, THE EGYPTIAN MARTYR 
A Desire for Martyrdom: 
This St. Serapion was a wealthy inhabitant of Binosah (Babousah) in Lower 
Egypt, with a strong love of giving alms. At the time of persecution, he heard 
that Armanius govern or of Alexandria arrived in the area to torture the 
Christians. Serapion came to encounter him, along with a friend called 
Theodorus and a third, a shepherd of cattle, named Thomas. And, when they 
confessed the Lord Christ before him, the governor cast them in prison.

92 
 
teaching against the Holy Spirit, considering Him as a created being, albeit 
higher than the angels, was very quickly spreading . Those letters are 
counted as the first methodical theological research about the Holy Spirit. 
St. Serapion Writings: 
1- Against the followers of Mani: a work that revealed the eloquence of St. 
Serapion in both the theological and philosophical fields. He only criticized 
the main points in the views of the followers of Mani, in particular their 
Dualism view, (concerning the god of light and the god of darkness); their 
objection about the Old Testament and some parts of the New Testament . 
He also proved the contradiction and lack of logic within their views. 
2- His Letters: A comforting letter he wrote to bishop Evgokius who was ill; 
a letter to the monks in Alexandr ia, in which he used the expression 
“Homosius Trias ,” meaning (The Trinity equal in Essence); and a 
condolence letter to some disciples of Abba Anthony after he reposed in 
the year 356 AD. 
3- Other works which, according to some scholars, were his, like A Sermon 
on Virginity ; A Letter to the Confessors ; and some fragments of 
Interpretations of the Book of Genesis, referred to by St. Jerome. 
4- The Divine Liturgy by St. Serapion 1 This version represents the 
Ecclesiastical Liturgy in Egypt in the 4th century (Probably referring to an 
earlier period). This Liturgy carried a reflection of the views of the School 
of Alexandria in the 3rd century concerning the Divinity of the Logos ‘The 
Word,’ after adding to it what suited the 4th century in response to the Arian 
heresy. 
So many prayers that came in this Liturgy are the same as those included in 
the Liturgy of St. Mark, concerning the Anaphora (The Ecclesiastical system) 
of the Ethiopian Church. 
All prayers address God, being the Father of the Only Begotten-Son, and it 
gives Him thanks for the sake of His compassion, proclaimed through the 
salvation works of our Lord Jesus Christ. 
Of the Divine Liturgy by St. Serapion: 
• I implore You, O Lord, to send Your Holy Spirit to our minds . Grant us to 
understand Your inspi red Holy Bible , to be able to  interpret them with 
uprightness and worthiness. 
So that all believers present here would benefit from them. 
Grant us the spirit of light, to recognize You as the Truth. And Jesus Christ 
whom You sent (John 3:17). Grant us the Holy Spirit, to be able to proclaim 
 
1 Fr. ‘Tadros Y. Malaty’ covered this Liturgy in his book “Christ in the Eucharist Sacrament”…

88 
 
contemplation, he soon returned to his monastery, to be called by the pope now 
and then, to enjoy his company and his shining countenance. 
Bishop of Nicius: 
Almost ten years in his papacy, the diocese of Nicius became vacant by the 
repose of St. John . Pope Peter called the monk Serabamon and ordained him 
as a bishop on that diocese, which made the congregation there very happy. 
On his hands, God performed so many miracles and signs; among them was 
that near his city, there were locations for idol worship, which he kept praying 
to the Lord Christ until these sites were all destroyed and inundated by water . 
The idol worship was ultimately uprooted from his whole diocese. He also 
managed to eradicate the heresy of Sabilius, who taught that the Father, the 
Son, and the Holy Spirit were one Hypostasis. 
 Performing Signs and Miracles: 
His biographer Pope Alexandros I talked much about how St. Serabamon 
opposed Arius and Meletius. He also said about the saint: “ Living in his city  
became like living in the monasteries of monks . The miracles and signs 
performed by him were not less than those performed by the Apostles Peter 
and Paul. He healed the sick and drove the unclean spirits out, screaming and 
begging him not to torture them with his prayers.” 
His Care for the Poor and the Rich: 
His city became like one family; the rich were urged by him to provide the 
poor generously with their necessities. 
His Martyrdom: 
After Emperor Diocletian (284 -305) denied the faith, he was told how 
bishop Serabamon hindered idol worship by his teachings. When the emperor 
visited Alexandria, he called him in. Once the saint arrived at Alexandria, he 
was arrested and spent the night in prison, wh ere he joined Pope Peter and 
some priests who saw his countenance shine like an angel. Emperor Diocletian 
tortured the bishop with every tool he had , and the Lord Christ kept healing 
him of every wound . And when the emperor saw how a multitude of people 
proclaimed their faith in the Lord Christ because of him , he decided to give 
him to Ariana the governor of Ansenah to torture him and to cut his head off if 
he persists on his faith. Then, it happened that Ariana was in Alexandria at that 
time, so he took the saint with him by boat. When they reached Nicius, and the 
boat stopped and could not be moved, they took the saint to the northern side 
of the city, where they cut his head off , and he received the crown of 
martyrdom. Afterward, his people came and moved his body with great honor

passages.text:
105 
 
eternity. The emperor called him and asked him to live in the royal court and 
to accompany him whenever he would go to the Church. And,  Innocentius I 
(401-417 AD), the pope of Rome at that time, was inspired by God that 
Severianus would eventually be entrusted on a great multitude, so the pope 
honored him and revered him, and he became beloved by all. 
In the Greek City of Gabala: 
When St. Severianus noticed how everyone was honoring him, he decided 
in secret for fear that he would lose his labor, to forsake the glory of this world. 
And, an angel of the Lord appeared to him and told him to go to a city called 
Gabala in Greece, where he woul d be in charge of a multitude of believers. 
Then, he set forth at night with his disciple Tadros, whom he clothed with the 
monastic attire. They both were guided by an angel to a monastery headed by 
a saintly man. That Abbot was told in a night vision abou t the coming of 
Severianus, and he came out to receive him and told him about what he saw. 
As he became well known in that region, an uncountable number of people 
came to see him. Emperor Theodosius II (402 -450) reconstructed an old 
monastery for him to dw ell in, and he came to be the cause of comfort for so 
many souls. He continuously taught and guided his monks to become as holy 
as angels. On his hands, God made so many signs, among which was that the 
daughter of the governor of the city was possessed by an unclean spirit. She 
told her father: “If you send Severianus out of our city, I shall get out of your 
daughter.” On learning about it, the saint wrote on a piece of paper: “In the 
name of Jesus Christ, go out of her.” Once the girl read what was written in the 
article, the unclean spirit screamed and came out of her. 
When some sorcerers, along with some soldiers, came to force themselves 
upon his monastery, God struck them with blindness for three days until the 
saint prayed on their behalf, and God healed them. 
Ordained as a Bishop on Gabala: 
Philadelphus, the bishop of the city of Gabala, was told by God through a 
dream that St. Severianus would sit on his throne after his departure. So, he 
informed his people about it. When Severianus, eventually was o rdained as a 
bishop on the city of Gabala, he strove to shepherd his people. It happened that, 
in that city, a Jew called Sectar was boasting about his wide knowledge, and 
he came to debate with St. Severianus. He ended up, along with so many 
sorcerers, be ing convinced of the soundness of the Christian Faith and 
proclaimed their belief in the Lord Christ. In his time, Egypt flourished with 
her monks, the way Constantinople flourished with having St. John 
Chrysostom.

he would finish his prayers, the fever and headache would forsake him. By that 
way, this monk was able to overcome the adversary thoughts. 
5. Controlling the Mind: The saint was asked: “How could man reject the 
talk of laymen in temporal issues; and how could he keep his mind with God , 
as it is written?” She answered: “This is like sitting at a banquet with many 
kinds of foods. If you eat with greed and covetousness, you would be guilty. If 
you eat without greed or covetousness, then you are not guilty. It is the same 
if you listen to the talk of laymen, but keep your heart with you, and have no 
pleasure in what being said. you would be unharmed.” 
6. The Features of a Teacher: It is befitting of a teacher to be a stranger to 
the desire of authority, pride and vainglory; lest he would pr obably fall by 
flirtation and lose his vision by gifts. But it is befitting of him to be 
longsuffering, meek and humble, as much as he can, and does not seek 
appearances, but cares for all and loves everyone. 
7. Enduring Tribulations: Let us try to enter t hrough the narrow door. For 
unless a tree endures the tempests of winter, it would not be able to produce 
fruit. For us, this age is like a stormy winter; it is only by enduring the 
tribulations and the temptations, we would inherit the Kingdom of Heaven. 
8. Sanctification of the Body: In a debate concerning the body between a 
Christian and a Mani -follower, the Christian said: “By letting the body walk 
according to the Divine law, you will find it on the side of its Creator.”  
 
THEODORA, EMPRESS 
This saint Theodora (~500-548 AD) was the wife of Emperor Justinian I 
(527-565). She was one of the most prominent women of the old , known for 
her beauty, iron will, riches and firmness, along with her broad knowledge. 
In the year 523, Justinian married her, and in the year 527, she was crowned 
as an empress. She had an active role in the theological debates and was very 
vibrant in other activities . Contrary to her husband, she loved St. Severus of 
Antioch and supported the non-Chalcedonian Egyptian Church. 
She had a significant role in the ethical reforms, cared for pious works, and, 
together with her husband, they cared for building churches and hospitals. 
She reposed in the year 548 AD. Her portrait in the mosaic was found in the 
Basilica of San Vitale in Ravenna. 
   [Cross: Dictionary of the Christian Church, p. 1358] 
 
 
THEODORA, THE BURRIER OF MARTYRS

physician was bandaging his amputated leg, the saint kept on weav ing the 
baskets and talking joyfully to us and giving thanks to God. And, St. Steven, 
who has lived such an exalted spiritual life, noticed our amazement to what 
was going on and noticed that we were not able to watch him, while he was 
enduring that necessary amputation of his leg. When he perceived our thoughts 
and felt our grief, the good man told us: “Do not let it saddens you, my children, 
and do not let it weakens your faith; for God never does anything wrong, on 
the contrary, He always reserves for us a happy ending. How often those body 
parts of mine deserved to be punished and amputated? To be punished here is 
far better than to be punished in the world to come.”  
On saying this, he gave us comfort, and bid us farewell, saying: “Do not 
ever be offended to see temptations of this kind dwell on the saints; for by them 
God edifies us, grants us comfort and holds us fast in his laws.” I narrated these 
things to keep you from wondering why the saints fall under such temptations.” 
 [Budge: The Paradise, Vol. 1; pp. 131-2] [Palladius: Lausiac History, Ch. 21] 
 
STRATONICE, ST. 
She was a martyr of Cyzicum in Mysia in Asia Minor. She was martyred 
along with her husband Seleucus during the persecution stirred up by Emperor 
Diocletian (284-305 AD). On account of t hat, her husband was the leading 
pagan magistrate of the town; she had the chance to watch how a significant 
number of Christians being arrested and violently tortured. With time, she was 
impacted by their perseverance and endurance, and as a result, she proclaimed 
her faith in Christianity. And, she managed to convince her husband to follow 
suit. Her father Apollonius, made a great effort to make them return to their 
paganism. However, when he failed to do so, he became one of their vicious 
opponents. Afte r prolonged and severe torture, and with several miracles 
performed on their hands in the Lord's name, they both received the crowns of 
martyrdom. The Western Church celebrates them on the 31st of October. 
 [A Dictionary of Christian Biography, Vol. IV, p. 743] 
 
SUSAN, ST. 
This saint was born in the region of Edessa (El-Roha) to a noble family. She 
was given the name Susan (Sawsan), which means the Lily flower. She was 
raised by her parents as a true Christian, so she used to begin her day and end 
it with prayers. She used to go regularly to the church to have communion in 
the Holy Sacraments. Her blessed life, delicate behavior, genuine humility, and 
her love for the poor and the needy made her the object of admiration of her

her that her salvation is near. On the next day, the governor ordered to resume 
her torture, and then he ordered to cut her head off . At that moment, a lighted 
dove came down on her head, which made many of those present proclaim 
their faith in the Lord Christ. 
 [Butler: September 7] 
 
REGULUS, THE BISHOP , ST. 
St. Regulus (Rieul) is the intercessor of the city of Senlis . He is said to be 
the first bishop in the city , for he lived in the 3 rd century. After that , the 
Cathedral of Senlis was burnt out with all the records of its former bishops . It 
is said that after he proclaimed his faith in the Lord Christ, he set forth to 
France where he preached Christianity. And, he went to Paris to search for the 
relics of the martyrs: St. Denis, St. Rusticus, and St. Eleutherius. Then, he took 
upon himself to convert the inhabitants of Senlis; to Christianity . He reposed 
around the year 250 AD. 
  [Butler: March 30] 
 
REPARATA, THE VIRGIN (The martyr) 
This lady, St. Reparata was from Caesarea of Palestine . When she was 12 
years old, she was arrested during the persecution of Emperor Decius (249 -
251), because of her being Christian. Once the governor saw her, admiring her 
beauty, he tried to seduce her by tender words. But, when he failed in making 
her worship his idols, he ordered to torture her by casting her into a furnace of 
fire. In there, like the Three Young Men, she was not harmed, but kept singing 
praise to God, and proclaimed to the governor from inside the furnace that she 
holds fast to her Christ. Finally, when the governor ordered his men to cut her 
head off, she walked wi th them singing praise . Finally, when she was 
beheaded, her soul was seen coming out of her body in the form of a dove, 
flying up toward Heaven. Her relics were eventually moved to Italy, where she 
was honored by several dioceses. 
 [Butler: October 8] 
 
RESTITUTA, THE VIRGIN (The martyr) 
This lady St. Restituta was a Roman virgin of noble origin, and was 
martyred in the year 271 AD in the town of Sora in Italy. She became the patron 
saint of that city where she was buried . It was said that the Lord Christ 
appeared to her and instructed her to go to Sora, and an angel led her to that

Earlier on, Genevieve 's poor parents received the Christian faith and 
forsook the idol -worship. Then, her father needed her to shepherd his s mall 
flock of sheep, in which the girl found a great chance to spend the whole day 
on the pasture land, practicing a life of prayer and worship of her beloved 
groom Jesus Christ . On the other hand, Genevieve 's mother tried to let her 
daughter stop spending  long hours worshipping God, with no avail . It 
happened that on a feast day, intending to punish her daughter for disobeying 
her, she ordered her to stay home and not to accompany her to church. Pleading 
with her mother with tears, not to deny her the enjo yment of the feast of her 
heavenly groom, the mother in anger, slapped her daughter on the face . In 
return, she was inflicted by blindness for two years. Then, with a contrite soul, 
she gave her daughter some water, asked her to pray o ver it, and then washed 
her eyes with it and God healed her on the spot. When her parents passed away, 
Genevieve went to live with her God-mother in Paris, where she dedicated all 
her time praying and helping others . Yet, she was subjected to ridicule and 
scoffing, even after St. Germanus visited her once again. 
Her Severe Illness: 
Genevieve was inflicted by a severe illness that left her in a coma that lasted 
for three days, and she was on the brink of death . However, God gave her a 
night vision to comfort her, in which she saw the saints in their glory and the 
wicked in their sufferings. She saw her soul had set forth as though to Mount 
Golgotha, to see the Lord  Jesus Christ crucified . This vision became so 
engraved in her heart and gave her the support she needed in her strife.  
Once more, she was inflicted by leprosy , and she was abandoned by 
everyone, but God healed her to become a guide to the virgins in Paris. 
Knowing the Inner Thoughts of Others: 
For her great love of the salvation of her brethren, God granted her the grace 
of understanding the inner thoughts of others and what was going on in their 
minds, and she used that to exhort them to repentance . A girl who vowed 
virginity fell into the sin of adultery, on meeting with the saint, who exhorted 
her to repent. The girl perceived that the saint had complete knowledge of the 
place, date, and time of her sin, and the girl felt shame and did repent sincerely. 
Building a Church: 
Saint Genevieve once revealed to some priests her longing to build a church 
in the na me of St. Dionysius , the martyr. They explained to her that they 
couldn't do that without having the needed building materials. Yet, the next 
morning they, miraculously found all the building materials required in a forest 
nearby, which they used to build that church.

651 
 
of her happiness. She answered that she was exultant because God used her to 
save the two sisters from the captivity of the devil. 
Finally, when the governor ordered to cut her head off, she cried out, saying: 
“I thank You, O Lover and Savior of the souls for inviting me to Your Heavenly 
Paradise.” 
With the Noble Young Man Theophilus: 
On her way to execution, a lawyer by the name of ‘Theophilus’ approached 
her, and mockingly asked her: “Where are you going , ‘Dorothy’?” She 
answered him: “I am going to the Garden of my Groom .” Then, he, with a 
scoff, said to her: “I seek from you, O bride of Christ, to send me some roses 
and fruits from the Garden of your Groom .” She answered him: “I shall 
certainly do as you requested.” On reaching the arena of martyrdom, a peasant 
child approached her carrying a plate containing three fruits and three roses 
with green leaves, even though it was winter. She said to him: “Please go and 
present them on my behalf to the lawyer ‘Theophilus’ and tell him that these 
roses and fruits are from the Garden of Jesus, my Groom.” The child went his 
way, and she approached the swordsman to enjoy the crown of martyrdom 
around the year 303 AD. 
In the House of Theophilus: 
While ‘Theophilus’ was at home narrating to his friends what he had done, 
and how he had scoffed the virgin ‘Dorothy;’ behold, that chi ld came in and 
presented to him the plate of roses and fruits, saying: “This is a gift for you 
from my sister ‘Dorothy,’ she plucked from the Garden of her Groom.” Then 
the child immediately disappeared. ‘Theophilus’ was amazed and cast himself 
on the ground, thanking God for His work with him, and before all those who 
were present, he confessed that the Lord Christ was his God and the Savior of 
the whole world . Then, he shouted aloud: “Blessed are You Jesus, my God, 
Groom of ‘Dorothy;’ and blessed are all those who believe in You, and who 
die for the sake of faith in You.” 
When one of those present hastened to inform the governor what had 
happened, he did not believe until he called ‘Theophilus,’ who confessed his 
faith before him . Then, he was put under severe torture and was finally 
crowned with the crown of martyrdom. 
It was said that ‘Dorothy’s body was carried to Rome, where it was kept in 
a church carrying her name, on the banks of the River ‘Tiber.’  
It became a tradition to paint the p ortrait of the saint carrying roses and 
apples, and in the celebration of her feast, a special rite is practiced to bless the 
roses and apples. 
 [Butler: The Lives of the Saints, February 6]

This saint Theodora was a woman who dedicated her life and energy to 
serve the martyrs during the persecution stirred up by Emperor Diocletian 
(284-305 AD), And when the available cemeteries were all filled by the tombs 
of the martyrs; she had them buried in her land on Flaminian Way, about 26 
miles from Rome . In that land, she hid the martyrs Abundius , the priest, 
Abundantius, the deacon, Marcianus, and Joannes. 
The West celebrates this saint’s feast on the 17th of September. 
 [Henry Wace: A Dictionary of Christian Biography, Literature, Sects & Doctrines; 4 
Vol.; London 1877-1887] 
 
THEODORA, THE CANONESS 
This saint Theodora was a Church woman (Canoness), to whom St. Basil 
the Great wrote a magnificent letter (# 173 [302]), in which he explained the 
strength of the rules of the Evangelical life which she adopted . And, he 
apologized to her that he ceased from writing more in his letter, lest it w ould 
probably fall in somebody’s hand, and he would read it. 
[New Advent; Fathers of the Church; Letters of St. Basil of Caesarea: 173]  
 
THEODORA, THE REPENTANT, ST. 
This is the story of an innocent God -loving soul, which, due to the lack of 
discernment, might drop and fall to the bottom . It is the story of the human 
being who is eager to have everybody saved, no matter how bad his/her sins 
were, to be installed as a holy son/daughter of the Mighty God. Theodora was 
the second Magdalene who knew, by her love for God, how to trample the sin 
under her feet, to live a holy life for Him. 
The Happy Wife: 
This saint Theodora was brought up in the 5th century in the days of Emperor 
Zeno (474-491 AD) of a noble family , and she had great beauty, piety , and 
wealth. She was married to a rich and pious young man, and she lived with 
him a life of peace and joy . Amid the riches and the multitudes of banquets, 
she got acquainted with a rich young man who admired her wisdom and well-
balanced nature. Her husband noticed this admiration but was sure of the purity 
of the young man . But, with time, the devil started to plant the seeds of evil 
thoughts in him toward Theodora, which he tried hard to fight for his respect 
for her. However, with the growing temptation and at the prop er chance, he 
revealed to the lady how he felt towards her. Because she thought he was pure 
in mind, she was shocked to hearing what he said. However, with time and the

DOROTHEUS, ST. 
(The martyr) 
This St. ‘Dorotheus’ was a priest in the city of ‘Tyre’ in ‘Phoenicia’ 
(nowadays Levant). Probably, he became the bishop of that city. 
When Emperor ‘Diocletian’ (284-305 AD) stirred up persecution against 
Christians, he suffered much in his city, was exiled for a while, and then came 
back to his diocese. In that period, he attended the Nicene Ecumenical Council 
in the year 325 AD . And when Emperor Julian the Apostate ’ (360-363 AD) 
reigned and renewed persecution against Christians, he exiled again to 
‘Odyssopolis in ‘Thrace’ (nowadays the port of ‘Varna’ in Bulgaria). 
Even in his exile, he was not left alone in peace. Although he was over 115 
years o f age , he was arrested and was beaten so fiercely that he became a 
martyr at the age of 117 years in the year 362 AD. 
[Butler: The Lives of the Saints, June 5] 
 
DOROTHY, THE VIRGIN, ST. 
(The martyr) 
The Virgin Bride of Christ: 
‘Dorothy’ (Dorothea) was a virgin in ‘Caesarea of Cappadocia,’ daughter of 
an elite Roman judge by the name of ‘Tadoros’ and his wife ’s name was 
‘Theodora.’ When the persecution against Christians got intense, they fled 
from Rome to ‘Cappadocia’ and resided in the city of ‘Caesarea.’ There, God 
gifted them with their daughter ‘Dorothy,’ and they were greatly comforted. 
The blessed girl exalted in virtue, particularly in humility, meekness , and 
chastity. Besides her God-given gifts of beauty and prudence, she had a well -
developed mind and was unique in her time. Many proposed to her in marriage, 
but she declined , for her heart was so kindled with love for her Heavenly 
Groom that she vowed to keep her virginity. Out of admiration, everybody used 
to call her “The Bride of Christ.” 
With Governor ‘Sopricius’: 
The fame of ‘Dorothy’ spread fast, and when governor Sapricius (Fabricius/ 
Apricius), came to visit ‘Caesarea,’ some people informed him of her great 
beauty and prudence  and told him that she was keeping Christians from 
worshipping the gods of the emperor . ‘Sapricius’ called her to appear before 
him, and once he talked to her, he felt that she was unique. The governor asked

165 
 
God also granted the saint the grace of casting demons out  and performing 
miracles. This given powers made some je alous people accuse her of 
deception. However, St. Germanus came to her defense. 
Attempting to Burn her Alive: 
It was said that the heathen king Attila the Hun  (434-453 AD) , after 
defeating Austria, headed toward France with an army of half a million 
soldiers. When he came close to Paris , the people planned to flee away to the 
surrounding fortified cities , but St. Genevieve convinced some women that 
Attila would not touch Paris . They, in turn, convinced their husbands to stay . 
However, some people thought that she was a sorcerer, and they plotted to burn 
her alive. Again, St. Germanus sent his deputy from Italy, a pious priest, to act 
in her defense, mainly that her prophecy was realized. 
Her Courage and Love for the Others: 
Another king of the Salian Franks  by the name Childeric  I (458-481 AD), 
came and put Paris under siege. This led to such a great famine that many poor 
people died on the streets . Greatly distressed for the news, Genevieve led a 
caravan of more than ten boats loaded with wheat, across the river to bring 
food to the inhabitants suffering from hunger , and out of her great love and 
compassion on people, she twice bravely sought from king Childeric  I to 
release the war captives, and twice she got her request. 
With Selinia: 
Genevieve once encountered a girl of a noble family, by the name Selinia . 
Talking to her about the virgin life and how the virgins were like angels , the 
girl broke her betrothal with a wealthy young man to lead a life of virginity. In 
retaliation, that young man intended to kill both girls , but they fled and took 
refuge in the church, where the closed gate opened for them then closed behind 
them in a miraculous exalted way. 
Her Asceticism: 
St. Genevieve only ate on Sundays and Thursdays, only bread of barley and 
boiled beans, and drank only water. She clothed herself with sackcloth, slept 
on the bare ground without a mattress a fter spending several hours praying at 
night. Finally, she reposed in peace around the year 500 AD. 
Among the miracles that happened after her departure to heaven, which 
reflected her intense love and compassion on people, was one that took place 
in the year 1129 AD, when a plague spread in France. The people carried the 
saint's coffin and paraded along the streets of the city, and the plague stopped 
at once. The church there, still celebrates the anniversary of that miracle up till

667 
old, after leading an angelic life on earth, St. Anthony the Great met him. St. Paul addressed 
him by name, and they talked about the wonders of God and praised Him. At sunset, a raven 
flew down from a palm tree and brought a full loaf of bread to them, even though it was the 
raven’s habit to bring only half a loaf to St. Paul. On the third day, St. Paul asked St. Anthony 
to bring him St. Athanasius’ vestment, which he then gave to St. Anthony to bury him in it. 
When St. Anthony returned, he found that St. Paul had departed while bowing down in 
prayer. Then, two lions came and dug in the sand to bury St. Paul. 
St. Anthony the Great:  He was born around 251 A. D. in the city of Coma, Egypt 
(Qiman El-Arous). When he was eighteen years old, he heard the Gospel reading: “If you 
want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in 
heaven; and come, follow Me” (Matt. 19:21), and so he sold his possessions, placed his sister 
in a house of virgins, and dwelt in a small hut to learn from a saintly hermit there. After some 
time, he went into the western desert to struggle on his own in a tomb, that was carved in the 
mountain. At the age of thrity -five, he settled at the eastern bank of the Nile at Pispir ( Dayr 
al-Maymūn), where he lived as a hermit, so many came to him and became his disciples. He 
went into the inner desert at Mount Colzim to live in peace and silence. Nonetheless, his love 
compelled him to visit Alexandria to support the martyrs in 316 A. D., and to support St. 
Athanasius against Arianism in 352 A. D. Many people came to be his disciples, and he 
departed in 352 A. D. 
St. Pachomius (Father of the Koinonia):  He was born in upper Egypt around the year 
290 A. D. He became Christian in the city of Esna in Upper Egypt because of their generosity 
and their love for their enemies. He left the army and was baptized around the ye ar 290 A. 
D. He became the disciple of St. Palamon the hermit, till an angel appeared to him and guided 
him to establish the system of the monastic communal life (coenobitic monasticism). He was 
a successful leader who loved the salvation of souls, so he e stablished many monasteries in 
Upper Egypt following strict rules. He also established a convent for nuns under the 
leadership of his sister. His monastic rules were translated to Greek and Latin. St. Basil the 
Great used them, and they were used in the Gaul in the fifth century. They were also adopted 
by Benedict, the father of western monasticism, and by Caesarius of Arles. 
St. Ammonas: He was contemporary of St. Anthony. He was born in 275 A. D., and 
when he was twenty-two years old, his uncle forced him to get married, so he lived with his 
wife as ascetics in Nitria. After eighteen years, his wife asked him to live in solitude away 
from her, so he went out to Mount Nitria and many gathered around him. So, he established 
the semi-eremitic monasticism, in which the monks are not required to have daily fellowship 
in worship or in meals, except for Saturdays and Sundays only. Usually, the monks of this 
order lived in cells or caves that were close to each other, around the church. 
St. Macarius the Great: (around 300–390 A. D.) He is the founder of the semi-eremitic 
order of monasticism in the wilderness of Scetis. He visited St. Anthony at least twice. His 
father forced him to get married, but then God allowed his virgin wife to depart

396 
 
he established a monastery for men, he dedicated it under the name of St. Victor 
(Boctor) and became its spiritual father and head . He built another one for 
women in the name of St. ‘Salvator.’ The monastic movement soon spread 
there, and thousands of monks and nuns populated the monasteries.1 
Indeed, ‘Cassian’ was p receded by St. ‘Honoratus’ (350-429 AD), who 
founded a monastery on one of the ‘Lerins’ islands (off the French Riviera) in 
the year 410 AD . ‘ Honoratus’ order was chiefly borrowed from that of St. 
Pachomius2, and the monastery carried the name of St. ‘Honoratus’ up to this 
day and enjoyed an excellent celebrity status during the 5th and 6th centuries, 
and it was a nursery for illustrious bishops and remarkable ecclesiastical 
writers.  
However, through his two famous books 3, St. ‘Cassian’ was credited for 
establishing an elaborate system for the monastic life for the first time . His 
system carried the monastic ideas of the East, particularly Egypt. He provided 
the West with a monastic system they could accept, which paved the way to 
the ‘Benedictines Order.’  
St. ‘Castor,’ the bishop of ‘Apt’ (in the southeast of France) was the one 
who requested from St. ‘Cassian’ to write about the rules of the monastic life. 
Therefore, St. ‘Cassian’ wrote his book: “De Institutis Coenobiorum ” about 
the rules of the monastic fellowship mixed with absolute basics of the life of 
seclusion, and he dedicated it to St. ‘Castor.’ 
When St. ‘Cassian’ opened up the arms of love before all people of all races 
who longed for the love of Christ; he was joined by a multit ude of disciples 
from all over the world. The West no longer was envying the East. Yet, his role 
was limited when some people started to have doubts about ‘Cassian's’ 
Orthodoxy, because of the attacks made by some of the followers of St. 
‘Augustine’ on him, accusing him of having ‘Pelagian’ leanings4. 
St. ‘Benedict’ (480-547 AD), who established the highest monastic order in 
the West, and whose fame even surpasses that of ‘Cassian,’ yet was indebted 
to him; on account of that most of the laws of the ‘Benedict's’ monastic order 
were directly taken from those of ‘Cassian.’ 
Of His Writings:  
 The monasteries are an extension of the early ecclesiastical life around the 
                                                 
1 K.S. Latourettie: A History of Christianity, 1953, p. 133. 
2 Butler, Alban: The Lives of the Fathers, Martyrs and Other Principal Saints, Vol. I, D. & J. Sadlier, & 
Company, 1864. 
3 "De Institutis Coenobiorum" (Institutes of the Coenobia) & "Collationes Patrum in Scetica Eremo" 
(Conferences of the Desert Fathers). 
4 ‘Pelagianism’ is the belief that original sin did not tain t human nature and that the mortal will is still 
capable of choosing good or evil without special Divine aid.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Volume 1, p. 197
passages.text:
197 
 
The young man dwelt beside the River Nile and spent all his time praying 
in strict asceticism. Yet, when thoughts of boredom attacked him, he cried out 
to the Lord to guide him. An angel of the Lord appeared to him in the form of 
a man wearing a long robe, with leather cross-like Eskeem and a cover on his 
head. He sat weaving palm leaves for some time, got up to pray, then returned 
to work, and so on. The angel said to Anthony: “If you do so, you will never 
get bored." That  came to be the attire of the monks, and the work of hand 
happened to be one of the basics of the monastic life. 
One day, a woman and her maidservants came down to the river to wash 
their feet. Turning his head away, waiting for their departure, they start ed to 
undress to bathe. When the saint admonished her on such a behavior, she 
answered him: “If you are a monk, you should dwell in the inner wilderness, 
for this is not a place befitting for monks." On hearing these words, the saint 
said to himself, “This is the voice of the angel of the Lord rebuking me." He 
instantly forsook the location and set forth to the inner wilderness. That was 
around the year 285 AD. The saint dwelt in a cave on Mount ‘Al-Kalzam’ to 
practice the life of seclusion, North-West of the Red Sea. However, in that new 
location, the demons kept fighting against him, sometimes in the form of 
women and other times in the way of horrible wild beasts. 
His Order of Seclusion: 
In about the year 305 AD, he had to break his seclusion to meet with  some 
beginners who came to him longing to be trained under his supervision. He 
helped and guided them, then resumed his life of seclusion later on. Thus he 
was the founder of the movement of monasticism, his life revealed the concept 
of the Christian monasticism, particularly the order of seclusion: 
4- St. Anthony came out to be a monk without any intention to become a 
member of the clergy. His movement was a civic one, not a clerical one; he 
did not want to interfere with the ecclesiastical structure. Even, when 
Emperor Constantine I sent to him seeking his blessing, he delayed his 
response to the message, and when asked by his disciples why he did so, he 
said, “I am preoccupied to respond to the message of God, the King of 
kings." However, when he was pressu red, he answered the emperor’s 
message, for the sake of the Church peace. 
5- His intense love of seclusion did not close his heart toward the holy 
congregation, but, in his seclusion, he believed in being a member of the 
Church. That is why he eventually came  down to help Pope Athanasius 
the Apostolic (who was once one of his disciples). Moreover, on his 
entrance into Alexandria, the whole city was shaken, and its inhabitants 
came out exultant to welcome the man of God; that even some Arians 
came back to the Church.

307 
 
and keep it in your heart.”1  
The Silence: 
Fr. Yousef asked the elder Fr . Nistherous: “What can I do to be able to 
control my tongue?”  Then, the elder asked him in turn: “When you talk, do 
you feel comfortable?” and the answer was in the negative. So, the elder said: 
“If you do not feel comfortable, why then do you have to talk? Would you 
rather not keep quiet.?  and if you were involved in a discussion , let your 
listening be much more than your talking.” 
I shall not Seek my Needs from Anyone: 
When one of the brothers saw Fr . Nistherous wearing two overcoats, he 
asked him: “If a poor man comes to you and ask s for one, which of them will 
you give him?” The Father answered: “The second one .” The brother asked: 
“If another comes to you asking?”  He said: “I shall cut the one I still have 
into two, give him half and cover myself with the remaining half .” The 
brother still asked him: “ If a third one comes seeking what is left on you, 
what will you then do?” T he elder said: “I shall give him all I have, and go 
somewhere to dwell, where God will cover my nakedness , but I shall never 
seek my need from anyone else.” 
The Work of the Monk: 
Fr. Nistherous said: “The monk should bring himself every morning and 
evening to give an account by saying: ‘What have I don e of what God 
wanted me to do? a nd what have I done of what He did not want me to do?’ 
This is what we should keep doing all our lives , and this was the way Abba 
Arsanius has lived since he cared to stand befo re God daily without sin. You 
should pray to God, the way you would in the presence of someone else since 
God is present with you.  Do not make yourself a legislator , and do not judge 
anyone. 
The monk who vows, perjures, lies, curses, slanders , or laughs lo udly; 
would be considered out of order and acting strangely haughty because, 
whoever honors himself and elevates it above what it is worth, will perish.” 
As for the second St. Nistherous; he had gifts and miraculous powers.  
Once, he was asked by one of th e most prominent monks of h is time St. 
Poemen or St. Pastor, about his spiritual powers and how he got them . St. 
Nistherous answered: “Once I became a monk, I said to myself: ‘When a 
donkey is beaten, it will never answer back .’ That is how I kept going and 
how I lived until I reached the condition de scribed by David in his Psalm: "I

passages.text:
108 
 
not ever interfere in something that does not c oncern you; to live in comfort 
all the days of your exile." Fr. Macarius, who happened to be present, asked 
him, “What could the familiarity do? ” He answered him: “It is like a strong 
burning hot wind; wherever it reaches, it causes everything to fly away before 
it, and it corrupts the fruits of trees." Then, Fr. Macarius asked, “Does vain talk 
have the same bad influence? ” The saint answered, “There is nothing worse 
than the uncontrolled tongue, and it is the father of all evil desires."  
Some brethren heard about the saint ’s gift of discernment and intended to 
put it to test to see if he would be ever provoked to anger. So, they asked him: 
“Are you Agathon, the one whom we hear that he is haughty? ” The saint 
answered: “Yes, that is me." Then they asked him : “Are you Agathon the 
scoundrel and deceptive?” He replied: “Yes, that is me." But, when they asked 
him: “Are you Agathon the heretic? ” He answered: “Far from it, I am not a 
heretic!” When asked why he endured all the other insults except for being a 
heretic, he answered: “I see all the other charges in myself; and accepting them 
would benefit me; but to be charged with being a heretic, it implies being 
separated from God, which I deny." Hearing that, they were amazed by his 
great wisdom and grace. 
At the beginning of his monastic life, he used for three years, to put a small 
stone inside his mouth to train himself in silence. But what was more important 
than just being silent with the tongue was being silent within his heart. He 
never allowed himself to condemn anyone; but could educate himself as well 
as others, by both his silence and his words. 
He remained caring for his salvation until his last breath. While on his 
deathbed, when he was asked by the brethren, what did he was seeing, He said 
that he was seeing the judgment of God. And when pressing him to elaborate, 
he said: “Do me a favor, and stop talking now, for I am busy." Then, he reposed 
with joy while they saw him departing as though he was biding his beloved 
friends' farewell. 
Of His Words: 
 The recognition of God’s will: So should be the concept of the saints; for 
man has been created in the image and likeness of God, he should recognize 
the will of God; listen to the truth and submit to it.  
 The effectiveness of prayer: Asked by the brethren conc erning the fight 
against adultery, he said, “Cast your weakness before God, to find comfort.” 
 The narrow road:  Whoever finds and walk along the way of the saints, 
would be pleased by the sorrows, for the way to salvation is full of sorrows. 
 The humility and self-love: Humility is the crown of the monk. You cannot 
live a life acceptable to God, as long as you are in love with yourself. 
 Love of possessions: If you long for the King of Heaven, forsake the riches

passages.text:
169 
 
Abba Anthony his Role Model: 
St. Sisoes was acting as if Abba Anthony the Great was watching him and 
listening to his instructions to his disciples. He strove to imitate that great 
teacher in all his life: in his asceticism, in his spiritual practices, in his 
commitment to silence and his longing for prayers. Therefore, his fame spread, 
and so many people came to him requesting to be his disciples. At this point, 
he had to forsake his love for silence and seclusion, to fulfill a higher goal, 
namely loving care of his disciples. Abba Sisoes’s brother came to visit him in 
the cave of Abba Anthony, where he was staying. The saint amiably said to his 
brother: “In this cave, a lion used to live; now it is inhabited by a fox.” 
St. Sisoes always was complaining that he did not reach the statue of St. 
Anthony. Once, a monk asked him: “Father! Have you not reached the level of 
St. Anthony?” He answered: “If I had only one of the virtues of that monk, I 
would have become a torch of Divine Love.” 
The Repentant of the Wilderness: 
St. Sisoes was such a helper to his disciples, even  in their weaknesses and 
sins. With his love and perseverance, he used to guide them to repentance. The 
contrite heart was his steady virtue that always highlighted his guidance and 
teachings to his disciples. To a recluse saying to him one day, “Father, I always 
place myself in the presence of God.”; he replied: “It would be much more to 
your advantage if you place yourself below every creature, to be securely 
humble.” Therefore, having been all the time watching for the Divine Presence, 
he always felt his weakness and lowliness. He was called The Repentant of the 
Wilderness, because what happened with him in the moments of his repose, in 
the presence of St. Ammon, the disciple of Abba Bamu: When St. Sisoes lay 
upon his deathbed, his disciples surrounding t he older saint saw that his face 
shone like the sun. They asked him what he saw. Abba Sisoes replied that he 
saw St. Anthony, the prophets, and the apostles. His face increased in 
brightness, and he spoke with someone. The monks asked: “With whom are 
you speaking, Father?” He said: “The angels had come down for my soul and 
I was entreating them to give me a little more time for repentance.” The monks 
said, “You do not need repentance, Father.” St. Sisoes said with great humility: 
“I do not think that I have  even begun to repent. ” After saying that, his 
countenance shone so brightly; and was heard saying: “ The Lord says: Bring 
to Me the Repentant of the Wilderness .” Then, he delivered his soul, and a 
sweet fragrance filled the whole place. 
His Love for Serenity and Seclusion: 
After the end of the Liturgy, he used to run like an arrow back to his cell.

172 
 
set, some people came knocking on the door. The saint asked his disciple: 
“Offer them something to eat.” Here, the bishop said to the disciple: “Let them 
wait for a while, lest they would think that Sisoes eats so early.” The saint 
looked at him. Then he instructed his disciple to go ahead and offer the new 
guests food. When the guests saw the food, they asked the disciple: “Do you 
have guests?” When he sa id: “Yes.” They sorrowfully said: “Why did you 
make the elder eat so early? Do you not realize how he would torture himself 
many days because of this one meal?” On hearing this, the bishop made a 
metanoia before the older saint and said to him: “Forgive me , Father, for I 
thought humanly, while you followed the commandment of the Lord.” 
His Repose: 
On his deathbed, St. Sisoes was heard crying out loud: “Behold! St. 
Anthony and a cloud of prophets and angels have come to take my soul away.” 
Then his countenance shone, sat a little while quietly, and then cried out again: 
“Now, the Lord Himself comes to me.” So, he delivered his soul around the 
year 429 AD, after living as a recluse for 62 years on Mount Anthony. 
Of his Sayings; 
* For 30 years, I have not asked  the Lord to forgive my sin, but instead, 
I say in my prayers: O my Lord Jesus Christ, cover me up because until now I 
sin with my tongue. 
* To answer a question: “Is it of benefit for the monk to escape?” He put 
his finger on his mouth and replied: “If you protect yourself from this, my son, 
this is the true escape.” 
* To answer another question: “What is sojourning?” He replied: 
“Sojourning is keeping silent. Wherever you may be, ask yourself: What have 
I to do with this matter?” 
* To a brother who sought  from him: “Tell me a word of benefit.” He 
said: “Why do you seek words? Do like what you see.” 
* “Be reproached; Cast your will behind you. You will be without worry, 
and you will find comfort.” 
* To a brother who sought from him: “Tell me a word of wisdo m.” He 
answered: “What should I say other than Go read in the Old Testament, then 
go to the New Testament.” 
* To a question from brother Joseph: “How long does it take for a man to 
put an end for lust.” He answered: “ Whenever a lust moves within you, cut i t 
off instantaneously.” 
* To a question by a brother: “If I am sitting in the desert and a barbarian 
comes to kill me and if I am stronger than he, shall I kill him?” The old man 
said to him, “ No, leave him to God. Whatever the trial is which comes to a

290 
 
purity and chastity. Right afterward, that evil man was inflicted with blindness; 
and he confessed to his son about what happened . He sought from him to 
deliver him to the authorities to get his punishment, somehow realizing that it 
was better for him to be chastised here than to lose his eternity. 
When Abba Danie’, the hegomen of Scetis, heard about that, he attended 
her funeral and considered her as a martyr. He sought to have her body buried 
in a monastery ne ar Alexandria (the 18 -miles monastery). Some of the 
monastery’s monks protested about the burial of a murdered woman’s body 
among the bodies of the hermit Fathers. But, Abba Daniel was able to convince 
them to honor such a pure young woman by having her bo dy buried in the 
tomb of the Fathers. 
 [Deacon Yousif Habib: Abba Daniel, p. 63] 
 
THOMAS OF AQUINAS 
This Thomas of Aquinas is the Doctor of the Catholic Theology. He lived 
in the 13 th century (1225-1274 AD). He was born in Roccasecca in Aquino, 
Italy. He was the youngest son of Count Lundulf of Aquino, with a connection 
to the emperor of France . When he reached five years of age, he joined a 
Benedectine school in Monte Cassino, where his father introduced him  to the 
head of the monastery. In the year 1240 AD, he went to the University of 
Naples to study a course in Arts . There, he was drawn to the new, study -
oriented Dominican Order. However, he was strongly opposed by his family , 
and he was kidnapped and conf ined in the city of Roccasecca for 15 months. 
But his firm will prevail. In April 1244, he re -joined the Dominican Order, 
lived in Paris during the period 1245 -1248, where he was influenced by Fr.  
Albertus Magnus. In the year 1256 AD, he became a professor  of theology. 
And in the year 1272, he went to  Naples where he established a Dominican 
school; and strove to show his famed theological work: ‘Summa Theologica.’ 
 
THOMAS, THE HERMIT, ST. 
St. Thomas, the hermit, was born in Shanshif in the province of Akhmim to 
two pious parents who raised him by the ethics of the church . His heart was 
inflamed by the love of God, and because of his longing to a life of meditation, 
he set forth to a neighboring mountain to practice his spiritual activity. He 
loved prayer and praise, and he had a beautiful voice. He was quite serious in 
his asceticism, to eat only once a week, to memorize the Holy Bible by heart, 
to keep all its commandments, and practice its Gospels with joy. As the sweet 
fragrance of Christ spread through him, some brethren living in the mountain

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Volume 2, p. 300
passages.text:
300 
 
the 16 years of his papacy (401-417), St. Innocent I, showed a lot of activity in 
his work, even though we do not know much about his personal life. 
This saint was in Rome when the Gothic army led by Alaric I (395-410 AD) 
put it under siege in the  years 408-410 AD. He saw how his people perished 
from hunger and how the corpses were scattered along the streets , causing a 
spread of the plague. The Senators attempted to make an acceptable deal to 
remove the siege, but Alaric I kept despising their delegates.  
On the 24th of August 410 AD, Rome fell to the Goths. The saint at the time 
was in Raphina to try to convince Emperor Honorius (W: 395 -423) to send 
help to his city and to try to buy peace with the invaders with money. But once 
Rome fell, it was utterly destroyed within six days, and the invaders left it in 
ruins. Afterward, Alaric I and his men set out toward the South to invade the 
prosperous strongholds. The saint returned to his city to mourn it with 
bitterness. During his days, the northwest of Africa entered into a controversy 
with the followers of Pelagius, who intended to confirm the human freedom 
exaggeratedly, disregarding and denying the Divine grace and the original sin. 
St. Augustine led the opposition reaction, and strongly confirmed the work of 
Divine grace, to the extent of disregarding human freedom . The bishops of 
north-west Africa wrote to the pope to call Pelagius  in and excommunicate 
him. St. Innocent I reposed on the 12th of March 417. 
 
INNOCENT, THE MONK 
St. Palladius (363 -425 AD) tells us about a priest -monk in the Mount of 
Olives by the name of Innocent, with whom he lived for three years, which 
was characterized by extreme simplicity, to do things that might seem to other 
people as quite odd. When he was young, Innocent worke d at the royal court 
in the days of Emperor Constantius II (337-361 AD), and he got married and 
had a son called Paul, who also worked in the royal court. That son eventually 
had diverted to evil and raped the daughter of a priest . Upon hearing about it, 
his father, Innocent, got so embittered in the soul, to ask God, saying, “Lord, 
give him such a spirit, that his flesh may no longer find an opportunity to sin,” 
and so, God did. That son ended up on the Mount of Olives, wearing irons and 
chastised by the spirit.  
Innocent saw a mother weeping on her son , who was paraly zed and 
possessed by an evil spirit. He took the young man to the small church which 
he built by himself and kept in it a relic of St. John the Baptist. He kept praying 
from the third to the ninth hour, then took the boy back to his mother healed of 
paralysis and free of the evil spirit.  
It was also said that he once saw a poor older woman weeping because her

passages.text:
385 
 
PAUL, THE MONK 
One of the desert fathers told this story about a monk by the name of Paul  
(Boulus) from somewhere in Lower Egypt and he lived in Thebes:  
He used to hold a serpent by his bare hands and split it into two . Some of 
the brethren made metanoia before him, and said: “Tell us brother; what did 
you do that made you qualified for such a marvelous grace ?” He answered 
them: “Forgive me, fathers. Once the man acquires purity, everything would 
submit to him and obey him. Like the way , Adam was in Paradise before he 
disobeyed the Divine commandment.” 
 [Light Publications: Sayings of the Elder Fathers, 1983, p. 258 (Arabic)] 
 [Bendicta Ward: The Sayings of the Desert Fathers] 
 
PAUL, THE SIMPLE, ST. 
This saint was a marvelous example of a simple man, who by the grace of 
God, could strive to reach a high ascetic level, even though he started it at his 
60th years of age. This St. Paul (Boulus) was a very simple and pious farmer 
who got married to a very beautiful girl . After living together for so many 
years, he started to take notice o f so many rumors about his wife' s evil 
behavior. However, whenever he inquired fr om her about the matter, she 
would pretend to be a pure woman . Eventually, by himself, he saw her in the 
evil act . On that day, he forsook the house to her and set forth to Abba 
Anthony the Great, hoping to become one of his disciples. 
Getting to know that this simple farmer was sixty years old, Abba Anthony 
advised him to go back to his field and plow; on account of that it would be 
difficult for him to practice the monastic life at his age . Before his 
persistence, he sought from him to join a monastery in  the valley to practice 
with the brethren what suit his old age; but the old man persisted on not 
leaving that mountain. 
Here, Abba Anthony had no other choice but to put him under tough tests; 
and was amazed by his endurance, perseverance , and obedience . Among 
those tests that he left him four days without food or drink while watching 
him lest he would collapse. He s ought from him to  remain a whole week 
outside his cave, under the heat of noon and the severe cold nights, without 
leaving his place; and sought from him, after weaving eight meters of a cord, 
to loosen it and weave it anew . In all that he was obedient, worked with joy 
and extreme simplicity. 
On seeing his persistence with the spirit of piety, Abba Anthony accepted 
him as a recluse and sought from him to build for himself a cell on the way 
between the base of the mountain and his own cell.

PIUS I, POPE OF ROME 
Saint Pius I (140 -155 AD) succeeded St. Hyginus (136 -140 AD) on the 
See of Rome. He was formerly a citizen of Aquileia in Italy and said to be the 
brother of Hermas author of the book The Shepherd in the 2nd century AD.  
He was ordained as a bishop around the year 140 AD. He cared to oppose 
the heresies faced by the Roman Church in his time, by the followers of 
Valentinus and Marcion. The first Valentinus, originally from Egypt, and he 
dwelt in Rome between the years 136 and 165 AD, hoping to be ordained as 
a bishop. His book carried a lot of Gnostic thoughts. While the second 
Marcion, was considered one of the most influential Gnostics personalities.  
Pope Pius I cared so much to commit the priests to practice the Holy 
Sacraments with great caution and elaboration. So, he issued a creed that 
says: “A priest who spills the chalice after the sanctification, has to remain in 
a condition of repentance for 40 days, and if he spills a drop of it, he has to 
remain in a condition of repentance for three days; along with wiping the 
place of a spill with towels  and burning them.” He also cared to incr ease the 
number of ministers serving the Kingdom of God, so he ordained 12 bishops 
and 18 priests. He was said to be martyred on the 11 th of June in the year 155 
AD, even though some scholars in the West, believe that he reposed without 
having his bloodshed. 
 [Butler’s: Lives of Saints; July 11] 
 
PERGENTINUS (The martyr) 
This saint was one of those who enjoyed the crown of martyrdom in the 
days of Emperor Decius (249 -251 AD) in the city of Arezzo in the region of 
Umbria. St. Pergentinus and his brother Laur entinus were of a noble family; 
they were arrested while still young students, brought before the governor 
Tibertius and charged of being Christians. He set them free, probably for the 
sake of their noble origin or for their young age; counting the mild 
chastisement was enough to make them stop practicing their worship and to 
live in fear and terror. However, once they found themselves free, they set 
forth to practice their Christian worship publicly, and with greater zeal, they 
even began to preach among t he pagans. God granted them the grace to 
perform miracles, that drew many people to the Christian faith. The governor 
put them again under arrest, then gave the order to cut their heads off, to

passages.text:
465 
 
prayers, and to be healed by the miracles granted to him by God. 
In Faran: 
It was also said that by Divine order, he set forth to the wilderness of 
Faran (in Saudi Arabia), where he remained for five years bringing the lost 
souls back to the fold of  faith. Then, St. Pijimi returned to a cave near his 
birth-town of Feesha. That cave became a center for preaching the Gospel 
and to guide the deviants, as well as a place to comfort the  tough and the 
sick. 
An Encounter with Abba Shenouda: 
It was also said  that Abba Shenouda the Archimandrite, in a night vision 
saw that he was carried to heavens and was shown the place prepared for St. 
Pijimi. He was quite impressed and decided to go to Feesha to get his 
blessing. There, after he rested and had some food , both saints praised God, 
prayed, and were comforted by the word of God. 
His Repose: 
When St. Pijimi was told about the day of his repose , he informed his 
disciple, and on the 1st day of Kiahk, he was inflicted by intense fever. On the 
11th of Kiahk, he saw a group of saints coming for him, along with angels, to 
carry his soul to its place of comfort. 
 [A monk in the Syrian Monastery (Virgin Mary’s Monastery): 
 The Biography of the Great Saint Abba Pijimi, the Hermit] 
 
PIOR, ABBA 
Abba Pior (Pihur; in Coptic) his name means (Of the god Horus) and he is 
a different saint from Abba Or the abbot.  He loved the monastic life at a 
young age, and he set forth to St. Anthony the Great in the year 325 AD and 
became one of his disciples for a few years. When he r eached his 25 years of 
age, he longed for a life of seclusion , so he asked the permission of St. 
Anthony and set forth to the region of Nitria around the year 330 AD.  There, 
he dwelt in an isolated cell between Nitria and Scetis. However, he kept 
coming back to Scetis for the rest of his life.  Abba Pior dug a well and kept 
drinking its bitter water for 30 years until he reposed. His visitors used to 
bring their own water with them to drink. It was said that God made the bitter 
water sweet in his mo uth. He kept growing in his asceticism until he got to 
eat only dry bread with five olives a day and persisted on not seeing any of 
his relatives.

[Baring-Gould: September 22] 
[Butler: July 3] 
 
PIAMON, THE VIRGIN, ST. 
St. Piamon lived with her mother in one of the villages in Upper Egypt. 
She lived with a holy monastic spirit, spending her life in spiritual watching, 
eating once every day at sunset , and earning her living weaving linen. That 
blessed virgin was worthy of enjoying the gift of knowing what was going to 
happen before it would happen. 
So, one time there was a controversy between her village and a 
neighboring one because of the  irrigation of their land  from the Nile’s water. 
As a result of the quarrels, some of the inhabitants of both villages were 
killed. So, the inhabitants of the other village who were known for their 
violence, planned on a sudden attack on their opponents. Th e Lord revealed 
that planning  to that virgi n Piamon. She hastened to tell the matter to the 
elders of her village , who had a great fear of confronting them, so they 
planned to ask for reconciliation. So, they sought from her if she wished to 
save her village and her household to go to meet with them by herself! 
Not wishing to go to them, she instead ascended to the roof of her house 
and spent the night in unceasing prayers and metanoias, crying out to God, 
saying: “O Lord, the Judge of the whole earth; Who has no pleasure in 
oppression; I implore You O Lord when the prayers and supplications of your 
maidservant reach You, let Your power stop the enemy at the spot where they 
are now.”  Then, three miles from her village, those violent people felt a 
superior power that froze them , and they could not mov e forwards anymore. 
They were told later that it was because of the prayers of that saint. They 
instantly sent to the other village to seek reconciliation, with a message in 
which they told them: “Give thanks to God; for the prayers of Piamon which 
kept us from coming against you.” 
 [W. Budge: The Paradise of the Holy Fathers, Vol. I, pp. 152-3] 
 
PIERIUS, ST. 
Father Pierius has been the dean of the School of Alexandria in the 2nd half 
of the 3 rd century, in the days of Pope Theonas (282 -301 AD). He was a 
cultured priest, a prominent interpreter of the Word of God and a great 
preacher. The historian Eusebius (260 -340 AD) said about him: “He was 
known for his intense poverty, along with his richnes s in the philosophical 
knowledge, his depth in spiritual contemplations, his strife in the 
interpretation of the spirituals and his eloquence in the public debates in

The two guards were cast again in prison, where Lucina served them. 
Pompinius replaced his father Paulinus as the jail officer, and he declared that 
those two guards were magicians. Then, he ordered that they get executed by 
the sword. In this way, they received the crowns of martyrdom. 
  [Baring-Gould: Lives of the Saints, July 2]  
 
PTOLEMAEUS (The martyr) 
During the long Church history, many people have carried the same name 
of Ptolemaeus; among them: 
• Ptolemaeus, the disciple of Valentinus in the 2 nd century AD, which was 
mentioned by St. Irenaeus. 
• Ptolemaeus, the martyr: celebrated in the West on the 19 th of October. He 
was martyred in Rome around the year 161 AD. His contemporary St. 
Justin, the martyr, has testified to him. 
It was said that a married woman was living in a sinful life, and then 
became aware of the Christian faith through this St. Ptolemaeus. After she 
repented, she started to lead a pious life.  Having tasted the sweetness of the 
fellowship with God and enjoyed the holy life, her heart was so inflamed by 
zeal, that she kept asking her husband to receive the faith also. However, he 
kept insulting her and badly treating her that she had to leave him. So, the 
husband told the governor that his estrange d wife was a Christian, and 
accordingly, she was arrested. In the court of justice, her mentor St. 
Ptolemaeus stood before t he governor Urbicius to defend her, and on 
proclaiming his faith, he was condemned to death himself. 
A Christian man by the name of Lucius, who was there during the trial, 
protested before the governor that Ptolemaeus was condemned for no crime 
he committed, which would be contrary to the wisdom of the emperor and 
the council of the elites.  This man also fell under the same verdict. Then, the 
same situation was repeated with a third man, although his name was not 
mentioned. 
 [Justine Mart: Apology 2:2; Eusebius: Hist. Eccl., vol. IV, 17:2-13]  
 
• Ptolemaeus, the soldier: (20 December) was mentioned by St. Dionysius, 
the 14th pope of Alexandria (247 -264 AD) in a letter he sent Fabian the 
bishop of Antioch. The pope narrated what happened in Alexandria during 
the persecution in the era of emperor Decius (249 -251 AD). Among those

Jerome's response. 
Once more, when a controversy between St. Jerome and Rophinus erupted 
about Origen's teaching, although they were good friends since their 
childhood, St. Pammachius declared his denunciation of their fierceness in 
the argument. 
When his wife Paulina passed away in the year 397 AD, both St . Jerome 
and St . Paulinus, the bishop of Nola, wrote him letters of condolence and 
advised him to funnel all his abilities to wards deeds of love . St. Paulinus  
wrote to him, saying: “Your wife now is a deposit for you, and an intercessor 
for your sake before the Lord  Jesus Christ. She would be receiving through 
you a lot of blessings in Heaven when you distribu te her treasures over here 
on earth. Don't remember her by vain tears, but by participating in the deeds 
of mercy. She would be honored by your virtues and fed by the food you 
offer to the poor.” St. Jerome also wrote him another letter inviting him to a 
life of dedication. 
St. Pammachius did distribute much of his wealth on the poor, to practice 
a monastic life; that St . Jerome wrote to him saying: “Although Paulina has 
fallen asleep, the church has gained the monk Pammachius.  According to his 
birth and marriage, he is a nobleman. He is generous in his giving and loft in 
his humility” [Letter # 66 ]. He also said in the same letter, that what 
Pammachius has gained now was the fruit of Paulina; for what she longed to 
see him as while she was alive, has been r ealized by her death . By doing so, 
Pamachius proved to be the wisest of the wise, the greatest and the noblest 
among them, and the most prominent monk. 
Also, St . Pammachius established with Fabiola an inn (hospital) in the 
area of Portus, to be a refuge fo r the strangers who were coming to Rome, in 
particular the sick and the poor among them . In his love for the unity of the 
church, St . Pammachius opposed the Donatic dissension 1 with a spirit of 
humility. He sought from them  to return to the bosom of the c hurch. For his 
good ecclesiastical work, St . Augustine, the bishop of Hippo, wrote St . 
Pammachius to thank him in the year 401 AD. 
St. Pammachius turned his house in Coelian Hill into a church , and 
according to some, the church of SS. Giovany and Paulo (John and Paul) was 
built on its location later on. 
St. Pammachius reposed in the year 410 AD, during the attack of the 
Gosians and the Alaric on Rome . He is celebrated by the w est on the 30 th of 
August. It was said that he was ordained as a priest, but th at was doubted by 
 
1 The ‘Donatists’ were a rebellious congregation in North West Africa, and found some sympathizers in 
Italy, that accused the other believers with infidelity.

St. Pacian had a famous expression: “My name is Christian and my title is  
Universal (Catholic) .” He departed on the 9th of March in the year 390 AD. 
      [Butler's Lives of Saints, Mar. 9] 
 
PAESA, ST. 
Lady St. Paesa was born in the city of Menouf to wealthy parents during 
the 4th century AD, and she was raised in a holy life. Since her childhood, she 
loved the worship of God and serving the poor . When her parents departed, 
she longed to join a house of virgins . She started distributing her wealth on 
the needy, and she gave hospitality to strangers in her ho me. However, the 
devil did not leave her alone but provoked some wicked people to lure her 
heart gradually to evil, until she completely got transformed and gave herself 
up to sin; and turned her house to a brothel. 
On hearing about what happened to her, the fathers of the Scetis were very 
sad, so  they spent some time in prayers and fasting for her, and then they 
sought from St . John the Short to go and talk to her . St. John the Short 
yielded to their reques t. When the time came for her to receive him; he 
entered into her house while singing the psalm: "Though I walk through the 
valley of the shad ow of death, I will fear no evil;  for You are with me” (Ps. 
23:4). When he sat down, he looked at her and said, "Why did you belittle the 
Lord Jesus Christ, and follow this evil way?" She trembled and her heart was 
melting from the words of the saint who bent his head and started weeping . 
Inquiring from him why he was cr ying, he told her that he could see demons 
playing on her face. She asked him if there would be possible repentance for 
her. The saint opened before her the door of hope, providing that she would 
abandon that unclean place and go with him to the wilderness . When it was 
evening, he told her to lie down far away from him . Then, when he got up at 
midnight for his prayer, he saw a pillar of light coming down from Heaven 
and angels carrying her soul . Approaching, he found out that she already 
passed away. He prostrated himself to the ground thanking God for His work 
with her, to hear a voice, saying that her repentance was received at the 
moment she uttered it, for she did it from the depth of her heart. 
He buried her body and set forth to the wilderness to tell the fathers about 
what happened, for which they glorified God . The church celebrates her

counted the priests in Rome slothful and easygoing; and violently attacked the bishop of Rome... He 
drew some bishops to his side, but the 14th  pope of Alexandria St. ‘Dionysius’ (247 -264 AD) 
condemned him on this dissension... He counted his group as the Holy Catholic Church, and he 
considered everybody else as infide.

asked the Lord to hold the sun until he would reach them; which the Lord

“Don't you remember the Lord's words; If you have faith as a mustard seed,
