Book 1: Introduction to the Coptic Catechism 
15 
faithful, leading to many being killed. Rather, it will suffice to present an extremely concise 
rectification of the accusations levelled against St. Dioscorus.18 
St. Dioscorus and Eutyches : Eutyches was an archimandrite and the abbot of a 
monastery in Constantinople with about three hundred monks under his guidance. He was an 
old ascetic, gifted with eloquence of speech; but he was not a true theologian. He played a 
significant role in the split that occurred in the Church in the fifth century.  Eutyches enjoyed 
great fame throughout the see of Constantinople: within monastic circles, the imperial court, 
and among the people. This was due to his intelligence, eloquence, his ascetic life, and his 
close relationship with the emperor, especially through his relative Chrysaphius, the chief 
minister. 
In reality, Eutyches represented neither Alexand rian theology nor Antiochian 
theology. His extreme zeal against the Nestorianism that was rife in this region, and his 
defense of the Alexandrian formula led him to another heresy: he fell into the error of saying 
that there were two natures before the uni on; but only one nature after it, for  the divine 
nature absorbed the human nature, and the latter ceased to be.  
It is not difficult for any scholar to discover the character of Eutyches  and his theology 
by simply reading his responses during his trials at the  councils of Ephesus in 448 and 449 
A. D. He was not by nature a theologian and he was largely ignorant of th e system of 
Alexandrian theology. He would sometimes use  orthodox expressions that contradict his 
main ideas. Perhaps this was because his theological understanding was shaky, or perhaps he 
intended to deceive, or perhaps he feared losing his fame, position, or priesthood.  
Eutyches’ appeal to the emperor and bishops:  Leo, the bishop of Rome wrote to 
Eutyches, lauding his zeal in defending against Nestorian dualism. At the same time, he wrote 
to Flavian, urging him to be kind to Eutyches. But Leo later changed his mind, perhaps when 
he heard that the emperor had written to St. Dioscorus, the pope of Alexandria, inviting him 
to convene a council to discuss this matter. Leo, who had no real knowledge of the nature of 
the conflict between Alexandrian and Antioc hian Christology, sent his tome (letter) to 
Constantinople on June 13, 449 A. D.; not to reconcile the parties, but to undermine the 
position of the Alexandrian theologians. 
The Second Council of Ephesus in 449 A. D.: Emperor Theodosius II, who convened

‘Anthony,' among whom are: 
ANTHONY, THE SYRIAN The martyr: 
He was a 20 years old Syrian, a stone builder who was known for his great 
zeal against the idol worshipping. He lived as an anchorite for two years; then 
he returned to his hometown. There, he found the people worshipping the false 
gods. So, he went into their temple and broke all the idols down. He was 
expelled from the city, and he went to ‘Apamaea'. And, when its bishop 
assigned him to build a Ch urch, the pagans were stirred up against him and 
killed him. 
ANTONIUS AL-BEBAWY: The martyr: 
St. ‘Anthony’ (Andona) was born in ‘Beba’ in Upper Egypt by pious and 
merciful parents. Hearing about the sufferings of the martyrs, he set forth to 
‘Arianus,' the governor of ‘Ansena.’ and confessed the Lord Christ before him. 
The governor ordered his men to throw spears at him, but he was not harmed. 
Then, for the fear of that the audience would be encouraged to believe in his 
Christ, he ordered him chained and se nt him to ‘Armanius,’ the governor of 
Alexandria. He sent with him ‘Abimachus’ and two other saints. ‘Armanius’ 
put the three in prison, crucified ‘Anthony’ upside down and tortured him, but 
God was glorified in him. Then, he was sent to the governor of ‘Al-Farma,' 
where he met with ‘St. Mina’ in the prison and both rejoiced by seeing each 
other. The governor of ‘Al-Farma’ ordered combing ‘Anthony’s body with 
sharp iron-teeth combs, and then he cut his head off by the sword. The saint 
received the crown of martyrdom. 
 
ANTHONY, FATHER OF THE MONKS, ST. 
He is considered worldwide as ‘The Father of the Monastic Family ’ and 
‘The Founder of the Monastic Movement ’ in the whole world, even though 
there have been some monastic movements prior to his. 
The saint was born in the village of ‘Komn Al-Aros’ – Beni-Sweif around 
the year 251 AD, to wealthy parents. When his father died, he stood before his 
corpse, contemplated in the mortality of the world, and his heart kindled 
toward eternity. In the year 269 AD, entering into the church, he heard the 
gospel saying: “If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to 
the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow Me ” (Matt. 
19:21). Anthony considered it a personal message for him, and it touched  his 
life. Moreover, when he returned home to his young sister ‘Dios,' he 
proclaimed to her his decision to sell his portion of the inheritance and give its 
proceeds to the poor, to dedicate his life to worship God. On her part, his sister 
also insisted on joining a convent in Alexandria.

Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God 
667 
old, after leading an angelic life on earth, St. Anthony the Great met him. St. Paul addressed 
him by name, and they talked about the wonders of God and praised Him. At sunset, a raven 
flew down from a palm tree and brought a full loaf of bread to them, even though it was the 
raven’s habit to bring only half a loaf to St. Paul. On the third day, St. Paul asked St. Anthony 
to bring him St. Athanasius’ vestment, which he then gave to St. Anthony to bury him in it. 
When St. Anthony returned, he found that St. Paul had departed while bowing down in 
prayer. Then, two lions came and dug in the sand to bury St. Paul. 
St. Anthony the Great:  He was born around 251 A. D. in the city of Coma, Egypt 
(Qiman El-Arous). When he was eighteen years old, he heard the Gospel reading: “If you 
want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in 
heaven; and come, follow Me” (Matt. 19:21), and so he sold his possessions, placed his sister 
in a house of virgins, and dwelt in a small hut to learn from a saintly hermit there. After some 
time, he went into the western desert to struggle on his own in a tomb, that was carved in the 
mountain. At the age of thrity -five, he settled at the eastern bank of the Nile at Pispir ( Dayr 
al-Maymūn), where he lived as a hermit, so many came to him and became his disciples. He 
went into the inner desert at Mount Colzim to live in peace and silence. Nonetheless, his love 
compelled him to visit Alexandria to support the martyrs in 316 A. D., and to support St. 
Athanasius against Arianism in 352 A. D. Many people came to be his disciples, and he 
departed in 352 A. D. 
St. Pachomius (Father of the Koinonia):  He was born in upper Egypt around the year 
290 A. D. He became Christian in the city of Esna in Upper Egypt because of their generosity 
and their love for their enemies. He left the army and was baptized around the ye ar 290 A. 
D. He became the disciple of St. Palamon the hermit, till an angel appeared to him and guided 
him to establish the system of the monastic communal life (coenobitic monasticism). He was 
a successful leader who loved the salvation of souls, so he e stablished many monasteries in 
Upper Egypt following strict rules. He also established a convent for nuns under the 
leadership of his sister. His monastic rules were translated to Greek and Latin. St. Basil the 
Great used them, and they were used in the Gaul in the fifth century. They were also adopted 
by Benedict, the father of western monasticism, and by Caesarius of Arles. 
St. Ammonas: He was contemporary of St. Anthony. He was born in 275 A. D., and 
when he was twenty-two years old, his uncle forced him to get married, so he lived with his 
wife as ascetics in Nitria. After eighteen years, his wife asked him to live in solitude away 
from her, so he went out to Mount Nitria and many gathered around him. So, he established 
the semi-eremitic monasticism, in which the monks are not required to have daily fellowship 
in worship or in meals, except for Saturdays and Sundays only. Usually, the monks of this 
order lived in cells or caves that were close to each other, around the church. 
St. Macarius the Great: (around 300–390 A. D.) He is the founder of the semi-eremitic 
order of monasticism in the wilderness of Scetis. He visited St. Anthony at least twice. His 
father forced him to get married, but then God allowed his virgin wife to depart

197 
 
The young man dwelt beside the River Nile and spent all his time praying 
in strict asceticism. Yet, when thoughts of boredom attacked him, he cried out 
to the Lord to guide him. An angel of the Lord appeared to him in the form of 
a man wearing a long robe, with leather cross-like Eskeem and a cover on his 
head. He sat weaving palm leaves for some time, got up to pray, then returned 
to work, and so on. The angel said to Anthony: “If you do so, you will never 
get bored." That  came to be the attire of the monks, and the work of hand 
happened to be one of the basics of the monastic life. 
One day, a woman and her maidservants came down to the river to wash 
their feet. Turning his head away, waiting for their departure, they start ed to 
undress to bathe. When the saint admonished her on such a behavior, she 
answered him: “If you are a monk, you should dwell in the inner wilderness, 
for this is not a place befitting for monks." On hearing these words, the saint 
said to himself, “This is the voice of the angel of the Lord rebuking me." He 
instantly forsook the location and set forth to the inner wilderness. That was 
around the year 285 AD. The saint dwelt in a cave on Mount ‘Al-Kalzam’ to 
practice the life of seclusion, North-West of the Red Sea. However, in that new 
location, the demons kept fighting against him, sometimes in the form of 
women and other times in the way of horrible wild beasts. 
His Order of Seclusion: 
In about the year 305 AD, he had to break his seclusion to meet with  some 
beginners who came to him longing to be trained under his supervision. He 
helped and guided them, then resumed his life of seclusion later on. Thus he 
was the founder of the movement of monasticism, his life revealed the concept 
of the Christian monasticism, particularly the order of seclusion: 
4- St. Anthony came out to be a monk without any intention to become a 
member of the clergy. His movement was a civic one, not a clerical one; he 
did not want to interfere with the ecclesiastical structure. Even, when 
Emperor Constantine I sent to him seeking his blessing, he delayed his 
response to the message, and when asked by his disciples why he did so, he 
said, “I am preoccupied to respond to the message of God, the King of 
kings." However, when he was pressu red, he answered the emperor’s 
message, for the sake of the Church peace. 
5- His intense love of seclusion did not close his heart toward the holy 
congregation, but, in his seclusion, he believed in being a member of the 
Church. That is why he eventually came  down to help Pope Athanasius 
the Apostolic (who was once one of his disciples). Moreover, on his 
entrance into Alexandria, the whole city was shaken, and its inhabitants 
came out exultant to welcome the man of God; that even some Arians 
came back to the Church.

162 
 
According to St. Athanasius, while Abba Anthony was sitting one day by 
his monastery, he saw somebody ascending to heaven, and a multitude of saints 
was welcoming him. Inquiring about him, he was told that he was Abba Amon. 
Thirty days later, some hermits came over from Mount Nitria, to inform St 
Anthony that their father has departed to heaven. 
The C optic Church celebrates his feast on the 20 th of Bashons; and the 
Greek Church on the 4th of October. 
 
 
 
 
AMON, THE RYTHIAN, FR. 
He was called that way because he lived in the region of ‘Rythio’ by the city 
of ‘El-Tur’ in Sinai. He was an Egyptian monk who lived as an anchorite in the 
region of ‘Kanub’ (Abu Quir) at the beginning of the fourth century AD. When 
the persecution was stirred up by Emperor ‘Valens’ (364-378 AD), he was 
exiled to Palestine, and from there, he returned to the wilderness of Sinai. He 
witnessed by himself the invasion of the pagan Arabs on the monasteries of 
Sinai when they destroyed the monasteries and dispersed their monks. At that 
time, Amon set forth to ‘Rythio,' which became the center of a gathering of the 
monks of Sinai. He li ved there for a long time until Rythio ’ was invaded as 
well. And, he then left it and set forth to ‘Manf,' then to Scetis to live among 
its hermits as a disciple to Abba Bemen. When he once asked Abba Bemen 
about the evil thoughts; his answer was: “It is within the power of the enemy 
to bring them to our minds, but it is within our power not to accept them!” 
 
AMON, ABBA 
This saint was the disciple of Abba ‘Poemen’ (Bemoa). He came once to 
visit Abba ‘Sisoes’ (Shishoy) in wintertime. And he noticed that Abba  Sisoes 
was very sad and depressed after he left the life of seclusion in the wilderness, 
so he said to him: “Why are you so sad, O father? How could you have 
managed to live alone in the wilderness at your advanced age? ” The old man 
looked at him with admonishment and said: “What are you saying Amon?! Is 
feeling freedom in the desert not better than anything else?!” 
 
AMON, THE BISHOP OF HERMOPOLIS

stayed alive in the frozen lake, including a young man called Melito. The 
governor ordered to break the hands and legs of those who were still alive, 
and to cast them into fire. So, the guards did what they were orde red and 
carried the saints’ broken bodies in a wagon to be burned. However, they kept 
Melito until the end, with the hope that he might change his mind when he 
would find out that he became alone. But his mother, a poor widow, 
admonished the guards on their wrong consideration and approached her son, 
who smiled at her with thanksgiving. With the power of the Holy Spirit, she 
exhorted her son to abide until the end, then carried him and cast him by 
herself into the wagon among his fellow martyrs. The guards burned the 
bodies of the martyrs and threw the ashes in the river, but the believers 
managed to haul some of the precious relics, and kept them in Caesarea. 
 [The Synaxarion: 13 Baramhat] 
 [Butler: March 10] 
 
MARTYRS OF ST. ANTHONY MOUNTAIN 
On the 26 th of Baba, the Coptic Church celebrates the memory of seven 
martyrs who were martyred at the hands of the Barbarians, on the Mountain 
of St. Anthony, the Father of all monks. 
 [The Synaxarion: 26 Baba] 
 
MARTYRS OF THE ARIAN HERESY 
When the Arian Emperor Constan tius II (337 -361 AD), the son of 
Constantine the Great (306 -337 AD), approved the heresy of Arius (250 -336 
AD), he sent someone called Gregory of Cappadocia to Alexandria guarded 
by 500 horsemen, to be appointed as the patriarch of Alexandria, instead of 
the 20 th Pope Athanasius the Apostolic (328 -373 AD), who rejected and 
opposed that heresy. The emperor ordered his envoy to kill whoever would 
disobey him. When the people of Alexandria refused to accept him, he killed 
several thousands of them. In the mean time, Pope Athanasius fled away and 
hid for six years. Then, the pope went to Constantinople to face the emperor. 
However, the emperor ordered his men to place him on a boat without food 
or drink, with the hope he would perish of hunger and thirst or drown  along 
the way, through a miracle, the boat came to land in Alexandria peacefully, 
where his people greatly rejoiced, brought him to the Church; and drove 
away Gregory the intruder and all his followers. 
During the whole period (337 -361 AD) of the reign of  Emperor 
Constantius II, the Arian persecution against the Orthodox prevailed over the

279 
 
did not cease to visit all the Pachomian monasteries . He also had  very 
admirable spiritual sayings, few of which survived, in which he urged all t o 
study the Holy Bible and to observe the Pachomian rules.  
A Delegation to meet Pope Athanasius: 
When the 20th Pope St. Athanasius the Apostolic (328-373 AD) returned 
with honor back to his seat, according to a prophecy by St. Pachomius , St. 
Horsiesius sent a delegation of monks to greet him . In their way, when the 
delegation knew that St. Anthony the Great was in the outer mountain, they 
decided to visit him there to get his blessing . St. Anthony received them with 
a warm welcome, and getting to know that St. Pachomius had already reposed, 
he comforted and encouraged them . Then, the delegation continued on their 
way to Alexandria to meet the pope.  
Monastic Dissensions:  
As the plague spread, after claiming the lives of St. Pachomius , St. 
Petronius, and so many other Abbots of these Cenobitic monasteries, a sort of 
confusion spread among many of the brethren who sought to occupy those 
leading positions. This made the work of St. Horsiesius very difficult. He tried 
to provoke the spirit of humility among t hem by his spiritual sermons, in 
addition to his humility and compassion.  
It was Apollon, the Abbot of the monastery of Moncose  in the province of 
Qena, who ignited the first spark of dissension , seeking the financial 
independence of his monastery and the right to keep what would be more than 
its needs. St. Horsiesius tried to counsel him, sometimes by compassion and 
other times by firmness,  in particular, that other monastery Abbots tried to 
follow his example. The saint's heart was so grieved. 
St. Horsiesius soul became embittered , and he longed to relinquish the 
leadership to someone else or to have a partner to help him . He fervently 
prayed, and in a night vision, the Lord guided him to seek the assistance of St. 
Tadros, the disciple of Abba Pachomius. He was comforted by that vision , 
particularly that St. Tadros was much cherished by him and by all the others, 
because of the sweetness of his humility.  
St. Horsiesius called for an assembly of the Abbots of the monasteries, 
except for Fr. Tadros, and sought their counsel. They greatly rejoiced and sent 
to call Fr. Tadros to become co -head of the monasteries along with St. 
Horsiesius, who quietly retreated to the monastery of Chensbosque  until the 
matter was settled. Yet, he returned when Fr. Tadros insisted not to accept this 
assignment without having his blessing . Convincing Fr. Tadros to accept 
working with him, he set out to the monastery of Chensbosque. Then, he 
moved to the monastery of Moncose, from which the first spark of dissension

of St. Paul, and shook their heads as if they were asking St . Anthony what to 
do. St. Antony knew that they were sent from God. He marked the place on 
the ground and they dug the grave with their claws ; according to St. Antony's 
directions. St. Anthony then buried the holy body. 
St. Anthony carried the garment of palm t ree fibers and presented it to 
Pope Athanasius who gr eatly exulted to have it, and kept wearing it every 
year in the feasts of Christmas, Theophany , and Resurrection . Many signs 
were shown by that garment. 
In the location where St . Paul the First Hermit used to live, a monastery 
was built where earthly angels dedicated all their lives to that of joyful praise 
for the Lord. 
 
PAUL, THE MONK 
About Abba Ur (Hur), we know that he had a disciple by the name of Paul 
(Boulus) who cared much for the life of prayers, even though he 
misunderstood its meaning . He considered his prayers as a race to recite the 
greatest number of church praises. H e was eventually corrected by St . 
Macarius.  
About him it was said: 
He did not approach the hard handworks or the assignments of selling and 
buying; except for the littl e things he eats every day . However, he was very 
advanced in one thing, which was praying without ceasing. He set for himself 
a rule; to pray 300 prayers every day. He used to put some little pebbles in his 
pocket, and then he used to hold in his hand one of them for every prayer he 
prayed. One day, he came to St . Macarius, saying: “Father, I am very sad .” 
When the elder monk asked him the reason for his anguish, he answered: “I 
heard about a virgin who spent thirty years of her monastic life, reciting 500 
prayers every day . On hearing that, I despised myself, for I am not able to 
pray more than 300 prayers every day.” 
Here, St. Abba Macarius told him: “I lived for sixty years in the monastic 
life, reciting only fifty prayers every day; work ed for  what was e nough to 
earn my need of food; and receive d the brethren who come to seek my 
counsel. Now, here you are who pray 300 prayers every day, condemned by 
your thoughts. You probably, either do not pray them with purity; or you can 
do more of other things and you do not want to.” 
 [The Diocese of Beni-Suef: The Garden of Monks; pp. 24-25] 
 [Budge: The Paradise, vol. 2, art. 356]

records.question: Who was St. Paul the First Hermit's wife?
records.answer: St. Paul the First Hermit did not have a wife. The passages describe that he went into the wilderness during the persecution of Decius around 250 A.D. after his brother Peter took his share of the inheritance by force. There is no mention of him having a wife in the sources provided [1][2].

A group of ninety-seven confessors: men, women , and children, were 
brought to the governor , and  he ordered  the executioners to burn the  
believers' left feet using red hot heated iron and to pluck out their right eyes 
then sear them with red hot metal. Afterward, he sent those courageous

Another group from Gaza was arrested while gathering in prayer and 
listening to the Word of God. Among them was a girl named Thea (Tia), who

ordered that she would be whipped and t ortured. When another girl from

In the apostolic age, many practiced a kind o f monasticism, seeking to enjoy the 
perfection of the Gospel. The eschatological direction of the Church made the believers long 
for the coming of their Bridegroom, so some preferred to live a life of virginity, consecrating 
all their time for worship to p repare themselves for the heavenly wedding. In the second 
century, the Christian virgins in Smyrna and Corinth used to walk in liturgical processions 
behind the priests and in front of the widows. Moreover, many groups of virgins were found 
living in Alexandria and in many cities around the world. Articles about virginity represented 
an essential aspect of the writings of the Church Fathers in the first three centuries. 
Virgins used to live together, while men preferred to leave the cities to live in simple huts 
in villages and were often called “consecrated.” Some people felt a thirst for the angelic life 
so they fled to the wilderness. We know of only a few of these, such St. Paul the Hermit who 
lived in the wilderness for almost ninety years (between 250–340 A. D.). 
St. Anthony established the monastic movement and is considered the father of all monks 
in the entire world, even though many preceded him. This is because of his strong relationship 
with St. Athanasius, who wrote about him to the Roman world. It is also because he opened 
his cave after twenty years of solitude to disciple monastic leaders, converse with 
philosophers in the simplicity of his faith, and receive rulers. He had an active role in the 
Church and went to Alexandria to support the martyrs and stand against the Arians. 
St. Pachomius, founder of cenobitic monasticism, felt that the order of solitude may not 
work for all those who want to become monks, so he started a monastic community within 
the walls of monasteries, and the hermits praised him for doing so. 
St. Macarius the Great, St. Ammonas and others started the order of communities (or the 
semi-eremitical order). Many came from around the world to practice the ascetic life in 
Egypt, and to write about it and take these orders back to  their countries. It is important to 
note that the leaders of the three orders were not biased for their monastic styles, but instead 
they used to visit each other and praise each other’s orders. 
The monastic movement of women started side by side with tha t of men, and monks 
helped build convents. Female leaders arose and had great influence, like Amma Sarah, 
Amma Theodora, and Amma Syncletica. Moreover, some Egyptian and foreign women were 
disguised in the apparel of men and led ascetic lives in monasterie s of men, and their 
asceticism, struggles, and spirituality exceeded many. 
875. Who were the most important monastic leaders? 
St. Paul of Thebes (the first hermit):  St. Jerome documented his biography in 374 or 
375 A. D. St. Paul grew up in northern upper Egypt and was well educated in Greek and 
Egyptian sciences. When he was sixteen years old, he received a big inheritance from his 
parents. During the persecution of  Decius (around 250 A. D.), he went into the wilderness 
after his brother, Peter, took his share of the inheritance by force. When he was 113 years

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Volume 3, p. 387
passages.text:
387 
 
father's huge inheritance.  
By orders from the governor, he was stripped from his clothes, whipped , 
and had flames placed on his sides. They put iron tools in his mouth and ears; 
cut his tongue off and set poisonous serpents upon him , but God sent His 
Archangel Suriel to comfort, support , and heal him . The governor then sent 
him to Alexandria; and in the prison there, he met with his friend  ‘Isy’ (Ba-
isy) and his sister Tekla.  The three of them were exulted in spirit . The Lord 
Jesus Christ appeared to proclaim that the thr ee saints would testify to His 
Name and their bodies, as well as their souls, would stay together.  
The head of St . Paul was cut off on the seashore, where some believers 
came, shrouded his body and kept his relics with them. 
The church celebrates his martyrdom on the 9th of Amshir.  
 
PAULA, THE ELDER, ST. 
St. Paula is considered the most famous Roman woman as far as her piety 
and dedication to the Lord are concerned . Besides, she had vast wealth , 
honor, and sharpness of mind. She was born on the 15 th of May 347 AD to a 
very rich family among the Roman elites . Her man Toxotius  passed away 
when she was only thirty-two years old and a mother to a son and four 
daughters: 
1- The son was named Toxotius, after his father's name. 
2- The oldest daughter was  named Blesilla, after her maternal grandmother . 
She passed away three months after she completely changed her worldly 
lifestyle and lived in repentance . St. Jerome wrote a condolence letter to 
her mother, to assure her that she has gone to Paradise. 
3- The second daughter was Paulina, the wife of Pammachius.  After his 
young wife Paulina passed away, he distributed most of the possessions he 
inherited on the poor and he pursued an ascetic life, even though he was 
one of the elites. 
4- The third daughter was Eustochium , who accompanied her mother all the 
way on a very tough ascetic road that angered her relatives . When her 
mother passed away in Bethlehem ; she was on the brink of collapse . 
However, St. Jerome came to her support and exhorted her to complete the 
mission of her mother. 
5- The fourth daughter was Rufina, who passed away in her youth in 386. 
Her Widowhood: 
St. Paula lived with her husband an ideal family life, to become a role 
model in Rome for the virtuous matrimony in the Lord . The man she dearly 
loved passed away, when she was only thirty-two years old . She was so

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Volume 3, p. 389
passages.text:
389 
 
daughters. 
Paula's heart was day by day i nflamed with the longing to the Heavenly 
life; while the atmosphere in Rome was suffocating for her because of the 
fame of her noble fami ly and the criticism she got from her family elders , so 
she planned to leave Rome and go somewhere else to worship God in 
tranquility and peace away from her family and her old friends. 
In the year 385 AD, she sailed along with her daughter Eustochium  to 
Cyprus. There, they visited St . Epiphanius, the bishop of Salamis , and from 
there, they sailed to Antioch, where they met with St . Jerome. Then all of 
them set forth to the Holy places in Palestine , and from there, they went to 
Egypt to see some of its desert monks and hermits. 
In Egypt: 
St. Paula accompanied St . Jerome on his trip to Egypt and was most 
probably with him when he met with St . Didymus the Blind, the d ean of the 
School of Alexandria. She studied at his school for one month; then set forth 
together with St . Jerome to the wilderness of Nitria. In Nitria , they stayed a 
long time . St. Jerome described the effect of that period on the life of that 
saintly widow, he said that she was excited and joyful to see these saints and 
longed to imitate their lives. The fathers received her with joy, for which she 
glorified God and felt unworthy of such an honor . She met with the two 
Macariuses, St. Serapion and others . She visited them in their cells, 
prostrated herself at their feet, feeling that the Lord  Jesus Christ was in every 
one of them. She tolerated the harsh traveling between the cells and spen t the 
nights in the open wilderness with joy and enthusiasm beyond the endurance 
of any woman . She forgot her fatigue and all her needs because of her 
spiritual joy. 
In Bethlehem: 
In the next year, she set forth to Jerusalem to live in Bethlehem. There, she 
built a guest -house to gi ve hospitality to strangers, a monastery for monks 
and a convent for the nuns. 
In the convent, she  lived along with her daughter Eustochum  a serious 
monastic life, and according to the convent' s rules, all practiced the work of 
the hand, particularly sewing for the nuns or those outside. 
Paula lived among the nuns as a mother who drew them with her love, 
tenderness and she was their role model . Even though she and her daughter 
partook of ministry and work, yet she was firm . If, for instance, she noticed a 
nun talk too much or showing anger ; she would ask her to separate herself 
from the congregation, to pray outside , and to eat her meals alone for a 
certain period.

passages.text:
Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church – Volume 1  
668 
ascetic life in a small hut in a village for about ten years under the guidance of an ascetic. He 
longed for solitude, and so he moved to Scetis and a cherub accompanied him on the way. 
He loved worship and asceticism, so many came from the East and the West to the wilderness 
to become his disciples. 
St. Shenoute the Archimandrite: He was the abbot of the White Monastery in Athribis 
(or Atripe), in the wilderness of Thebes for over fifty-six years (fourth or fifth century A. D.). 
He led 2200 monks and 1800 nuns. He was called the “Archimandrite” as he practiced 
solitude from time to time, and he encouraged the monks at his monastery to retreat to the 
wilderness after practicing the life of fellowship. In the year 431 A. D., he accompanied St. 
Cyril the Great to the Ecume nical Council of Ephesus. He is known for  purifying Coptic 
literature of Hellenistic cultural influences, and did not allow any foreigners to join his 
monastic communities. For this reason, he was regarded as a political leader and a social 
reformer, besides the depth of his spirituality. 
Amma Sarah : The first monastic group of women in the world was in the city of 
Alexandria, following the rule of St. Syncletica. St. Athanasius documented her biography 
and teachings. Moreover, St. Pachomius established two convents for nuns, while many nuns 
lived in solitude in the desert. Many mothers came from foreign convents to Egypt, like St. 
Melania the Elder (374 A. D.) and her granddaughter Melania the Younger (418 A. D.). Also, 
we cannot forget to mention St. Mary of Egypt who repented in Jerusalem and lived for forty-
seven years in the wilderness across the Jordan not seeing the face of another human being, 
except St. Zosima twice in the last two years of her life.  
Many nuns were given the gift of true leadership and spiritual discernment, like St. Sarah 
of whom it was said that she lived for sixty years on the banks of a river, but never lifted her 
eyes to look at it. Many of her sayings were preserved in the sayings of the desert fathers and 
mothers.  
St. Hilaria: In the fourth century, the daughter of Emperor Zeno fled to Scetis where she 
led a life of asceticism in the attire of a male monk. When her sister, Theopiste, was possessed 
by an evil spirit, the elders of the wilderness sent her to St. Hilaria to pray for her, and did 
not know that St. Hilaria was a woman. She prayed all night for her and embraced her. 
Theopiste was healed, and she told the emperor about the monk, “Hilarion,” who healed her 
and was embracing her, so her father was disturbed. He called for her to come to the palace, 
where she revealed to him that she was his daughter after he had promised not to prevent her 
from going back to her cave. 
St. Syncletica: Some historians regard her to be the equal of St. Anthony, the star of the 
wilderness; for as St. Anthony was the father of all monks, St. Syncletica was a mother to 
that group of virgins which transformed the fertile valley of Egypt into a dwelling place for 
the grace of God. She was born to noble parents who settled in Alexandria to be close to the 
School of Alexandria. They had two sons and two daughters, so they wanted to educate them 
in all sciences, which were only offered in the School of Alexandria. This family was shocked

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Volume 3, p. 385
passages.text:
385 
 
PAUL, THE MONK 
One of the desert fathers told this story about a monk by the name of Paul  
(Boulus) from somewhere in Lower Egypt and he lived in Thebes:  
He used to hold a serpent by his bare hands and split it into two . Some of 
the brethren made metanoia before him, and said: “Tell us brother; what did 
you do that made you qualified for such a marvelous grace ?” He answered 
them: “Forgive me, fathers. Once the man acquires purity, everything would 
submit to him and obey him. Like the way , Adam was in Paradise before he 
disobeyed the Divine commandment.” 
 [Light Publications: Sayings of the Elder Fathers, 1983, p. 258 (Arabic)] 
 [Bendicta Ward: The Sayings of the Desert Fathers] 
 
PAUL, THE SIMPLE, ST. 
This saint was a marvelous example of a simple man, who by the grace of 
God, could strive to reach a high ascetic level, even though he started it at his 
60th years of age. This St. Paul (Boulus) was a very simple and pious farmer 
who got married to a very beautiful girl . After living together for so many 
years, he started to take notice o f so many rumors about his wife' s evil 
behavior. However, whenever he inquired fr om her about the matter, she 
would pretend to be a pure woman . Eventually, by himself, he saw her in the 
evil act . On that day, he forsook the house to her and set forth to Abba 
Anthony the Great, hoping to become one of his disciples. 
Getting to know that this simple farmer was sixty years old, Abba Anthony 
advised him to go back to his field and plow; on account of that it would be 
difficult for him to practice the monastic life at his age . Before his 
persistence, he sought from him to join a monastery in  the valley to practice 
with the brethren what suit his old age; but the old man persisted on not 
leaving that mountain. 
Here, Abba Anthony had no other choice but to put him under tough tests; 
and was amazed by his endurance, perseverance , and obedience . Among 
those tests that he left him four days without food or drink while watching 
him lest he would collapse. He s ought from him to  remain a whole week 
outside his cave, under the heat of noon and the severe cold nights, without 
leaving his place; and sought from him, after weaving eight meters of a cord, 
to loosen it and weave it anew . In all that he was obedient, worked with joy 
and extreme simplicity. 
On seeing his persistence with the spirit of piety, Abba Anthony accepted 
him as a recluse and sought from him to build for himself a cell on the way 
between the base of the mountain and his own cell.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Volume 3, p. 384
passages.text:
384 
 
of St. Paul, and shook their heads as if they were asking St . Anthony what to 
do. St. Antony knew that they were sent from God. He marked the place on 
the ground and they dug the grave with their claws ; according to St. Antony's 
directions. St. Anthony then buried the holy body. 
St. Anthony carried the garment of palm t ree fibers and presented it to 
Pope Athanasius who gr eatly exulted to have it, and kept wearing it every 
year in the feasts of Christmas, Theophany , and Resurrection . Many signs 
were shown by that garment. 
In the location where St . Paul the First Hermit used to live, a monastery 
was built where earthly angels dedicated all their lives to that of joyful praise 
for the Lord. 
 
PAUL, THE MONK 
About Abba Ur (Hur), we know that he had a disciple by the name of Paul 
(Boulus) who cared much for the life of prayers, even though he 
misunderstood its meaning . He considered his prayers as a race to recite the 
greatest number of church praises. H e was eventually corrected by St . 
Macarius.  
About him it was said: 
He did not approach the hard handworks or the assignments of selling and 
buying; except for the littl e things he eats every day . However, he was very 
advanced in one thing, which was praying without ceasing. He set for himself 
a rule; to pray 300 prayers every day. He used to put some little pebbles in his 
pocket, and then he used to hold in his hand one of them for every prayer he 
prayed. One day, he came to St . Macarius, saying: “Father, I am very sad .” 
When the elder monk asked him the reason for his anguish, he answered: “I 
heard about a virgin who spent thirty years of her monastic life, reciting 500 
prayers every day . On hearing that, I despised myself, for I am not able to 
pray more than 300 prayers every day.” 
Here, St. Abba Macarius told him: “I lived for sixty years in the monastic 
life, reciting only fifty prayers every day; work ed for  what was e nough to 
earn my need of food; and receive d the brethren who come to seek my 
counsel. Now, here you are who pray 300 prayers every day, condemned by 
your thoughts. You probably, either do not pray them with purity; or you can 
do more of other things and you do not want to.” 
 [The Diocese of Beni-Suef: The Garden of Monks; pp. 24-25] 
 [Budge: The Paradise, vol. 2, art. 356]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Volume 4, p. 232
passages.text:
232 
 
THECLA OF PALESTINE (The martyr) 
This St. Thecla was mentioned by the historian Eusebius, the bishop of 
Caesarea. She was martyred in Gaza along with her brother Agapius the soldier 
in the 2nd year of the persecution stirred up by Emperor Diocletian (304). After 
they confessed their faith in the Lord Jesus Christ, she was condemned to death 
by being devoured by the wild beasts, and she received the crown of 
martyrdom. Whereas her brother Agapius suffered many tortures in Caesarea 
of Palestine and was also martyred [Martyrs of Palestine 3:6]. The martyrdom 
of this saint is celebrated by the Coptic Church on the 26th of Mesra. 
 [Eusebius: Martyrs of Palestine, 3:1] 
 
THECLA, ST. PAUL’S DISCIPLE 
This St. Thecla was a disciple of St. ‘Paul the Apostle. She was considered 
as the first female martyr in Christian history, in the same way, St. Steven was 
considered as the first male martyr. She endured so many mortalities, ev en 
though her blood was not shed. Many Fathers viewed her as a small model of 
the Virgin Church adorned with every virtue, coming directly after the Virgin 
St. Mary. And, some of the Fathers used to commend any great female saint by 
calling her: The New Thecla. 
This saint raised in  Iconium in Asia Minor . She was known for her great 
beauty, high ethics , and great fortune beside her excellent education. Her 
father, who was one of the elites of the city, cared to educate her that she 
excelled in philosophy, poetry; and was eloquent, daring, yet full of decency. 
Many young men wished to propose to her, but her parents chose for her a 
wealthy young nobleman by the name of Thamyris. 
In the year 45 A D, St. Paul and St. Barnabas passed through the city of 
Iconium, i n their first preaching trip (Acts 13:51) . Thecla happened to be 
sitting on the window sill of her house when she saw St. Paul. Then, the Spirit 
of God drew her to be intrigued by his words about the Lord Jesus. She met St. 
Paul, listened to him, proclaimed her faith, and then got baptized.  
During her continuous association with St. Paul, she felt a great longing for 
a life of virginity. Then, she cast off her vain adornments and stopped caring 
for jewelry, banquets , and worldly celebrations . This change in her life 
confused her mother, who tried hard to convince her to resume her early one 
and to get married  and have children who would s upport her in her old age . 
But, the saint firmly proclaimed her desire for virginity for the Lord’s sake . 
Here, the mother started to threaten her and resorted to Thamyris to help 
convince her daughter to get married . The man flirted with her, counting he 
could draw her heart to the pleasures of the world . Yet she persisted on her

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Volume 3, p. 145
passages.text:
145 
 
wondered within themselves whether there were any others out there, who 
surpassed them spiritually to learn from them and follow their path. Among 
those Fathers were St. Anthony the Great, to whom the Lord revealed the 
existence of St. Paul the First Hermit, St. Zosima th e Priest, whom the Lord 
guided to St. Mary the Egyptian, and St. Macarius the Great,  to whom the 
Lord revealed the two married women in Alexandria, who lived by the spirit 
of love, sanctity, and asceticism. 
A Married Couple Living better than a Monk: 
Such a thought came upon one of the saintly elder monks, and a Divine 
voice informed him that there was a virtuous wife called Mary living with her 
husband Ephcharistos in a village in Egypt at a spiritual level higher than 
him. By the guidance of an angel, the elderly monk set forth to that village, to 
meet with that couple who did surpass him spiritually. Knocking at their 
door, the woman opened for him, while her husband was still away 
shepherding a flock of sheep. In the evening, Ephcharistos came home and 
joined in welcoming their guest. After they prepared dinner for him, the 
monk refused ultimately to eat until they would tell him about what was 
going on in their lives. Ephcharistos did not want to talk about their private 
life together. He just said: “I a m a shepherd, and this is Mary, my wife.” The 
elder monk persisted on knowing more about them and revealed to the man 
that it was God who sent him to them. Here, the man started talking with the 
fear of the Lord. He said: “I shepherd the sheep we inherited  from our 
parents, and whenever we make a little profit by the help of God, we divide it 
into three portions: one for the poor, one to accommodate the strangers and 
the third for our personal needs. Since we got married, my wife lives with me 
like a sister . Each of us sleeps separately. At night we wear sackcloth, and 
during daytime, we put on our regular attires. No one knows anything about 
our lives.” Here, Mary looked down and supplicated to the elder monk to 
keep their life secret until they repose.  
 
MARY MAGDALENE, ST. 
The Lord Christ healed St. Mary Magdalene (from ‘Magdala’) by driving 
seven unclean spirits out of her. She was one of the women who served the 
Lord in Galilee (Luke 8:1 -2). She also was present when He was crucified 
and went to His tomb  along with two others, to find the grave empty. 
According to the Gospel of St. Mark, she was the first to see the Lord Christ 
after His resurrection (Mark 16:9), and St. John added that the Lord entrusted 
her to carry a message to His brethren (John 20:11-18). 
Among the women who were mentioned in the Gospel, there was “The

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Volume 2, p. 85
passages.text:
85 
 
A Favorite Disciple of St. Jerome: 
She was the daughter of St. Paula, the 3 rd of 4 daughters, yet the only one 
who followed the monastic life of her mother up till the end. 
Paula was of a noble family in Rome. When her husband Toxotius died, she 
dedicated her whole life to God in simple living, voluntary poverty and 
faithfulness, while spending all her time in worship and works of love. On 
seeing her mother doing all that, Eustochium, who was a 12 years old young 
girl at the time, absorbed her mother’s kind of behavior. And when St. Jerome 
came to Rome from the East in the year 382 AD, the two of them put 
themselves under his spiritual guidance. Such action stirred up Hemetus, the 
girl’s uncle, and his wife against them. They e xerted all effort to change the 
little girl’s mind from that monastic way of living and to lure her toward the 
pleasures of this world. The young girl Eustochium did not listen to them; on 
the contrary, she put on the attire of virgins; and she became the first dedicated 
virgin among the noble ladies of Rome. In the year 384 AD, St. Jerome wrote 
a beautiful long letter to this saint concerning ‘The Virgin Life1,’ an important 
message that concerns all virgins in general and not just St. Eustochium. 
When St. Jerome decided to travel to Palestine because of the troubles 
which he had in Rome, Paula agreed to join him. She was accompanied by 
Eustochium and some other women. In Palestine, they visited the holy sites in 
the Holy Land, before they set out t o Egypt where they had a chance to meet 
with the monks of Nitria. Finally, they settled in Bethlehem. 
In Bethlehem, three monastic congregations of nuns were established under 
the leadership of Paula, helped by her daughter Eustochium. They both helped 
St. Jerome in translating the Holy Bible to the Latin language (The Vulgate). 
And according to their request, he wrote comments on some of the books of 
the Holy Bible, and even dedicated some of his books to them, saying, “These 
two ladies are capable of judg ing books more so than most men.” In the year 
403 AD, St. Paula fell ill, and her daughter Eustochium kept serving her and 
praying for her in the cave of Bethlehem. And when she reposed on the 26th of 
January in the year 404 AD, Eustochium threw herself on her reposed mother, 
kissing her eyes and longing to be buried together with her. St. Jerome 
comforted her and tasked her to work in the service of the nuns’ convents. 
Her Departure: 
After her mother reposed, Eustochium took upon herself also the 
responsibility of caring for the congregation of the dedicated and widowed 
women in Bethlehem. She was in charge when a mob invaded their house,

557 
or St. Abu-Sefein the Martyr? He went to his house with such bitterness in his soul that he 
fell asleep in his chair …  and in his sleep he saw the heavens open, and the Lord of Glory 
seated on His throne, and Fr. Bishoy Kamel going forth to welcome  the saints to paradise 
and present them to the Lord Christ; and Fr. Bishoy exulted in those martyrs. The soul of 
the servant from Sydney rejoiced, and he telephoned me to tell me how much the late Fr. 
Bishoy cares while in Paradise and how he rejoices in the martyrs. 
When a church named after Pope Cyril VI was founded in Los Angeles, someone said 
to me that a person came forward bearing an envelope with a large sum of money and told 
the Coptic priest: “A group of us, Christians and Indians, gathered together and learned that 
this is the Church whose members were  martyred in Libya because they were Christians . 
Thus, we consider the establishment of your church in this area to be a blessing for us all.” 
1441. How does St. John conclude the Book of Revelation , regarding the Day of the 
Lord? 
St. John concludes the Book of Revelation by describing the heavenly Jerusalem  — or 
as St. Augustine  calls it, “The heavenly Church ”1360 — the glories and blessings of the 
heavenly Church, and the desire of our Lord Jesus Christ to come quickly (Rev. 22:20 –21) 
to take His bride the queen to His throne.  
Many authors, poets, and philosophers such as Plat o depict ideal cities  (in their 
estimation) prescribing for them  laws, arrangements,  and principles dictated by  their 
philosophy and way of thinking . However, very soon, mistaken or unrealistic principles  
infiltrate their models, and their ideal cities turn out in fact to be  deficient and riddled with 
shortcomings.  
St. John does not imitate their example but rather, ascending by the Spirit, his vision is 
of a true, ideal, and immortal Church, which is in essence “ the tabernacle of God … with 
men” (Rev. 21:3). As this was difficult to depict or express in human language, he recorded 
for us what he actually saw, but in simple symbols that leave it to us to go deeper into them 
and savor the nature of  this singular, heavenly city ; so far as  our spiritual stature allows us 
to comprehend through the guidance of the Holy Spirit. 
1442. What is meant by “a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the 
first earth had passed away” (Rev. 21:1)?  
The earth in which we now live and the heaven under which w e live witness to the 
power of our Creator and His sublime care. He has not left us wanting for anything. For the 
earth with all its laws, resources, and marvels is there to serve us,  and the sun, moon , and 
 
1360 Cf. St. Augustine of Hippo, City of God 20.17 (NPNF I/2:436).

359 
 
up, resulting in keeping him awake in prayers. As for fasting, he trained himself 
to fast the whole week and eat only on Saturdays. His prayers and fasting got 
to hand in hand with his intense love for the word of God. He memorized most 
of the Holy Bible by heart. The Book of ‘Jeremiah’ had a special place in his 
heart; that it was said that he used to se e the prophet Jeremiah during his 
reading of his Book; that he was called ‘Bishoy the Jeremian.’ 
He considered hand-work as a significant part of building his spiritual life. 
He believed in the saying : “If anyone will not work, neither shall he eat. ” (2 
Thess. 3:10). His friend Abba ‘John the Short’ said about him that when a rich 
man brought to him plenty of gold as a donation, he told him: “The dwellers 
of the wilderness have no need of gold and should not have any of it. Go instead 
to the villages of Egypt and distribute it to the poor. God bless you.” After the 
man went his way, and the saint returned to his cell, Satan came to him, saying: 
“You fatigued me so much, O Bishoy .” And, the saint answered him: “Since 
your fall, and all your fatigue is in vain.” 
His Fellowship with our Lord Jesus; 
Through his pure heart, he used to meet often with the Lord Jesus Christ on 
a friendship level . He used to see Him, to talk with Him , and to enjoy His 
Divine proclamations. It was said that, having been so persiste nt in his great 
ascetic life and prayers that the Lord Jesus Christ appeared to him, saying: “My 
chosen vessel ‘Bishoy,’ peace be with you; I saw your labor and strife, and 
behold, I shall always be with you!”  
Another time, as our saint remained a long time fasting, the Lord appeared 
to him, saying: “You labored too much, My chosen vessel Bishoy!” The saint 
answered Him: “It was You O Lord who labored for me, but I have not labored 
at all!” 
A third time, the Lord appeared to him, saying: “Rejoice, My chosen vessel 
Bishoy. Do you see this mountain? I shall send you monks to fill that mountain 
to worship Me.” The saint asked Him: “Will You sustain them, Lord, in such a 
barren wilderness?” The Lord answered: “If they love one another and keep 
My commandments, I shall sustain them in everything!” The saint asked Him: 
“Will You save them from all the anguishes and afflictions mentioned in the 
Gospel?” The Lord answered: “Whoever fears, obeys Me and keep My 
commandments; I shall save him from all temptations! ” He then blessed him 
and ascended. 
Again the Lord appeared to him surrounded by angels. The Lord comforted 
him and blessed him . The saint worshipped Him and washed His feet with 
water in a basin, then the Lord ascended . St. ‘Bishoy’ drank from that water 
and left a portion for his disciple . The saint sought from him more than once 
to drink it, but the disciple was too slow. Then, when St. ‘Bishoy’ went to check

His Love for the Salvation of All Souls: 
Saint ‘Bishoy’ had a disciple named ‘Isaac,’ who descended to the world 
and was seduced by a Jewish woman to forsake his faith, and he was converted 
to Judaism and lived with her . When he happened to encounter some monks, 
he asked them to tell St. ‘Bishoy’: “Your son, the Jewish ‘Isaac,’ has fallen and 
seeks from you to pray on his behalf to God to save him.” On hearing that, the 
woman said: “Even if ‘Bishoy’ come to me, I shall seduce him.” On returning 
to the monastery, the monks forgot what happened. Then, they were asked by 
the saint: “Has someone asked you to tell me something? ” They answered in 
the negative. The saint asked them whether they have encountered the Jewish 
‘Isaac,’ so they told him what happened and what ‘Isaac’ and the Jewish 
woman said. At that moment, they saw the saint retreat three steps backward 
and make the sign of the Cross on himself at each stage. Astonished, the monks 
said; “Even you, father, fear that woman?” St. ‘Bishoy’ humbly answered: “My 
children, the woman was the cause of the fall of ‘Adam,’ ‘Samson,’ ‘David’ 
and ‘Solomon.’ Who would be the poor ‘Bishoy’ to challenge her?!  Nobody 
can overcome the tricks of Satan in wo men, except that one whom God is 
with.” He kept praying and fasting for the sake of his son ‘Isaac’ until God 
saved him, and he came back and repented. 
Forsaking Scetis: 
In the year 407 AD, the first attack of the Berbers on the wilderness of 
‘Scetis’ took place. At that time, the monks escaped from the desert. St. ‘John 
the Short ’ asked St. ‘Bishoy’: “ Do you fear death, O man of God? ” He 
answered him: “No, but I fear a Berberian would kill me and goes to hell 
because of me!” 
St. ‘John the Short ’ went to mount ‘Kalzam,’ near the monastery of Abba 
‘Anthony’ where he reposed . Whereas, St. ‘Bishoy’ went to ‘Ansena’ (the 
village of ‘Sheikh Abbadah’ near ‘Mallawy’), and he lived in the mountain . 
There, he formed a close relationship with ‘St. Abba ‘Paul of Tamouh,’ and 
sought from the Lord not to be separated from him when they would repose , 
and God granted them their wish. 
St. ‘Bishoy’ remained in his expatriation until he reposed on the 8th of Abib 
in the year 417 AD, after reaching 97 years of age. He was buried in the castle 
of ‘Meniat el-Saqar’ near ‘Ansena.’ When St. ‘Paul of Tamouh’ reposed, St. 
‘Athanasius’ of ‘Ansena’ gathered the two saints'  bodies and buried them 
together in the monastery of abba ‘Bishoy’ in ‘Ansena’ (Monastery of El -
Bersha). The bodies of these two saints were returned to the wilderness of 
‘Scetis’ during the patriarchate of the 52nd pope Abba ‘Yusab I’ (831-849 AD).

BISHOY, ST. ABBA 
Our great saint abba ‘Bishoy’ represents the simple life striving in the Lord, 
that was founded upon the love fellowship with the Lord Jesus Christ. He had 
a personal relationship with Jesus that broke the obstacles down to open up the 
heart by the Holy Spirit that the Heavenly Groom would transfigure within it 
and reign with power and dominion! 
St. ‘Bishoy’ was born in ‘Shansa,’ a village in the governorate of ‘El-
Menufyia,’ around the year 320 AD. He was one of six brothers, whose father 
reposed when they were relatively young, and their mother raised them  up. 
One day the mother saw an angel who came to tell her: “The Lord says to you: 
‘Give Me one of your children to serve Me all the days of his life. ’” She 
answered: “Sir, they are all for the Lord. Let Him take whomever He chooses.” 
The angel put his hand on this saint, and said: “This is a good laborer for the 
Lord.” Being weakly built and frail in the body, his mother asked the angel to 
choose another one; but he answered her: “The Lord said ‘My strength is made 
perfect in weakness.’” (2 Cor. 12:9). 
In Scetis (Shiheet): 
Having reached twenty years of age in the year 340 AD, the young ‘Bishoy’ 
set forth to the wilderness of ‘Scetis,’ where he became a disci ple of Abba 
‘Bemwah’ (Bemen), the disciple of St. ‘Macarius’ (300-391 AD). There, he 
worshipped in seclusion for three years without going out of his cell. He grew 
in virtue and had his heart inflamed with love for God. 
Life in Seclusion: 
When Abba ‘Bemwah’ reposed in the Lord, his two disciples Abba ‘Bishoy’ 
and Abba ‘John (Yeĥness) the Short,’ spent the whole night praying to seek the 
guidance of God . An angel appeared to them and said that Abba ‘John the 
Short’ should remain alone in that location . In obedience, Abba ‘Bishoy’ left 
the place forsaking his friend, and d ug for h imself a cave near the southern 
rock, about two miles away from Abba ‘John the Short.’ 
His Strife: 
As he loved prayer, he made a hole in a high spot on the cave wall, then he 
fixed a wedge in it and tied one end of a rope around it . Then, he used to tie 
the long hair of his head with the other end of that rope; so that whenever his 
head would get heavy and drop down due to sleepiness, the rope would pull it

The Book of Revelation speaks symbolically about the state of the Church during her 
struggle on earth until the day she meets our Lord Jesus her Bridegroom . It then begins to 
tell us of her heavenly matrimonial home  — that is, the eternal kingdom, prepared for us 
since the foundation of the world. This kingdom is not alien to the true believer but is rather 
an extension of what he enjoys here on earth as a token of heaven, and it is what he lives by 
in paradise from the moment of  his departure. Thus, in the last three chapters , the book 
begins to speak about the kingdom in which we live here, and  about the authority that we 
have over Satan and his soldiers as the beginning of an eternal journey  and a heavenly 
meeting with our heavenly Father face to face. 
1372. What is meant by Satan being bound for a thousand years (Rev. 20:1–3)? 
“Then I saw an angel coming down from heaven, having the key to the bottomless pit 
and a great chain in his hand. He laid hold of the dragon, that serpent of old, who is the 
Devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years; and he cast him into the bottomless 
pit, and shut him up, and set a seal on him, so that he should deceive the nations no more 
till the thousand years were finished. But after these things he must be released f or a little 
while” (Rev. 20:1–3) This angel who came down from heaven , has authority over hell, and 
is able to lay hold of and bind Satan is a symbol of the angel of the covenant: our Lord 
Jesus (Mal. 3:1) who came down from heaven and was nailed to the cr oss for the sake of 
humanity, having wiped out the handwriting of iniquity that was written against us. Thus, 
the devil has no place in us, and thus the believer is able to trample on Satan and his power. 
And as the Holy Bible says:1200  
“… now the ruler of this world will be cast out” (John 12:31).  
“Having wiped out the handwriting of requirements that was against us, which was 
contrary to us. And He has taken it out of the way, having nailed it to the cross. Having 
disarmed principalities and powers, He ma de a public spectacle of them, triumphing over 
them in it” (Col. 2:14–15).  
“And He said to them, ‘I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven. Behold, I give you 
the authority to trample on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and 
nothing shall by any means hurt you’” (Luke 10:18–19).  
“Because the ruler of this world is judged” (John 16:11).

An Encounter with St. Ephraim the Syrian: 
By a Divine arrangement,  Mar ‘Ephraim the Syrian ’ came once to meet 
with Abba ‘Bishoy.’ As St. ‘Ephraim’ talked in the Syrian tongue, while St. 
‘Bishoy’ talked in the Cop tic tongue; the later sought from God to give them 
both the ability to understand each other without the need for an interpreter, 
and God granted them that, and they managed to spend a tremendous spiritual 
time together. St. ‘Ephraim’ learned from St. ‘Bishoy’ about the monast ic 
experiences of the Egyptian fathers, particularly of St. ‘Macarius the Great.’  
After a week, St. ‘Ephraim’ left. Then, a brother came to seek St. 
‘Ephraim's’ blessing, but when St ‘Bishoy’ told him that he just left, the brother

able to because St. ‘Ephraim’ was carried away by a cloud. It was also said that 
St. ‘Ephraim’ has left behind his stick, in front of the cave of St. ‘Bishoy.’ 
Emperor Constantine visited Him: 
St. ‘John the Short’ once went to visit his friend St. ‘Bishoy,’ and while he 
was still outside his cell, he heard him talking to someone inside. Knocking on 
the door and entering, he found no one with the saint. Asking him with whom 
he was talking, he answered: “Emperor Constantine came to visit me and told 
me: ‘I wish I have abandoned my kingdom and became a monk; for I did not

The second interpretation: In St. Augustine’s1224 view, the war here is a spiritual war, 
rather than a physical one. The antichrist and his supporters Gog and Magog will use all 
methods of cruelty, violence, and deception to kill th e saints as they attempt to force them 
to stray from their faith.  However, God will support the two faithful witnesses Elijah and 
Enoch with the heavenly fire of the Holy Spirit that burns error, casts out fear, and sustains 
faith. By this fire the faithful will stand fast during the days of the two witnesses, and even 
more so after their martyrdom and the killing of the antichrist, and the Holy Spirit will 
rebuke many of those who followed the antichrist and resisted the Church that they might  
repent and turn from their evil. As for the devil, his end will be with the beast and the false 
prophet, when the wicked are cast into the lake burning with fire. 
1379. What is the millennial kingdom? And what is its true meaning? 
The Book of Revelation tells us that our Lord Jesus will rule on earth for a thousand 
years (Rev. 20:1 –15). During this period, Satan, who had previously entered into a battle 
against the Church, would be bound; and he, his angels, and his followers will be defeated 
in the Battle of Arm ageddon. Some have fallen into erroneous interpretations here because 
they failed to distinguish between the symbolic material contained  in the Book of 
Revelation and the literal, material interpretation of that material. Origen,1225 St. Dionysius 
of Alexand ria,1226 Methodius of Olympia ,1227 St. Basil of Caesarea ,1228 St. Gregory 
Nazianzus,1229 St. Epiphanius of Salamis ,1230 St. Jerome ,1231 and St. Augustine1232 all 
resisted this incorrect thought. 
This literal interpretation is adopted by  the Jehovah’s Witnesses, who believe that 
Christ will reign materially for a thousand years and establish an earthly kingdom. They  
also reject the doctrines of the Holy Trinity, the sacraments of the Church , and the 
veneration of saints. 
We need to understand that the Book of Revelation hides divine mysteries behind the 
veil of symbols. This leads us to the following conclusions: 
First: It is clear that the period of a thousand years is symbolic. St. Peter says, “But, 
beloved, do not forget this one thing, that with th e Lord one day is as a thousand years, and 
a thousand years as one day” (2 Pet. 3:8). The biblical millennium refers to the victory of 
the Church and the fulfilment of the message of the Gospel throughout the whole world.  It

His Papacy (1862-1870): 
After the repose of the great reformer the 110th pope ‘Cyril IV’ (1853-1862), 
the papal throne remained vacant for about 6 months, after which the bishops 
and the archons unanimously decided to choose the Hegumen ‘Michael Ăbdel 
Sayyed,’ the Abbot of the monastery of Abba ‘Macarius’ to sit on the throne. 
He was ordained on the 15th of June 1862, by the name of Pope ‘Demetrius II.’ 
After his ordination, he went accompanied by the State men and paid a visit 
to khedive ‘Saåiid Pasha,’ the Ottoman ruler of Egypt and Sudan. In their first 
encounter, the khedive gently told him: “Do not do like what your predecessor 
did. Just tell me about anything you would need, and I shall do it for you.”

The pope cried out to God to enlighten his mind. Afterward, the Virgin St. 
Mary appeared to him and gave him some water to drink, and behold his mind 
became ready for learning. The next day, he humbly began to make his teacher 
sit on his chair, and he sat at the feet of his teacher, who happened to be the 
church’s Cantor. 
Later on, the pope studied very intensely on the hands of the Scholars of the 
School of Alexandria, and he managed to acquire tremendous knowledge in 
various fields in a short time. Also, Pope ‘Demetrius’ was able to develop the 
rules for a Church calendar system using what became known as “The Apokty 
Calendar,” to determine the date of the feast of the resurrection. Nowadays, 
this system is still followed in the Eastern Churches. 
Before the development of this system, Christians used to fast the ‘Holy 
Forty Days, ’ directly after the feast of the Epiphany (Christ ’s Baptism),  
imitating the Lord Jesus, who fasted directly after his baptism. Then, they 
would fast the ‘Passion Week’ separately during the Jewish Passover week and 
would celebrate the Christian Passover on the Sunday following the Jew ish 
Passover. Few Christians used to celebrate the Christian Passover on the 14 th 
of Nissan (April) with the Jewish Passover, ignoring that the Christian 
Resurrection Passover took place after the Mosaic Passover.  
For that reason, Pope ‘Demetrius’ made enough effort to assign fixed dates 
for the Christian fasts and feasts, and he tied the ‘Holy Forty Days’ with the 
‘Passion Week.’ Then, he wrote about his new system to ‘Agabianus’ Bishop 
of Jerusalem, ‘Maximus’ Bishop of Antioch, the Patriarch of Rome, and others; 
who decided to follow it until this very day; except for the Church of Rome 
which, since the 16th century was following the ‘Gregorian Calendar.’ 
The popes of the Coptic Church are credited for establishing the proper date 
for the Christian Passov er, and they kept on sending Passover messages all 
over the world to make all Christians rejoice by celebrating that feast on the 
same day. 
His Piety: 
Because of his piety, he was given the spiritual ability to see through those 
people participating in the Holy Communion. He often asked some of them to 
present true repentance before being allowed to have a part in it.

the Roman Emperor ‘Septimius Severus’ (193-211 AD) against the Egyptian 
Christians, declared his persecution in which a significant number of believers

Marcorius (Abu-Seifein) by the name of St. Mark the Apostle, on the 26th of

the days of the Ottoman Sultan Moĥammed III (1595-1603 AD). He also was 
a contemporary of the Sultans Aĥmad I (1603 -1617 AD) and Mustafa I

The new pope started his papacy by visiting his people everywhere in the 
country. He also visited Jerusalem. In his travels, he wanted to strengthen his 
congregation's will and urge them to hold their faith fast. He was using what 
God granted him of vast knowledge, particularly concerning the Church  
doctrines. 
Troubles from Within the Church: 
It was surprising that the troubles that faced this new pope were  from 
within the c hurch. The problem originated when some of the rich Copts 
started to get married to more than one wife . Also, when the pope rebu ked 
them and then excommunicated them for acting against the Christian 
doctrines, they were provoked to anger and incited the Ottoman governor to 
arrest and imprison the pope . Aspiring to replace the pop e on the throne, the 
bishop of Damietta  joined forces with those immoral individuals . However, 
the congregation was united and stood firm, and pressured the governor to 
release their pope.  
Afterward, a holy Council was held, excommunicated those who married 
to more than one  wife, together with the bishop who took their side . It was 
strange that the Muslim governor himself acted against those deviants, drove 
them out of their jobs, and dispersed them everywhere after confiscating their 
wealth. 
Troubles with the Turks: 
The Copts showed their patriotism, when they refused to take part in the 
revolts against the Turkish governor, stirred up in the area from the city o f 
Tanta to the city of Cairo. Yet, when the Turks put those revolts down, they 
did not distinguish between those who were on their side or against them.

The Roman pope succeeded in drawing the king of Ethiopia to his side 
and convinced him to close the Coptic churc hes there and to force those 
baptized by the Copts to be re -baptized, and to re -consecrate their churches . 
However, the people in Ethiopia rebelled against him, with the support of the 
Coptic metropolitan. Civil war flared up, which lasted for six years, with so

Then in less than a couple of years, when pope ‘Peter IV’ reposed, the clergy 
and the congregation solidly decided to choose ‘Damianus’ as their new pope. 
However, because of the obsta cles created by those in control of the 
government at that time, his ordination was delayed for almost three years. 
Then, he sat on the papal throne on the 2nd of Abib 285 AM (26 June 569 AD). 
Keeping the Upright Faith:  
In his papacy, he opposed the heretics, including the followers of ‘Meletius’ 
of ‘Lycopolis’ (Assuit). He wrote several messages to clarify the upright 
Orthodox Dogma and teachings. He expelled the followers of ‘Meletius’ from 
the monasteries when they attempted to corrupt the minds of the monks.  
He also wrote a message responding to ‘Peter’ the Patriarch of Antioch (who 
succeeded Abba ‘Theophanius’), who sent him a fellowship message after his 
ordination. In the beginning, Pope ‘Damianus’ rejoiced to receive that message 
from the patriarch  of Antioch, but on studying its contents, he found that it 
contained a serious theological error concerning the nature of the Holy Trinity. 
That issue implied that there was no need to believe in the Holy Trinity. With 
the intention not to lose his friendship or adversely affect the unity between the 
two churches, Pope ‘Damianos’ wrote to ‘Peter’ the patriarch of Antioch an 
essay, in which he explained the teaching of the Ecumenical Councils and the 
saintly Fathers about the nature of the Holy Trinity, but  as patriarch ‘Peter’ 
persisted on his statements, pope ‘Damianus’ had to write him a very strong -
worded message, then held a council which condemned his heresy and 
excommunicated him. This, of course, caused controversy between the two 
churches, which endured for 20 years, until patriarch ‘Peter’ died. 
Pope ‘Damianos’ gave special attention to writing essays and (Mymers) to 
defend the Orthodox faith. His writings were characterized by the eloquence 
and the inflamed zeal, which drew so many heretics back to  the Orthodox 
Doctrine. 
The Chalcedonian church, backed up by the Byzantine civil authorities, 
confiscated all the Orthodox Church buildings in Alexandria. When their 
patriarch who was imposed on Egypt, died in the year 569 AD, they replaced 
him with another called ‘John.’ ‘John’ was originally an army leader, then they 
ordained him in ‘Constantinople’ before getting sent to Egypt to confiscate the 
revenues of the Orthodox churches. However, ‘John’ is a lover of peace and 
tranquility, he refrained from using force to commit the Copts to forsake their 
doctrines, but he left it entirely up to their choosing. As Pope ‘Damianos’ kept 
himself away in his cell in the Natron Valley, the intruding patriarch did not 
enter with him into any open controversy. 
In genera l, through all his reign, Pope ‘Damianos’ kept on teaching his 
people and held them fast to the Orthodox faith, and after a life abounding in

was a master in Ecclesiastical knowledge, and authored so many books on the 
rites and teachings of the church, for the benefit of his contemporaries. 
The Ordination of a Cyprian Bishop: 
Concerning the Ecumenical role of the Coptic church, Pope John XIII wrote 
messages to the bishops of Cyprus, the Pentapolis and Ethiopia; and ordained 
a Cyprian bishop – Abba Michael of Cyprus – a Coptic metropolitan on the 
islands of Cyprus and Rhode. The Coptic influence is still evident in the 
adornments and icons of the churches and the palaces there up to this day. One 
of our churches is still there by the name of St. Anthony; and a monastery 
which carries the name of Abba Macarius. The Copts were, officially, a sect of 
the population, as shown by the general census done by t he Ottoman Turks 
after they took over the island for imposing their taxes. 
The Pentapolis Dioceses: 
Christianity in Libya came to an end in the papacy of Abba John VI (1189-
1216), during the days of Salaĥ al -Din al-Ayyubi (1138-1193); after having 
been one of the most important centers of the Alexandrian throne. Yet there 
was still a Coptic bishop in the days of Pope John XIII, until the entrance of 
the Ottomans into North Africa in the 2 nd decade of the 16 th century AD, by 
the name of Curiacus, who, then f orsook his diocese and returned to Egypt, 
went to the monastery of the Virgin St. Mary, known as ‘The Syrian 
Monastery,’ where he spent the rest of his days. Among the dioceses of 
Pentapolis was Barqua, Bernika, Western Tripoli, Maraqia in Libya and Tunis, 
Derna, Quabes and Cyrenia in Tunis. 
A Portuguese Bishop on Ethiopia: 
As it was difficult for the Coptic pope to send a Coptic metropolitan to his 
children in Ethiopia due to the hostilities between the Mamluk Sultans in Egypt 
and the kings of Ethiopia; ki ng David II of Ethiopia sought from Portugal to 
send a Roman bishop there. A Portuguese named Poaz Parmodaz was sent, 
who was amazingly given the title Patriarch of Alexandria despite that was an 
obvious challenge to the brotherly rules and the decrees of the Ecumenical 
councils, the Nicene council in particular. 
Arabian Tribes Attack Abba Paul and Abba Anthony Monasteries:

Egypt lived in peace with their Muslim brethren, during the rule of Abu Saåid 
Qansuh al-Ghoury (1498-1500), as shown in celebrating the Nile Flood, and

Soon after, the governor resumed his violence and cruelty towards the 
saints. He ordered the hanging of ‘Cosman’ and ‘Damien’ on two crosses, then 
to stone them. However, the thrown stones, before touching their bodies, 
reversed their course and headed towards those who were throwing them. As 
for their brothers, they were chained, cast betw een the two crosses, and were 
being shot with arrows from a distance, but here too, the arrows were returned 
towards those who shot them. That miracle caused all guards to flee. Then, the 
governor ordered them unchained and cast all of them into a fiery fu rnace for 
three days and three nights. God saved them from the fire. Then, the governor 
put them on hot iron beds; but the Lord brought them up unharmed. 
When the governor got tired of torturing them, he sent them to the emperor 
to deal with them. When the mother ‘Theodata’ strengthened her children and 
rebuked the emperor on his cruelty and his worshipping of the idols, he ordered 
cutting her head by the sword, and she received the crown of martyrdom. Her 
body remained cast on the ground, and nobody dared to bury it. St. ‘Damien’ 
cried out to those present: “O you inhabitants of this city; is none of you have 
mercy to cover and bury the body of this old woman? ” ‘Boctor,’ the son of 
‘Romanos,’ came forward, took the body, shrouded it, and buried it.  
When the emperor got to know what ‘Boctor’ has done, he ordered exiling 
him to Egypt, where he eventually received the crown of martyrdom. The next 
day, he ordered cutting the heads of ‘Cosman,’ ‘Damien,’ and their brothers, 
all of whom received the crowns of Life in the Kingdom of Heavens. 
When the era of persecution came to an end, several churches were built in 
their names, where the Lord performed so many signs and wonders. 
These saints are celebrated by the Church of the West on the 7 th of 
September and the 4 th Thursday of the Great Lent and by the Coptic Church 
on the 22nd of Hator and the 22nd of Paona every year.

‘Zaåfaran,’ and the ‘Saysaban valley’ (northeast of Gharbiah governorate) in 
the Nile delta. When St. ‘Demiana’ reached the first year of age, she was

‘Damasus’ probably wrote the first three parts of the ‘Decretum 
Gelasianum’ on the Holy Spirit, and the canonization of the Holy Bible and 
the Roman See as the source of authority. The work as a whole is a product of 
Southern France at the end of the 5th century, and the beginning of the 6th. 
In his letter 22:22, St. ‘Jerome’ refers to ‘Damasus’ works on virginity,

DAMIAN, ST. 
(The martyr) 
This saint was martyred in Antioch. He endured vicious tortures unt il he 
delivered his soul into the Lord’s hand. 
[The Synaxarion: 23 Mesra] 
 
DAMIANOS, The 35th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA 
He was a prominent scholar in civil and religious matters. At a young age, 
he went to the monastery of St. ‘John the Short ’ and became a monk o n the 
hand of one of the saintly Fathers in ‘Scetis.’ There, he remained to strive for 
16 years, during which he was ordained as a deacon. ‘Damianos’ did absorb 
well the teachings of his spiritual Fathers and continued to strive day and night 
to get more k nowledge. He became very able in words and deeds and was 
clothed with the Divine grace. 
In the Enaton Monastery: 
When the 34th pope ‘Peter IV’ (567-569 AD) sat on St. Mark ’s throne, he 
chose ‘Damianus’ to be his secretary, and he moved him to the monastery  
known by the name ‘Pateron (means "the Fathers"),’ west of Alexandria. The 
pope wanted him to participate in carrying the burden of pastoral care, and he 
had to abandon the life of seclusion to be near his pope. In the ‘Patron,’ 
‘Damianos’ pursued an excellent course of life, and everyone loved him.
