153 
One God by highlighting the Trinity. This does not actually contradict divine oneness but 
supports it by revealing some of the mysteries of the One God and His relationship with 
humanity. Without Trinitarian faith, divine oneness would remain obscure. Trinitarian faith 
is a fundamental path to our salvation, touching our practical lives, our relationship with God, 
and our eternal future. Such faith causes no dissonance in a mind that is spiritual, but rather 
fulfills it and exalts it to meditate on divine mysteries with joy. 
St. Gregory of Nazianzus 360 understands the Old Testament as proclaiming the Father 
openly, but the Son in a more obscure manner. Then, the New Testament proclaims the Son 
clearly, and suggests the divinity of the Holy Spirit. Thus, the Trinity was revealed gradually, 
lest people become like those who are weighed down by eating more food than they can 
stomach, or like those who gaze upon the sun with eyes too weak to bear its light; lest they 
therefore lose even that wh ich was within their grasp. But as David says, gradually they 
ascend, progress, and grow from glory to glory (Ps. 84:7; 2 Cor. 3:18), as the light of the 
Trinity shines on those who are enlightened. 
180. Does the Holy Bible explicitly teach the doctrine of the Trinity? 
The Holy Trinity is evident at the baptism of our Lord Jesus (John 1:27–33), which is the 
template for our own baptism in the name of the three Hypostases according to St. Matthew 
(Matt. 28:19). We also find this doctrine in St. Paul’s blessing in  2 Cor. 13:14. The three 
Hypostases are also mentioned in John 14:16; Eph. 2:18; and 1 Pet. 1:21–22. 
The work and titles of both our Lord Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit in the Holy Bible 
attest to their divinity. 
From the Old Testament shines forth the threefold sanctification of “Holy, Holy, Holy,” 
found in the vision of Isaiah (6:3); and its connection to the phrase “who will go for Us?” 
(6:8). The three Hypostases are also evident in the Bible’s frequent use of the plural form of 
the name “Elohim” (plural) for God, sometimes even connecting it to God’s oneness: “Hear, 
O Israel: The Lord ( Jehovah) our God ( Elohim; plural), the Lord ( Jehovah) is one” (Deut. 
6:4). It is also used in certain phrases such as “And God ( Elohim; plural) said ‘Let Us make 
man in  Our image’” (Gen. 1:26), and again “Let Us go down and there confuse their 
language, that they may not understand one another’s speech” (Gen. 11:7). 
The Old Testament prepared the world to believe in the Holy Trinity, but it did not 
expressly reveal  the T rinity since most of the gentiles of the time were deeply mired in 
polytheism (the belief in many gods). The Israelites were drawn towards idolatry, and at 
times, worshipped the pagan gods and fell into their abominations, even after their victory 
over these same gentiles. 
 
360 St. Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 31.25–26 (NPNF II/7:325–326; PG 36:161).

records.question: eucharist
records.answer:
The Eucharist in the Coptic Orthodox Church is the sacrament of communion that unites the faithful with the Savior by partaking of His Body and Blood, which He gave up for us. This sanctifies the whole being, including the body, and blesses it with eternal glory [1].

The Eucharist is considered a sacrifice. The Church learned about sacrifice from the apostles, with St. Paul referring to an altar and the offering of the Eucharist as a sacrifice fulfilling Old Testament symbols (Hebrews 13:10; 10). Early Christian writings such as the Didache (around 100 A.D.) and the teachings of Church Fathers like St. Ignatius, St. Justin, St. Irenaeus, St. Cyril of Jerusalem, St. Cyprian, and St. Augustine confirm the Eucharist as a pure sacrifice [1]. The Church uses Greek terms θυσία (thysia; sacrifice) and προσφορά (prosphora; offering) for the Eucharist, and the altar is sometimes called τράπεζα (trapeza; table), emphasizing the sacrificial act as a loving self-offering of Christ rather than a senseless slaughter [1].

The Eucharist is the pinnacle of Christian worship because the believer spiritually participates in Christ’s sacrifice at Golgotha, partaking actively of His body and blood offered for them. The Holy Spirit offers the crucified and risen Lord’s body and blood so that believers may abide in Christ’s righteousness and be members of His body. Christ’s words, “My flesh is food indeed, and My blood is drink indeed” (John 6:55–57), affirm this union [2].

St. John Chrysostom describes the Eucharist as the salvation and beautification of the soul, a fountain of light and truth, and the means by which believers stand with angels, clothed in Christ’s kingly robe and the armor of the Spirit [4]. The Eucharist is the “medicine of immortality,” and believers are encouraged to partake frequently, even daily, as St. Basil teaches that daily Communion is excellent and advantageous [4][7].

The Eucharist is truly the Body and Blood of Christ. St. Jacob of Sarug, St. Cyril of Jerusalem, Origen, and St. Cyril the Great affirm that the bread and wine are truly transformed into Christ’s flesh and blood, and that faith is necessary to receive this mystery worthily [3].

Preparation for receiving the Eucharist involves examining one’s conscience, repentance, and sincere prayer. The Apostle Paul warns against receiving unworthily (1 Cor. 11:27–29) [7]. The believer should approach the Eucharist with reverence, realizing they are in heaven before God’s throne, contemplating the Trinity, and feeling united with Christ during the Divine Liturgy [5].

Partaking of the Eucharist results in abiding in Christ, uniting with Him, and sharing eternal life, as Christ promises in John 6:53–56 [5]. The Church continues to pray the Divine Liturgy and celebrate the Eucharist until the second coming of Christ, proclaiming His death and awaiting His glory [5][6].

The Eucharistic table is linked to the teaching table, inviting believers to delight in the teaching and share the banquet with others, caring for the poor and inviting all to the feast [6].

In summary, the Eucharist in the Coptic Orthodox Church is a true sacrifice and the real Body and Blood of Christ, a mystery of union with the Savior, a source of spiritual life and growth, and the central act of Christian worship and anticipation of Christ’s return [1][2][3][4][5][6][7][8].

The sources do not describe the Eucharist in other churches.

764. What is the mystery of communion in the eucharist? 
It is the mystery of uniting us the faithful with the Savior by partaking of His Body and 
Blood which He gave up for us. Thus, our whole being, including our bodies, is sanctified 
and is blessed by His eternal glory.  
765. Is the eucharist a sacrifice?  
First: The Church was introduced to the idea of sacrifice at the time of the apostles, for 
St. Paul says, “We have an altar from which those who serve the tabernacle have no right to 
eat” (Heb. 13:10). In his epistle to the Hebrews (Chapter 10), he speaks of the Old Testament 
sacrifices as symbols fulfilled in Christ’s redemption and in the eucharist. He also speaks of 
the eucharist as an offering when he compares the holy table of God to that of demons (1 
Cor. 10:20–21). 
Second: Around the year 100 A. D., the author of the Didache mentions the eucharist as 
a pure sacrifice. 1471 This was further confirmed by Fathers of the Church 1472 such as St. 
Ignatius, St. Justin, St. Irenaeus, St. Cyril of Jerusalem, St. Cyprian, and St. Augustine.  
Third: The Church uses two Greek words to refer to the eucharist: θυσία (thysia; 
sacrifice), and προσφορά (prosphora; offering). When talking about the eucharist, St. 
Ignatius refers to the Church assembly as the eucharistic θυσιαστήριον (thysiastirion; place 
of sacrifice or altar.1473 St. Clement of Rome says that the work of the bishop is the offering

refer to the altar. This term does not contradict the fact that the eucharist is a sacrifice, but it 
gives the sacrificial act of the eucharist a new meaning. In the New Testament, senseless 
animals were unwillingly slaughtered by the people on the altar for a sacrifice. However, on 
our altars, the Sacrifice offers Himself out of His immense love, to grant us life. He is not

believer then remembers the death and resurrection of His  life-giving Groom, not just in 
words and thoughts but by actively partaking of His body and blood that are offered for him; 
the secret of his life and his continuous spiritual growth. 
In the sacrament of the eucharist, the Holy Spirit offers us the crucified body of the Lord 
who rose from the dead, and His precious blood, to be in Him and He in us. Through Him, 
we are worthy to enter before His divine throne, abiding in Christ’s righteousness, as 
members of His body. Christ the Lord says, “For My fle sh is food indeed, and My blood is 
drink indeed. He who eats My flesh and drinks My blood abides in Me, and I in him … so he 
who feeds on Me will live because of Me” (John 6:55 –57). The Church hides in this Holy 
Sacrifice, and therefore bears Christ’s holiness and righteousness.

alone. His Body and His Blood He has set forth at the feast before them that sit at table, that 
they may eat of Him, and live with Him without end. Meat and drink is our Lord at His 
marriage supper: blessed is He who has given us His Body and  Blood, that in Him we may 
delight.”1510 
778. Is the eucharist, true Body and true Blood?  
St. Jacob of Sarug says, “The chosen apostles were concerned to believe the Son, not to 
argue or question Him like the daring ones. The bread He broke and called His flesh,  they 
knew it as flesh and they truly believed that His blood was being poured out.”  
St. Cyril of Jerusalem  says, “He once in Cana of Galilee, turned the water into wine, 
akin to blood, and is it incredible that He should have turned wine into blood? W hen called 
to a bodily marriage, He miraculously wrought that wonderful work; and on the children of 
the bride-chamber (Matt. 9:15), shall He not much rather be acknowledged to have bestowed 
the fruition of His Body and Blood? ”1511 And, “Since then He Himself declared and said of 
the Bread, This is My Body, who shall dare to doubt any longer? And since He has Himself 
affirmed and said, This is My Blood, who shall ever hesitate, saying, that it is not His blood? 
… Wherefore with full assurance let us partake as of the Body and Blood of Christ.”1512 
Origen says, “for ‘he who doubts is condemned if he eats, because he does not eat not 
from faith’ (Rom. 14:23), and as nothing is pure to him who is defiled and unbelieving, not 
in itself, but because of his defilement and unbelief.”1513  
St. Cyril the Great says, “For they knew not the beauty of the Mystery, and that fairest 
economy devised for it. Besides this, they full surely reasoned thus with themselves, How 
can the human body implant in us everlasting life, what can a thing of like nature with 
ourselves avail to immortality? Christ therefore understanding their thoughts (for all things 
are naked and, bared to His eyes), heals them again, leading them by the hand manifoldly to 
the understanding of those things of which they were yet ignorant … For if you suppose that 
My Flesh cannot put life into you, how can It ascend into heaven like a bird? … For this too 
is equally impossible for flesh. But if it ascends contrary to nature, what is to hinder it from 
quickening also, even though its nature be not to qu icken, of its own nature? For He Who 
made That heavenly which is from earth, will render it Lifegiving also.”1514

“with this gift do we adorn ourselves, with this we are beautified .”1483 He also says, “ This 
blood is the salvation of our souls, by this the soul is washed, by this is beautiful, by this is 
inflamed.”1484 
Then he says, “For this Table is the sinews of our soul, the bond of our mind, the 
foundation of our confidence, our hope, our salvation, our light, our life … when you see It 
set before you, sa y to yourself, ‘Because of this Body am I no longer earth and ashes, no 
longer a prisoner, but free: because of this I hope for heaven, and to receive the good things 
therein, immortal life, the portion of angels, converse with Christ.’”1485 
“This fountain is a fountain of light, spouting forth rays of truth. By it stand the Powers 
on high looking upon the beauty of its streams … They who share this blood stand with 
Angels and Archangels and the Powers that are above, clothed in Christ’s own kingly robe, 
and having the armor of the Spirit. Nay, I have not as yet said any great thing: they are clothed 
with the King Himself.”1486 
767. Is it possible to partake of the eucharist every week? 
There are two main reasons that some people offer for excusing themselves from 
receiving the eucharist every week. The first reason is feeling unprepared; while the truth is 
that to be prepared for communion is simply to feel unworthy, while sincerely praying for 
the work of God’s grace through repentance and prayer. The  second reason is when people 
lose the meaning of the eucharist because they pray the Divine Liturgy merely as a routine. 
The eucharist is the medicine of immortality. He who feels the need for this medicine should 
not stop partaking of the eucharist, or praying, or studying the Holy Bible, or striving to keep 
the divine commandments. Doing these things prevents us from practicing the rituals in a 
literal manner that is void of spirit, and instead fills the heart with love for God and love for 
others.  
768. Is it permissible for a person to receive the body and blood of our Lord every day? 
St. Basil talks about praying the Divine Liturgy daily: “Now, to receive Communion 
daily, thus to partake of the holy Body and Blood of Christ, is an excellent and advantageous 
practice; for Christ Himself says clearly: ‘He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has life 
everlasting’ (John 6:54). Who doubts that to share continually in the life is nothing else than 
to have a manifold life? We ourselves, of course, receive Communion four times a week, on

(1 Cor. 11:27–29). 
772. What results from partaking of the body and blood of the Lord? 
By receiving the body and blood of the Lord, the believer abides in Christ, unites with 
Him, and shares in the eternal life. Christ says, “Most assuredly, I say to you, unless you eat 
the flesh of the Son of Man and drink His blood, you have no life in you. Whoever eats My 
flesh and drinks My blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up at the last day. For My 
flesh is food indeed, and My blood is drink indeed. He who eats My flesh and drinks My 
blood abides in Me, and I am in him” (John 6:53–56). 
773. How do we feel when we participate in the Divine Liturgy? 
a. We should ask the Lord to grant us His fear, to realize that we are in heaven before 
the majesty of the throne of God.  
b. During the church readings, we should count ourselves among the multitudes and that 
Christ Himself (at that moment) talks to us.  
c. In the offering of the Lamb, we must contemplate the Trinity. The Father sent His 
Son to us; the Son is pleased to offer Himself as a sacrifice for our salvation; and the 
Holy Spirit leads us towards Jesus Christ and lift us up to heaven.  
d. In the institution narrative, we should consider ourselves in the upper room where 
Christ blessed and sanctified, granting us His body and blood.  
e. During communion, we should feel that Christ Himself is extending His hands to 
offer us His body and blood.  
f. After receiving the eucharist, we should consider ourselves as standing before the 
throne of God, praising and glorifying Him with the heavenly hosts.   
g. Upon leaving the church, we should occupy ourselves with talking to the Savior who 
raises us with Him, desiring to be one with Him as Mary Magdalene desired when 
He spoke to her and revealed that He was not the gardener as she thought, but the 
Lord Himself.  
774. Will the Church continue to pray Divine Liturgy until the second coming? 
The Apostle says, “For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the 
Lord’s death till He comes” (1 Cor. 11:26). By saying, “you proclaim the Lord’s death till 
He comes,’ the Apostle reveals the eschatological aspect of the life of the Church. The main 
role of the Church is to be united with Christ the Lord in His death, and in the continuous 
waiting for His second coming, so that she may partake in His glory and see Him face to

carry us to the bosom of His Father, wherein we partake of His glory and fulfill the pleasure 
of the Father, Son, and the Holy Spirit.  
St. Ambrose says, “So, as often as you receive, what does the Apostle say to yo u? As 
often as, we receive, we proclaim the death of the Lord (cf. 1 Cor. 11:26). If death, we 
proclaim the remission of sins. If, as often as blood is shed, it is shed for the remission of 
sins, I ought always to accept Him, that He may always dismiss my sins (cf. Matt. 26.28). I, 
who always sin, should always have a remedy.”1491  
775. What is the relationship between the table of the eucharist and the table of 
teaching? 
In his ninety-fifth homily on the reception of the holy mysteries, St. Jacob of Sarug links 
the eucharistic table with the teaching table. He says, “Come, you discerning, let us delight 
today in the teaching, the taste whereof is sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. Come and 
be filled with the table that is full of life, for its foods are unblemished for those who deserve 
them.” 
776. What is the role of this banquet in the lives of those who partake of it? 
First: Openness towards others. As the believer enjoys this banquet, he in turn desires 
to invite others to it. St. Jacob of Sarug says, “The King’s bride went out on the paths of the 
world to gather all peoples in order to delight them … She stood in the marketplaces and the 
corners of the earth to invite the assemblies and the crowds to the banquet.”1492  
He also says, “Who is capable of sacrificing the Son before His Father, if He had not 
offered Himself from before His sufferings? Our Lord is the High Priest and the perfect 
sacrifice and therefore, He offered  Himself before His Father … He died, but while being 
dead, He was alive. He is the Priest and the Sacrifice. Comprehending this mystery is beyond 
debate. He taught them to drink from the Cup of His blood and to make the nations, countries 
and the world dr ink from it … He sealed with His blood the new covenant, which He 
instituted for the remission of sins for the whole world.”1493 
Second: Caring for the poor. St. John Chrysostom says, “These words let us also listen 
to, all of us, as many as in this place approach with the poor to this holy Table, but when we

He also says, “The daily Communion of the Body and Blood of Christ is great and 
beneficial because the Lord declares: ‘Unless you eat of the flesh of the Son of Man and drink 
His blood, you have no life in you’ (John 6:53).”1488  
St. Augustine says, “Throughout these days the teachers feed you. Christ daily feeds you, 
That His Table is ever ordered before you. What is the reason, O Hearers, that you see the 
Table, and come not to the Banquet?”1489  
769. Why do we believe in the one Sacrifice that is offered on multiple altars? 
There are no multiple sacrifices like the High Priest used to offer in the past, for we offer 
the same sacrifice every day, or in other words we fulfill the remembrance of the sacrifice 
(ἀνάμνησις, anamnesis). We believe in one altar, despite its multiplicity, for they are all 
together the one holy tomb of the one body of Christ. St. John Chrysostom says, “Do we 
not offer every day? We offer indeed, but making a remembrance of His death, and this 
[remembrance] is one and not many … For we always offer the same, not one sheep now and 
tomorrow another, but always the same thing: so that the sacrifice is one … Christ is one 
everywhere, being complete here and complete there also, one Body … so also [He is] one 
sacrifice … It is not a nother sacrifice, as the High Priest, but we offer always the same, or 
rather we perform a remembrance of a Sacrifice.”1490 
770. Why do we mix the wine with water in the chalice? 
When the Lord was pierced in His side, blood and water came out. St. Augustine believes 
that mixing the Eucharistic blood with water indicates that water is a symbol of humanity 
which partakes in Christ’s suffering. 
771. How can we prepare ourselves to receive the body and blood of the Lord? 
The believer should examine his conscience before God and purify it through repentance. 
The Apostle says, “Therefore whoever eats this bread or drinks this cup of the Lord in an 
unworthy manner will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a man examine 
himself, and so let him eat of the bread a nd drink of the cup. For he who eats and drinks in

Thirteen: The declaration of Himself.  St. Augustine  says, “Ah yes, brothers and 
sisters, but where did the Lord wish to be recognized? In the breaking  of bread. We’re all 
right, nothing to worry about; we break bread, and we recognize the Lord. It was for our

Theophylact of Bulgaria says, “The eyes of those who receive the holy bread are opened 
to know Christ, for within the Body of the Lord is His great incomprehensible power.” 
Fourteenth: Acknowledging the mystery of the Christian Passover. St. Melito of 
Sardis says, “But the mystery of the Lord … through the body which was able to suffer … 
For, he himself led as a lamb and slain as a sheep, he ransomed us from the world’s service 
as from the land of Egypt, and freed us from the devil’s slavery as from the hand of Pharaoh; 
and he marked our souls with his own Spirit and the members of our body with his own 
blood.”1509 
The mystery of the Passover has been completed in the body of the Lord. For He who 
was led away as a lamb, and who was sacrificed as a sheep, by  himself delivered us from 
servitude to the world as from the land of Egypt, and released us from bondage to the devil 
as from the hand of Pharaoh, and sealed our souls by his own spirit and the members of our 
bodies by his own blood. 
Fifteenth: Continuous spiritual growth. St. Cyril the Great says, “The acquisition of 
a spiritual life through the Eucharist requires regular participation in the sacrament. The 
believer retains his spiritual life and grows in the Spirit as long as he is attached to Christ,

blood of Christ. But irregular participation in the Eucharist deprives the believer of eternal

records.question: confession
records.answer:
Confession in the Coptic Orthodox Church is a vital spiritual practice aimed at encountering God, the Physician of our souls. It involves acknowledging one's sins and weaknesses both privately before God and publicly before a priest, who is entrusted with the stewardship of the Mysteries of God. This practice is necessary because it helps the believer feel their need for God's mercy and love, preventing self-righteousness even over seemingly minor sins. True believers do not differentiate between big and small sins but seek to be unblemished stewards of heaven [1][2].

Christ gave His disciples the authority to forgive sins after His resurrection, emphasizing the continual need for repentance and confession in the world. Believers are called to be merciful and forgiving to others so that they may receive mercy from God. Repentance and confession are the beginnings of a transformation in life, both inwardly and outwardly, acknowledging God's love and grace that can transform the heart from corruption to incorruption [2].

Confession is also linked to baptism, where the confession of faith is a cornerstone of the Church and an entry into a divine covenant with God. Candidates publicly confess their faith in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, renouncing evil and pledging to persist in love for the Divine nature [3][7].

The Church, as the "mother of believers," shares in grief over sinners and intercedes for their repentance. The Church has the authority to forgive sins as granted by Christ, and confession before the Church is part of the believer's journey toward holiness and salvation [8].

The goal of confession is not only forgiveness but also correction and spiritual healing. Saints like St. Basil the Great and St. John Chrysostom emphasize the importance of self-accusation and repentance before being accused by others, leading to true cleansing and restoration [1][2][5].

In summary, confession in the Coptic Orthodox Church is a sacramental and spiritual practice involving:
- Private repentance before God and public confession before a priest [1][2].
- Receiving forgiveness through the Church's authority given by Christ [2][8].
- A transformation of life and heart through God's grace [2].
- A covenantal act linked with baptism and faith confession [3][7].
- A path to healing, mercy, and spiritual maturity [1][4][5].

743. Is it necessary to repent before God in our private rooms, and then again in the 
presence of the Father of Confession? 
The goal of confessing our sins is to encounter God, the Physician of our souls. Whoever 
does not feel his weakness or sins, will never feel the need for the heave nly Physician and 
will not therefore experience God’s love. Many times, we consider ourselves righteous, since 
we do not commit any dangerous sins that hurt others. A true believer, however, does not 
differentiate between big sins and trivial sins, since what truly concerns him is to be the icon 
of Christ, the Holy One’s ambassador, and an unblemished steward of heaven.  
St. Basil the Great  says, “it seems necessary that sins be confessed to those entrusted 
with the stewardship of the Mysteries of God (cf. 1 Cor. 4:1). For thus also those who repented 
of old are found to have confessed their sins before the saints. For it is written in the gospel 
that they confessed their sins to John the Baptist (cf. Matt. 3:6; Mark 1:5) and in the Acts of 
the Apostles, to the apostles, by whom they were also baptized (cf. Acts 2:37).”1444 
He also says, “On the other hand, where sin is concerned, be your own accuser (Prov. 
18:17), and do not wait for others to make the accusation. Thus, you will be like a just man 
who accuses himself in the first speech made in court, or like Job who was not deterred by 
the crowd of people in the city from declaring his personal guilt before all (Job 31:34).”1445 
744. Why does God the Lover of humanity use different ways of chastisement?  
God reveals His love and providence not only when He forgives, but also when He 
disciplines. When He chastises like a Father, He elevates us from pampered infancy to 
maturity. Without discipline, we may not feel the seriousness of sin, nor struggle to live a life 
of holiness. Therefore, we would lose our victory and heavenly crown.  
St. Basil the Great says, “We should learn, then, that it is because we have turned away 
from the Lord and disregarded His ways that God has inflicted these wounds upon us. He 
does not seek to destroy us, but rather endeavors to turn us back to the right way, just as good 
parents who care for their children are stern and rebuke them when they do wrong, not

729. What was Christ’s commandment to His disciples when He appeared to them after 
His resurrection?  
He said to them, “‘As the Father has sent Me, I also send you.’ And when He had said 
this, He breathed on them, and said to them, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins 
of any, they are forgiven them; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained.’” (John 20:21–
23). He gave them this authority to show them that the world always needs repentance and 
confession so that the believers may never cease to confess the Lord’s blessings as wel l as 
the fact that they are sinners and hence offer repentance every time they pray the Lord’s 
prayer, “Forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us.”  Therefore, 
Christ who is risen from the dead, calls them to be merciful with th e people that the Lord 
may be merciful with them as well.  
730. What are the important obligations of the believer who repents?  
First: He or she thanks God for His blessings, His mercy, and His salvation, so that he 
may have the boldness to seek forgiveness.  
Second: To admit that he is a sinner and unable to enjoy the holy life without God’s 
mercy and free grace.  
Third: To be merciful to those who sin against him and to forgive them, so that the Savior 
may open for him the way of salvation.  
Fourth: The believer’s focus on heaven, his anticipation of the eternal wedding and his 
love for others, elevates all his inner being as on the wi ngs of the Holy Spirit so that the 
person may know the heavenly Bridegroom, who prepares for him eternal glory. He also 
acknowledges his weaknesses, and the grace of God that is capable of transforming the heart 
from corruption to incorruption and from an earthly heart to a new heaven, and from humans 
to angels.  
Repentance to God and confession before Him in our private rooms and in the presence 
of a priest are the beginning of a change in one’s way of life, both at the inner level as well 
as the external behavior. It is a transformation in which we acknowledge the richness of 
God’s love, and hence offer the sacrifice of thanksgiving, in which we acknowledge our 
weaknesses and wickedness, confident in His salvific work and His ability to raise use from 
corruption to an angelic life that is acceptable to the Father . This is how are continuously 
cleansed in the spirit of hope. “If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you 
retain the sins of any, they are retained” (John 20:23).  
St. John Chrysostom says, “Repentance is the evangelical path through which the soul 
passes to the kingdom ,” and, “Therefore, beloved, when you commit sin, do not wait for 
another man to accuse you but, before you are accused and indicted, you yourself condemn 
what you have done. Then, if someone accuses you later on, it is no longer a matter of your

I delivered to you first of all that which I also received: that Christ died for our sins according 
to the Scriptures, and that He was buried, and that He rose again the third day according to 
the Scriptures” (1 Cor. 15:3–4). Pagans knew this, which is why their concern was to oblige 
the faithful to renounce Christ.  
Second: Since baptism is the gate by which one becomes a member of the Church, the 
confession of faith is the cornerstone on which the Church is built and is the reason for her 
existence.  
Third: The confession of faith is an entry into a divine covenant or like a signed contract 
with God and is kept in a book in heaven. St. Theodore of Mopsuestia  says of this: “We 
establish agreements and covenants with our Lord God by confessing the faith. By the 
mediation of the priest, we are prepared to enter His house, to see Him, to know Him and for 
Him to dwell within us that we may be counted among the citizens of that city and are counted 
trustworthy.”1355 Again, he says, “By confessing the faith, you associate yourself with God 
by the bishop and you enter into a covenant in which you declare that you will be persistent 
in seeking the love of the divine nature.”1356  
In the current Coptic rite, the baptized or the sponsor publicly repeats the main aspects 
of the faith after the celebrant priest before baptism. In the early Church, the candidate would 
declare his or her faith from inside the waters of baptism. This was done in the form of 
questions that the priest or bishop would ask and to which the candidate wou ld respond, as 
is mentioned in the Canons of St. Hippolytus.1357 
698. What are the main articles of faith in the baptismal confession of faith? 
The early Church focused on faith in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, as well as 
the confession of the catholic (universal) Church and the remission of sins.  The Canons of 
St. Hippolytus state that candidates for baptism should face the east and say, “I believe and 
kneel before You and before Your greatness, O Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.” Then, they are 
immersed in the water and stand facing the east. Another priest lays his hands on their heads 
and asks them: “Do you believe in God the Father the Pantocrator?” They would then respond 
saying, “I believe” and are immersed for the first time.  
After the first immersion, they are asked: “Do you believe in Jesus Christ, the Son of God 
who was born of the Virgin Mary by the Holy Spirit, who died and rose from the dead on the 
third day, who ascended to the heavens and sat at the right hand of the Father and will come

Minnesota: Liturgical Press, 2003): p. 46.

Minnesota: Liturgical Press, 2003) Canon 19: p. 133.

Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God 
557 
19  
The Sacrament of Repentance & Confession 
728. Why was our Lord Jesus called “a friend of tax collectors and sinners” (Matt. 
11:19)?  
The Word of God was incarnate to heal the souls wounded by sin. He has compassion on 
them for He is the loving physician who opened the gates of Paradise to a thief who was 
counted unworthy of living in the world (Luke 23:34) and accepted a sinful woman who was 
about to be stoned to death (John 8:1–12). He invited Himself into the house of a cold-hearted 
chief publican and a lover of money, even though the multitudes complained against Him 
(Luke 19:5). He knows how sin humiliates humanity and therefore, He is compassionate with 
sinners. He neither reproaches nor rebukes any broken heart, “He will not quarrel nor cry out, 
nor will anyone hear His voice in the streets. A bruised reed He will not break, and smoking 
flax He will not quench” (Matt. 12:19–20).  
He stands and knocks at the doors of our hearts, that we may also be compassionate 
towards Him and offer Him the heart which He purchased with His blood and even if we do 
not offer Him what He actually owns; He never forces Himself in, but stands outside weeping 
as He did when He entered Jerusalem (Luke 19:41). In sweetness, He calls the soul “My 
sister, my love,” and then He encourages her, revealing her inner beauty by saying, “O My 
perfect one” (Song. 5:2). He encourages the souls of the broken despite their defilement and 
evil.  
As much as the Lord’s sermons and parables — in public and in secret — revolved around 
the Kingdom, He emphasized the need for repentance and that we cannot approach Kingdom 
without repentance. And as much as He was tenderhearted and kind to repentant sinners, He 
seemed harsh with the cruel hearts of those who were unwilling to repent. He was generous 
with the sinners, adulterers, and thieves because they were eager to repent, but scolded and 
rebuked the Scribes and Pharisees who insisted in their stubbornness not to repent.  
It is important for us not to despise His love and longsuffering and hence be lax with sin, 
relying on the fact that the Savior is the Lover of humanity and the Forgiver o f sins, as St. 
Paul says, “Or do you despise the riches of His goodness, forbearance, and longsuffering, not 
knowing that the goodness of God leads you to repentance?” (Rom. 2:4). St. Basil the Great 
says, “he who has been chastised for his past sins and h as obtained pardon prepares for 
himself a judgment of wrath more severe than the former judgment if he sin again … ‘See, 
you have been made well. Sin no more, lest a worse thing come upon you’ (John 5:14).”1437 
 
1437 St. Basil of Caesarea, The Morals 11.2 (FOTC 9:87).

passages.text:
Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God 
559 
doing the right thing in confessing, but of your correcting the accusation which he makes … 
Peter certainly sinned gravely in denying Christ. But he was quick to remind him self of his 
sin and, before anyone accused him, he told of his error and wept bitterly (Matt. 26:69 –75; 
Mark 14:66–72). He so effectively washed away his sin of denial that he became the chief of 
the apostles and the whole world was entrusted to him.”1438  
731. Should someone who lives in sin constantly be in tears and fear? And with what 
hope must this person approach the Lord?  
During the events of the repeated church bombings at the end of the era of former 
Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak and the following years, our understanding of the concept 
of repentance in the Gospel and the writings of the Church Fathers was confirmed, in that it 
leads to an atmosphere of peace, true joy, courage, hope, and fearlessness in the face of death. 
It also triggers within us a desire for the salvation of all humanity, even for those who 
persecute the Church and resist the faith. Repentance is an invitation to experience a taste of 
heaven and communion with the Lover of all humanity! 
St. Jacob of Sarug begins his homily on repent ance with expressions that reveal the 
joyful biblical concept of repentance, which is in essence a delightful encounter with Christ 
Himself to enjoy His wondrous blessings, even if it was accompanied with some sorrow and 
regret because of our human weakness. 
In his introduction, the saint experiences the life of repentance as a journey that extends 
across the entire life. He invites us to speak openly with Christ, being the open Door for all 
humanity and the Way that leads us to the Father’s bosom.  
He sees the incarnate Son of God with His hands stretched on the cross to embrace the 
repentant together with the right-hand thief, leading them in, for He is the Door (John 10:9) 
and the Way (John 14:6), and accompanying them throughout the way as He did with th e 
disciples of Emmaus, when he says with them, “Was not our heart burning in us, as He spoke 
to us in the way?” (Luke 24:32).  
St. Jacob of Sarug  says, “O Son of God, open to me by Your love the great door; You 
are the door and the way of life to those who walk through You. O Good Friend, with You 
I walk to Him who sent You. The wicked is accompanied by many since he abides in the 
world. Through You, I come forward to speak to You, O Teacher of Life, for without You 
no man can see the Father.”1439 
The path of repentance takes the believer away from sin. Our Christ draws him back, 
speaks to him and gives him life so that he may see His great divine glory by His grace.  
 
1438 St. John Chrysostom, Discourses against Judaizing Christians 8.3.3–4 (FOTC 68:213–214). 
1439 St. Jacob of Sarug, On Repentance.

595 
calls for a healer for her, and says: ‘Happy is he who takes and dashes your littles ones against 
the rock!’ (Ps. 137:9). That is to say, shall dash all corrupt and filthy thoughts against Christ 
… For if it is said to Moses when he was desiring to draw nearer: ‘Take your sandals off your 
feet’ (Ex. 3:5), how much more must we free the feet of our soul from the bonds of the body, 
and clear our steps from all connection with this world.”1533 
786. How can we prepare ourselves for the partaking of the Body and Blood of the 
Lord? 
Partaking of the Body of Christ in the eucharist requires purity of the soul and not 
luxurious clothing. St. Cyril of Jerusalem says, “But now, having put off your old garments, 
and put on those which are spiritually white, you must be continually robed in white: of 
course we mean not this, that you are always to wear white raiment; but you must be clad in 
the garments that are truly white and shining and spiritual, that you may say with the blessed 
Isaiah, ‘My soul shall be joyful in my God; for He has clothed me with a garment of salvation, 
and put a robe of gladness around me’ (Isa. 61:10).”1534 
St. Basil was asked if a man who had an unclean drea m or a natural secretion could 
partake of the holy sacraments. His response was that he who was born anew through baptism 
is elevated above nature, through the work of the Holy Spirit. He says, “In the Old Testament, 
we learn of the horrific punishment tha t is inflicted on those who approach the Holies 
in their uncleanness (Lev. 15:31). But now we know that the One who is greater than the 
temple is present (Matt. 12:6). Hence, the Apostle warns even more that, ‘whoever eats or 
drinks in an unworthy manner eats and drinks judgement to himself’ (1 Cor. 11:29).”1535 
St. Clement of Alexandria says, “Thus, it is not just through external preparations, but 
through the preparation of the soul, by practicing a life of love and purity of heart and body, 
and making our behavior inside the church the same as our behavior in our daily lives. It is 
fitting for men and women to enter the church calmly, silently and in an orderly manner, 
filled with sincere love … that their bodies and hearts may be pure and ready for prayer.” 
With regards to washing the hands, and our purification from every sinful deed, St. Cyril 
of Jerusalem says, “You have seen then the Deacon who gives to the Priest water to wash, 
and to the Presbyters who stand round God’s altar. He gave it not at all because of bodily 
defilement; it is not that; for we did not enter the Church at first with defiled bodies. But the 
washing of hands is a symbol that you ought to be pure from all sinful and unlawful deeds; 
for since the hands are a symbol of action, by washing them, it is evident, we represent the 
purity and blamelessness of our cond uct. Did you not hear the blessed David opening this

111 
strongly out of all the Scriptures … not writing it out on paper, but engraving it by the 
memory upon your heart … I wish you also to keep this as a provision through the whole 
course of your life.”288 
St. Jerome says, “Our custom is, for the space of forty days, to deliver public lectures to 
those who are to be baptized.”289 
To confess the faith is to enter into a divine pact or to seal a covenant with God, recorded 
in the book of heaven. Theodore of Mopsuestia says, “They confess and they renounce – the 
two in one, without doubting – [making] a renunciation of the Evil One, and a confession of 
the heart in the name of the Divinity. By the hand of t he priesthood they make a covenant 
with the Divinity, that they will not again return to Satan by their doings. They give to the 
priest a promise by the words of their minds; and he brings in, reads [it] before the good 
pleasure of God. The chart which is the door of the royal house he holds in his hands; and 
from the palace he has [received] authority to inscribe [the names of] men.”290 He also says, 
“By confessing the faith, you attach your soul to God through the Bishop and establish a 
covenant, pledging to persist in loving the Divine nature.”291 
105. What are the articles of the present Creed?  
We can divide the Creed into fourteen articles: 
In truth, we believe in One God, 
God the Father, the Pantocrator, Creator of heaven and earth, and of all things seen and 
unseen. 
We believe in One Lord, Jesus Christ , the only-begotten Son of God, begotten of the 
Father before all ages. Light of Light, true God of true God; begotten not created; of one 
essence with the Father; by whom all things were made. 
Who for us men and our salvation, came down from heaven, was incarnate of the Holy 
Spirit and of the Virgin Mary,  
And became man. And He was crucified for us under Pontius Pilate,  
Suffered and was buried, and on the third day He rose from the dead  according to 
the Scriptures.  
Ascended into the heavens; He sits at the right hand of His Father,

It is interesting to notice that Origen, in his Homilies on Numbers, found in Scripture the 
implication that Pentecost is a symbol of forgiveness: “We have often and abundantly shown 
in many passages of the Scriptures that the number fifty contains the mystery of forgiveness 
and pardon. For there is both the fiftieth year which is called Jubilee by the Hebrews, in 
which there is remission of property, slavery and debt. There is also the tradition in the law 
that the fiftieth day after Passover is a feast day. Moreover, in the Gospel, when the Lord was 
teaching the parable of forgiveness and pardon, he introduces some debtors, ‘one who owed 
fifty denarii and the other five hundred’ (Luke 7:41).”1061  
527. Does the Church have the authority to forgive sins? 
The early Church considered herself a “congregation of saints” and attributed the 
authority to forgive the sin to God alone.1062 Origen says, “Moreover, just as the sun and the 
moon enlighten our bodies so also our minds are enlightened by Christ and the Church.”1063  
528. What is the role of the Church as “the mother of the believers”? 
About the motherhood of the Church, Origen says, “According to the Spirit, your Father 
is God; your mother is ‘the heavenly Jerusalem’ [See Gal. 4:26; Heb. 12:22]. Learn this from 
prophetic and apostolic witnesses. This Moses himself writes in a song, ‘Is He not your 
Father, who bought you? Has He not made you and established you?’ (Deut. 32:6).”1064  
He also says, “But the Apostle says about ‘the heavenly Jerusalem,’ ‘She is free who is 
the mother of us all’ (Gal. 4:26). Therefore, first, your Father is God who begot your spirit 
and who says, ‘I have begotten sons and exalted them’ (Isa. 1:2). But the Apostle Paul also 
says, ‘Let us submit to the Father of spirits and we shall live’ (Heb. 12:9).”1065 
St. Cyprian of Carthage also says, “He can no longer have God for his Father, who has 
not the Church for his mother.”1066  
529. Does the Church grieve over sinners? 
The Church together with her Head, our Lord Jesus Christ, will remain in a state of grief 
over sinners until they return to God and submit to the Father. Christ said, “I will not drink 
of this fruit of the vine, from now on, until that day when I drink it new with you in My 
Father’s Kingdom” (Matt. 26:29). Origen commenting on these words says that wine in

records.question: St Bishoy
records.answer:
Here is a summary of the life and spiritual significance of St. Bishoy according to the provided sources:

- St. Bishoy was born around 320 AD in the village of Shansa, El-Menufyia governorate, Egypt. He was one of six brothers raised by their mother after their father's early death [3].

- At age 20 (around 340 AD), he went to the wilderness of Scetis to become a disciple of Abba Bemwah, who was a disciple of St. Macarius the Great. He lived in seclusion, worshipping and praying intensely [3].

- After Abba Bemwah's death, St. Bishoy left the place in obedience to an angelic message and dug a cave near Abba John the Short, about two miles away. He practiced severe asceticism, including tying his long hair to a rope to keep himself awake in prayer and fasting extensively [3][6].

- He memorized most of the Holy Bible and had a special love for the Book of Jeremiah, to the extent that he was called "Bishoy the Jeremian" [6].

- St. Bishoy had a close fellowship with the Lord Jesus Christ, who appeared to him multiple times, spoke to him, and blessed him. On one occasion, the Lord appeared as an old man whom St. Bishoy carried, and the Lord promised that his body would never decay [2][6].

- His body is said to be preserved without decay in his monastery to this day [2].

- He had a disciple named Isaac who fell away to Judaism but was brought back through St. Bishoy's prayers and fasting [1].

- In 407 AD, due to Berber attacks on Scetis, St. Bishoy left the desert and lived in the mountain near Ansena, where he formed a close friendship with St. Paul of Tamouh. They wished not to be separated in death, and God granted this [1].

- St. Bishoy reposed on the 8th of Abib in 417 AD at age 97. He was buried near Ansena, and later his body was moved back to Scetis during the patriarchate of Pope Yusab I (831-849 AD) [1].

- St. Bishoy was known for his humility, love for salvation of souls, and great spiritual gifts, including the ability to see the deeds of others and to support them in repentance [5][6].

- He was visited spiritually by Emperor Constantine and by St. Ephraim the Syrian, with whom he had a miraculous understanding despite language differences [2].

- St. Bishoy's life exemplifies simple, devoted monasticism founded on love and fellowship with Christ, breaking down obstacles by the Holy Spirit [3].

This summary covers the life, ascetic practices, spiritual experiences, and legacy of St. Bishoy as described in the sources. The sources do not provide information on any differences between St. Bishoy and other churches or traditions.

His Love for the Salvation of All Souls: 
Saint ‘Bishoy’ had a disciple named ‘Isaac,’ who descended to the world 
and was seduced by a Jewish woman to forsake his faith, and he was converted 
to Judaism and lived with her . When he happened to encounter some monks, 
he asked them to tell St. ‘Bishoy’: “Your son, the Jewish ‘Isaac,’ has fallen and 
seeks from you to pray on his behalf to God to save him.” On hearing that, the 
woman said: “Even if ‘Bishoy’ come to me, I shall seduce him.” On returning 
to the monastery, the monks forgot what happened. Then, they were asked by 
the saint: “Has someone asked you to tell me something? ” They answered in 
the negative. The saint asked them whether they have encountered the Jewish 
‘Isaac,’ so they told him what happened and what ‘Isaac’ and the Jewish 
woman said. At that moment, they saw the saint retreat three steps backward 
and make the sign of the Cross on himself at each stage. Astonished, the monks 
said; “Even you, father, fear that woman?” St. ‘Bishoy’ humbly answered: “My 
children, the woman was the cause of the fall of ‘Adam,’ ‘Samson,’ ‘David’ 
and ‘Solomon.’ Who would be the poor ‘Bishoy’ to challenge her?!  Nobody 
can overcome the tricks of Satan in wo men, except that one whom God is 
with.” He kept praying and fasting for the sake of his son ‘Isaac’ until God 
saved him, and he came back and repented. 
Forsaking Scetis: 
In the year 407 AD, the first attack of the Berbers on the wilderness of 
‘Scetis’ took place. At that time, the monks escaped from the desert. St. ‘John 
the Short ’ asked St. ‘Bishoy’: “ Do you fear death, O man of God? ” He 
answered him: “No, but I fear a Berberian would kill me and goes to hell 
because of me!” 
St. ‘John the Short ’ went to mount ‘Kalzam,’ near the monastery of Abba 
‘Anthony’ where he reposed . Whereas, St. ‘Bishoy’ went to ‘Ansena’ (the 
village of ‘Sheikh Abbadah’ near ‘Mallawy’), and he lived in the mountain . 
There, he formed a close relationship with ‘St. Abba ‘Paul of Tamouh,’ and 
sought from the Lord not to be separated from him when they would repose , 
and God granted them their wish. 
St. ‘Bishoy’ remained in his expatriation until he reposed on the 8th of Abib 
in the year 417 AD, after reaching 97 years of age. He was buried in the castle 
of ‘Meniat el-Saqar’ near ‘Ansena.’ When St. ‘Paul of Tamouh’ reposed, St. 
‘Athanasius’ of ‘Ansena’ gathered the two saints'  bodies and buried them 
together in the monastery of abba ‘Bishoy’ in ‘Ansena’ (Monastery of El -
Bersha). The bodies of these two saints were returned to the wilderness of 
‘Scetis’ during the patriarchate of the 52nd pope Abba ‘Yusab I’ (831-849 AD).

promised to appear to them on the mountain at a particular time. The brethren

by monks cared to help him. Saint ‘Bishoy’ asked if he may carry him, and he 
did carry him and walked without feeling any labor . However, the older man 
started to get heavier and heavier; and the saint perceived that He was no one 
but the Lord  Jesus Christ Him self. He then looked at Him and said: “The 
heaven is not wide enough to accommodate You, and Your majesty shakes the 
earth; how can a sinner like me carry You? ” To this, the Lord  Jesus Christ 
smiled at him and said: “Because you carried Me, My beloved ‘Bishoy,’ your

kept in his monastery without de terioration up to this very day . Once the

BISHOY, ST. ABBA 
Our great saint abba ‘Bishoy’ represents the simple life striving in the Lord, 
that was founded upon the love fellowship with the Lord Jesus Christ. He had 
a personal relationship with Jesus that broke the obstacles down to open up the 
heart by the Holy Spirit that the Heavenly Groom would transfigure within it 
and reign with power and dominion! 
St. ‘Bishoy’ was born in ‘Shansa,’ a village in the governorate of ‘El-
Menufyia,’ around the year 320 AD. He was one of six brothers, whose father 
reposed when they were relatively young, and their mother raised them  up. 
One day the mother saw an angel who came to tell her: “The Lord says to you: 
‘Give Me one of your children to serve Me all the days of his life. ’” She 
answered: “Sir, they are all for the Lord. Let Him take whomever He chooses.” 
The angel put his hand on this saint, and said: “This is a good laborer for the 
Lord.” Being weakly built and frail in the body, his mother asked the angel to 
choose another one; but he answered her: “The Lord said ‘My strength is made 
perfect in weakness.’” (2 Cor. 12:9). 
In Scetis (Shiheet): 
Having reached twenty years of age in the year 340 AD, the young ‘Bishoy’ 
set forth to the wilderness of ‘Scetis,’ where he became a disci ple of Abba 
‘Bemwah’ (Bemen), the disciple of St. ‘Macarius’ (300-391 AD). There, he 
worshipped in seclusion for three years without going out of his cell. He grew 
in virtue and had his heart inflamed with love for God. 
Life in Seclusion: 
When Abba ‘Bemwah’ reposed in the Lord, his two disciples Abba ‘Bishoy’ 
and Abba ‘John (Yeĥness) the Short,’ spent the whole night praying to seek the 
guidance of God . An angel appeared to them and said that Abba ‘John the 
Short’ should remain alone in that location . In obedience, Abba ‘Bishoy’ left 
the place forsaking his friend, and d ug for h imself a cave near the southern 
rock, about two miles away from Abba ‘John the Short.’

As he loved prayer, he made a hole in a high spot on the cave wall, then he

head would get heavy and drop down due to sleepiness, the rope would pull it

(The martyr) 
‘Bishai’ (Abshai) was the brother of St. ‘Hur’ (Abahur) of Antioch. He was 
ordained as a priest because of his piety . His brother and his mother went to 
Alexandria, where they were martyred. Their brother, the priest, went there to 
take care of their bodies . Then, he felt the longing to partake in  their crowns. 
So, he set forth to the governor to proclaim his faith, endured sufferings until 
he died. In vain, the governor attempted to burn their bodies. 
The Church celebrates his feast on the 1st day of the short Coptic month: 
‘Nasie’ (the forgotten days). 
 
BISHAI, THE HERMIT, ABBA 
The biography of Abba ‘Bishai the Hermit ,’ known as Abba ‘Bishai’ the 
dweller of the two graves at the entrance of ‘Tod’ (Mount Tod, east of the Nile 
river opposite to ‘Armant’), was linked to those of SS. ‘Pasantaos’ and ‘Sorus.’ 
The three of them were considered among the first monks who became 
disciples of St. ‘Pachom,’ the father of the ‘Koinonia’ (Coenobite). 
He was a hermit who worshipped God from his early age and labored in his 
prayers day and night . He was also known for his love of the book of the 
prophet ‘Jeremiah;’ so that it was said that every time he read it, he would find 
the prophet ‘Jeremiah’ himself before him, kiss his head, then watch him 
ascending to heaven (which also happened to him when he read the other books 
of the prophets). 
Giving his body no rest, he loved doing metanoias and long watching of the 
nights. After completing his strife, he reposed in the Lord on the 25th of Kiahk. 
His body was buried in his church, from which many signs and wonders 
appeared. 
 
BISHAI, ST. ABBA 
The story of this saint reveals the fantastic plan of God for the salvation of 
every soul; how He uses every tool to draw them to Him, and how He sets 
them on the highest level if they receive His call and respond to it. 
This saint, also (called ‘Peter’), was born in the village of ‘Epsona,’ a suburb 
of ‘Akhmim.’ In his youth, he walked in an evil path; but God did not leave 
him there but allowed for him to fall ill, and in a night vision , He revealed to 
him the place of the eternal sufferings  which he was heading to . He bitterly

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Volume 1, p. 357
passages.text:
357 
 
wept, and raised his eyes to heaven and cried out: “My Lord and my God! If 
you heal me of this illness; I shall repent, return to You and worship You 
with all my heart .” ‘Bishai’ (Peter) was healed,  and he  did not forget his 
promise to the Lord, but he was inflamed in his heart with an intense longing 
to experience the monastic life. He forsook the sheep he was shepherding, and 
set forth to the monastery where he met with St. ‘Bigol,’ the uncle of St. 
‘Shenouda’ (who was to become the Archimandrite in Mount Adriba). 
His Monastic Life: 
God used the illness to bring that young man out of the covetousness of the 
body, which would destroy the soul . Once he tasted the real spiritual life, his 
heart got filled with so much joy to set forth firmly and be willing to do so 
many labors enduring daily so many harsh sufferings with a joyful heart.  
He lived with St. ‘Bigol’ in a  fantastic friendship, partaking together in 
monasticism and worship without ever getting bored, watching the nights, and 
opposing the temptations of the devil. 
God granted him an exalt ed capability beyond the limits of human 
endurance; he used to fast, in a way that defied imagination, for a whole month 
not tasting anything, and by a fantastic Divine allowance, he would stand the 
entire night praying. God, in His love, granted him to ha ve the deeds of other 
people revealed before his eyes, which he used to support them on the life of 
true repentance. Because of God's grace working in him, many people came to 
him from all over Egypt to seek his blessings . They benefited greatly by his 
spiritual sermons, and he also wrote essays for the monks and those in the 
world. 
Through the friendship of th is saint with St. ‘Bigol,’ he was present when 
the young Abba ‘Shenouda the Archimandrite;’ St. ‘Bigol's’ nephew, first came 
out in the wilderness in  his 7th year of age. He was clothed by his uncle the 
holy monastic Eskeem, in obedience to an angelic proclamation, and the 
presence of St. ‘Bishai.’ The three of them, despite the difference in age, 
worked with one spirit in a fantastic fellowship, realizing the saying of the wise 
‘Solomon’: “A threefold cord is not quickly broken.” (Eccl. 4:12). 
Each of them built for himself a cell on the mountain and another one near 
the church . I t so happened that while th ey were setting forth to visit A bba 
‘Jehnes’ (John) on Mount ‘Assiut,’ they heard a voice from heaven saying: “I 
have chosen you, O ‘Shenouda’ an Archimandrite.” 
St. ‘Bishai’ reposed in the Lord on the 5th of Amshir, and was shrouded by 
St. ‘Shenouda.’ From his body, many signs and wonders appeared, which were 
all documented by Abba ‘Shenouda,’ who wrote his biography and described 
his ascetic life.

passages.text:
359 
 
up, resulting in keeping him awake in prayers. As for fasting, he trained himself 
to fast the whole week and eat only on Saturdays. His prayers and fasting got 
to hand in hand with his intense love for the word of God. He memorized most 
of the Holy Bible by heart. The Book of ‘Jeremiah’ had a special place in his 
heart; that it was said that he used to se e the prophet Jeremiah during his 
reading of his Book; that he was called ‘Bishoy the Jeremian.’ 
He considered hand-work as a significant part of building his spiritual life. 
He believed in the saying : “If anyone will not work, neither shall he eat. ” (2 
Thess. 3:10). His friend Abba ‘John the Short’ said about him that when a rich 
man brought to him plenty of gold as a donation, he told him: “The dwellers 
of the wilderness have no need of gold and should not have any of it. Go instead 
to the villages of Egypt and distribute it to the poor. God bless you.” After the 
man went his way, and the saint returned to his cell, Satan came to him, saying: 
“You fatigued me so much, O Bishoy .” And, the saint answered him: “Since 
your fall, and all your fatigue is in vain.” 
His Fellowship with our Lord Jesus; 
Through his pure heart, he used to meet often with the Lord Jesus Christ on 
a friendship level . He used to see Him, to talk with Him , and to enjoy His 
Divine proclamations. It was said that, having been so persiste nt in his great 
ascetic life and prayers that the Lord Jesus Christ appeared to him, saying: “My 
chosen vessel ‘Bishoy,’ peace be with you; I saw your labor and strife, and 
behold, I shall always be with you!”  
Another time, as our saint remained a long time fasting, the Lord appeared 
to him, saying: “You labored too much, My chosen vessel Bishoy!” The saint 
answered Him: “It was You O Lord who labored for me, but I have not labored 
at all!” 
A third time, the Lord appeared to him, saying: “Rejoice, My chosen vessel 
Bishoy. Do you see this mountain? I shall send you monks to fill that mountain 
to worship Me.” The saint asked Him: “Will You sustain them, Lord, in such a 
barren wilderness?” The Lord answered: “If they love one another and keep 
My commandments, I shall sustain them in everything!” The saint asked Him: 
“Will You save them from all the anguishes and afflictions mentioned in the 
Gospel?” The Lord answered: “Whoever fears, obeys Me and keep My 
commandments; I shall save him from all temptations! ” He then blessed him 
and ascended. 
Again the Lord appeared to him surrounded by angels. The Lord comforted 
him and blessed him . The saint worshipped Him and washed His feet with 
water in a basin, then the Lord ascended . St. ‘Bishoy’ drank from that water 
and left a portion for his disciple . The saint sought from him more than once 
to drink it, but the disciple was too slow. Then, when St. ‘Bishoy’ went to check

passages.text:
75 
 
around, he decided to leave and returned home. He visited on the way some 
Asian cities, in Syria, Mesopotamia, and Nissibin; and God worked through 
him, wherever he w ent. The saint prepared a tomb for himself, on which he 
engraved the sign of the fish, a symbol of the Christian faith, and wrote a 
concise account of God’s work through him in the imperial palace. He reposed 
in the Lord around the year 167 AD. 
[Butler’s Lives of the Saints; Oct. 22] 
 
 
ABSADI, BISHOP OF EBSAY 
(The martyr) 
The word ‘Absadi’ (Bisada) means “the Humiliated." St. ‘Bisada’ was a 
bishop on ‘Ebsay’ (Monshaa), east of ‘Akhmim.’ 
In the days of emperor ‘Diocletian’ (284-305 AD), ‘Arianius,’ governor of 
‘Ansena’ called him for hearing how he was very vigilant in shepherding his 
people and holding them fast on the Christian faith. 
The bishop called his congregation and advised them to strive. He held a 
Divine Liturgy for them, in which all had the commu nion of the Holy 
Sacraments; then, he bid them farewell and delivered himself to the 
messengers of ‘Arianius.’ At first, ‘Arianius’ treated him decently on account 
of what he saw how awesome the bishop looked. He tenderly asked him to 
obey the orders of the emperor, to spare himself of the ’troubles, but the bishop 
bravely refused to burn incense before the idols. 
Therefore, the saint suffered long by the hinbazeen and by being cast in a 
furnace of fire, where the Lord kept him safe; and he ultimately recei ved the 
crown of martyrdom on the 27th of Kiahk. 
A monastery by the name of St. ‘Bisada’ is still there east of ‘Monshaa.'  
 
ABU AL-HASSAN AL-AMAH 
He was among the 11 th century Copts. He was a secretary of Calipha ‘Al-
Hafez.' He was known for his piety and  his care for reconstructing the 
churches. 
[Iris Habib Al-Masry: The Story of the Coptic Church; V. 3; 1981, p. 144]

the Consuls down. The case ended up by punishing and firing the judge and 
the governor, in addition to all those who took part in torturing the saint. 
And to calm the Christians down, the khedive gave the order to hold an 
official funeral for Sidhom Bishai. He also allowed the Cross to be raised in 
public at the front of the saint's funeral procession 1. That display was 
prohibited by the Egyptian rulers for so many centuries. They put the pure 
saint's body in a gasket covered with tin at the expense of the State. His burial 
was celebrated by all sects and was preceded by priests in their priestly attire 
and by deacons carrying banners and crosses. They brought him to the Church, 
where they prayed on him, then buried  his body in a unique tomb on the land 
of the Church, which was originally a cemetery for the Copts. On the night of 
his burial, a shining pillar of light was seen over his tomb and so many people 
took ashes from his tomb for the blessing. 
Finally, the relics of St. Sidhom Bishai were moved to St. George Cathedral 
in Damietta. And, it happened that in the year 1848, they intended to widen the 
church, so they had to move the body of the martyr to a special place on the 
south-west side of the Church, next to that of muåallem Banoub Farag and all 
the rest of his family. There, it remained until the year 1986. The feast of his 
martyrdom was continuously celebrated; until the day the Lord, intending to 
honor His Saint; the committee of the Church decided to move his blessed 
body with a grand celebration into a particular tomb in the court of the Church, 
in the days of the 116th pope Abba Kyrillos VI (1959-1971). One of the toes of 
the right foot of the Saint was placed in a tube in St. Mary Church in Dayrut. 
The Wonders of God through the Saint: 
Many signs appeared from the body of this saint, among which was that a 
rosary which was found in the hand of the saint after moving him, was offered 
to the bishop Abba Aghabius, who carried out the consecration of the blessed 
body. To get its blessing, a brother borrowed it from the bishop, but intending 
in secret to cut a portion of it, St. Sidhom Bishai appeared to him, unknown to 
the man and ordered him to bring it b ack; and so he did, confessed and got 
absolution. 
It happened once that a priest, while sick, came to receive the blessing of 
the martyr, and on leaving, before he reached the door of the Church, he was 
completely healed of his illness. Many other miracles were performed with so 
many visitors of the city and the Church.  
 [The Synaxarion: 17 Baramhat]

Abu el-Bishr ibn el-Muqaffaå, the Clerk: 
Sawires ibn el-Muqaffaå ascended the ladder of the State jobs in the era of 
the Ikhshidid dynasty (935-969) who ruled Egypt under the Abbasid Caliphate 
(750-1258), until he became a prominent clerk . He occupied a very high  
position that required a good knowledge of the Arabic language, beside the 
Coptic and the Greek languages. At that time, Sawires was known by the title: 
Abu el -Bishr el -Muqaffaå The Clerk . This did not imply that he had a son 
called El-Bishr, but indicated that he was a prominent and respectable man, as 
it was the custom in those days. 
His Monastic Life: 
After reaching the highest of jobs, Sawires forsook the glory of the world 
and his job, to become a monk in one of Egypt’s monasteries. He managed to 
get much benefit during his monastic life, since he perfected his religious 
education which was based mainly on the Holy Bible and the writings of the 
Fathers. Abu el-Bishr became distinguished in both fields. 
His Knowledge of the Holy Bible: 
According to the researchers, Sawires knowledge of the Holy Bible was 
amazing, so has been his knowledge of the writings of the Fathers; he 
surpassed that of all his contemporaries. This was obvious from his book: “The 
Precious Pearl in Explaining the Religious Doctrine”1 (this is different from 
another book almost with the same title 2), which indicated his extensive 
knowledge of the Holy Scriptures. It could be said that no other author in the 
Arabic language had his knowledge of the Holy Bible; and that his theological 
writings indicated his in-depth knowledge of the works of the Fathers of the 
Church, whether in Greek or Arabic. 
 
Ordained as a Bishop: 
He was chosen as a bishop on the city of El -Ashmonein, which was at the 
time a great bishopric rich in churches and monasteries. Nowadays, it is a small 
village affiliated with the province of El-Roda in the Assiut governorate, to the 
north-west of Mallawy. He was probably ordained by the 59 th Pope of 
Alexandria St. Macarius I (932-952 AD). 
His Debates:

SIDHOM BISHAI (The martyr) 
On the 17th of Baramhat in the year 1561 AM (25 March 1844), the Coptic 
Church celebrates the martyrdom of St. Sidhom Bishai. 
Sidhom Bishai was a trader of wood in the city of Alexandria. He used to 
go twice every year to Damietta to purchase lumber, which was imported 
through its harbor. Being an archdeacon who loved the old churches, Sidhom 
Bishai on hearing that the wooden roof of St. George el -Muzaĥem Church in 
the town of Basat in the district of Sherbin had collapsed; he took on himself 
the responsibility of repairing the damage done and provide d a full ship load 
of wood for that purpose. At the same time, during his visits to Damietta, he 
used to attend the Holy Liturgies in St. George Church. One time, it happened 
that a non -Christian stroked shoulder against him on his way to the church 
aiming to block him from going to the Church. But, seeing how muåallem 
Sidhom Bishai paid little attention to that evil man, he was provoked to anger 
and paid some street boys to insult him. Then, it happened that the Mofti 1 of 
the town was passing by; and thes e boys falsely accused Sidhom Bishai of 
insulting Islam, its “Prophet” and the “Quran.” Those false accusations, 
finding the expected fertile soil in the Moftis ears; he chose two of equally evil 
people around as witnesses. Through these people, they rigged the case against 
muåallem Sidhom Bishai. He was then 40 years of age, well known for 
meekness, kind-hearted and loving for all, not at all expected to utter what they 
falsely claimed that he has done. 
Torturing Him: 
Then, Sidhom Bishai was called in for trial. And, on his way to the court of

records.question: Anthony the Great
records.answer:
St. Anthony the Great, also known as the Father of the Monks and the Founder of the Monastic Movement, was born around 251 AD in the village of Komn Al-Aros (Qiman El-Arous), Egypt, to wealthy parents. After his father's death, he was deeply moved by the mortality of life and, at eighteen years old, he heard the Gospel reading from Matthew 19:21, which inspired him to sell his possessions, give to the poor, and dedicate his life to God. He placed his sister Dios in a convent and began living a life of asceticism in a small hut, learning from a saintly hermit [1][2].

He initially dwelt beside the Nile, praying in strict asceticism, but when disturbed by boredom and improper behavior nearby, he moved to the inner wilderness around 285 AD, living in a cave on Mount Al-Kalzam near the Red Sea. There, he faced spiritual battles with demons but persevered in seclusion [3].

Around 305 AD, he began to receive disciples, thus founding the monastic movement. His monastic life was characterized by intense love of seclusion, yet he remained connected to the Church, notably supporting the martyrs in Alexandria in 316 AD and defending St. Athanasius against Arianism in 352 AD. His entrance into Alexandria was so impactful that even some Arians returned to the Church [2][3].

St. Anthony lived as a hermit at Pispir (Dayr al-Maymūn) on the eastern bank of the Nile and later in the inner desert at Mount Colzim. He died in 352 AD [2].

He is known for the monastic attire inspired by an angel who appeared to him, teaching him to weave palm leaves and work with his hands, which became foundational to monastic life [3].

St. Anthony had a notable encounter with St. Paul the First Hermit, whom he visited in the desert. St. Paul lived for eighty years in solitude, sustained by a raven bringing him bread. When St. Anthony arrived, the raven brought a full loaf, confirming St. Anthony's divine mission. After St. Paul's death, St. Anthony buried him with the help of two lions who dug the grave [4][5].

St. Anthony's influence extended to many disciples and other monastic figures such as St. Serapion, St. Hilarion, and St. Sisoes, who sought to imitate his asceticism and spiritual practices [6][9][10].

In summary, St. Anthony the Great is the pioneering figure of Christian monasticism, known for his ascetic life, spiritual struggles, leadership of disciples, defense of the Orthodox faith, and lasting legacy in the monastic tradition [1][2][3][4][5][6][9][10].

‘Anthony,' among whom are: 
ANTHONY, THE SYRIAN The martyr: 
He was a 20 years old Syrian, a stone builder who was known for his great 
zeal against the idol worshipping. He lived as an anchorite for two years; then 
he returned to his hometown. There, he found the people worshipping the false 
gods. So, he went into their temple and broke all the idols down. He was 
expelled from the city, and he went to ‘Apamaea'. And, when its bishop 
assigned him to build a Ch urch, the pagans were stirred up against him and 
killed him. 
ANTONIUS AL-BEBAWY: The martyr: 
St. ‘Anthony’ (Andona) was born in ‘Beba’ in Upper Egypt by pious and 
merciful parents. Hearing about the sufferings of the martyrs, he set forth to 
‘Arianus,' the governor of ‘Ansena.’ and confessed the Lord Christ before him. 
The governor ordered his men to throw spears at him, but he was not harmed. 
Then, for the fear of that the audience would be encouraged to believe in his 
Christ, he ordered him chained and se nt him to ‘Armanius,’ the governor of 
Alexandria. He sent with him ‘Abimachus’ and two other saints. ‘Armanius’ 
put the three in prison, crucified ‘Anthony’ upside down and tortured him, but 
God was glorified in him. Then, he was sent to the governor of ‘Al-Farma,' 
where he met with ‘St. Mina’ in the prison and both rejoiced by seeing each 
other. The governor of ‘Al-Farma’ ordered combing ‘Anthony’s body with 
sharp iron-teeth combs, and then he cut his head off by the sword. The saint 
received the crown of martyrdom. 
 
ANTHONY, FATHER OF THE MONKS, ST. 
He is considered worldwide as ‘The Father of the Monastic Family ’ and 
‘The Founder of the Monastic Movement ’ in the whole world, even though 
there have been some monastic movements prior to his. 
The saint was born in the village of ‘Komn Al-Aros’ – Beni-Sweif around 
the year 251 AD, to wealthy parents. When his father died, he stood before his 
corpse, contemplated in the mortality of the world, and his heart kindled 
toward eternity. In the year 269 AD, entering into the church, he heard the 
gospel saying: “If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to 
the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow Me ” (Matt. 
19:21). Anthony considered it a personal message for him, and it touched  his 
life. Moreover, when he returned home to his young sister ‘Dios,' he 
proclaimed to her his decision to sell his portion of the inheritance and give its 
proceeds to the poor, to dedicate his life to worship God. On her part, his sister 
also insisted on joining a convent in Alexandria.

old, after leading an angelic life on earth, St. Anthony the Great met him. St. Paul addressed 
him by name, and they talked about the wonders of God and praised Him. At sunset, a raven 
flew down from a palm tree and brought a full loaf of bread to them, even though it was the 
raven’s habit to bring only half a loaf to St. Paul. On the third day, St. Paul asked St. Anthony 
to bring him St. Athanasius’ vestment, which he then gave to St. Anthony to bury him in it. 
When St. Anthony returned, he found that St. Paul had departed while bowing down in 
prayer. Then, two lions came and dug in the sand to bury St. Paul. 
St. Anthony the Great:  He was born around 251 A. D. in the city of Coma, Egypt 
(Qiman El-Arous). When he was eighteen years old, he heard the Gospel reading: “If you 
want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in 
heaven; and come, follow Me” (Matt. 19:21), and so he sold his possessions, placed his sister 
in a house of virgins, and dwelt in a small hut to learn from a saintly hermit there. After some 
time, he went into the western desert to struggle on his own in a tomb, that was carved in the 
mountain. At the age of thrity -five, he settled at the eastern bank of the Nile at Pispir ( Dayr 
al-Maymūn), where he lived as a hermit, so many came to him and became his disciples. He 
went into the inner desert at Mount Colzim to live in peace and silence. Nonetheless, his love 
compelled him to visit Alexandria to support the martyrs in 316 A. D., and to support St. 
Athanasius against Arianism in 352 A. D. Many people came to be his disciples, and he 
departed in 352 A. D. 
St. Pachomius (Father of the Koinonia):  He was born in upper Egypt around the year 
290 A. D. He became Christian in the city of Esna in Upper Egypt because of their generosity 
and their love for their enemies. He left the army and was baptized around the ye ar 290 A. 
D. He became the disciple of St. Palamon the hermit, till an angel appeared to him and guided 
him to establish the system of the monastic communal life (coenobitic monasticism). He was 
a successful leader who loved the salvation of souls, so he e stablished many monasteries in 
Upper Egypt following strict rules. He also established a convent for nuns under the 
leadership of his sister. His monastic rules were translated to Greek and Latin. St. Basil the 
Great used them, and they were used in the Gaul in the fifth century. They were also adopted 
by Benedict, the father of western monasticism, and by Caesarius of Arles. 
St. Ammonas: He was contemporary of St. Anthony. He was born in 275 A. D., and 
when he was twenty-two years old, his uncle forced him to get married, so he lived with his 
wife as ascetics in Nitria. After eighteen years, his wife asked him to live in solitude away 
from her, so he went out to Mount Nitria and many gathered around him. So, he established 
the semi-eremitic monasticism, in which the monks are not required to have daily fellowship 
in worship or in meals, except for Saturdays and Sundays only. Usually, the monks of this 
order lived in cells or caves that were close to each other, around the church. 
St. Macarius the Great: (around 300–390 A. D.) He is the founder of the semi-eremitic 
order of monasticism in the wilderness of Scetis. He visited St. Anthony at least twice. His 
father forced him to get married, but then God allowed his virgin wife to depart
