226 
1079. What is the monthly Church cycle? 
Every month is sanctified  by our monthly commemoratio n of St. Mary the Mother of 
God, the Theotokos, on the 21 st of each Coptic month. We look up to St. Mary as a living 
role model for the faithful and the First Citizen of the Church of the Lord Christ, learning 
from her to live as those who carry the Lord C hrist wherever they go; He who establishes 
His kingdom in our depths.  
On the 29 th of every Coptic month, we commemorate the annunciation, nativity [or 
Christmas], and resurrection of Christ (except for the months of Tobe and Meshir) . With 
these commemorations, t he believer is dissolved into  love through his union with the 
Savior every hour, every day, every week, and every month. 
And we commemorate the chief of the army of the Lord, Archangel Michael, every 12th 
day of the Coptic month. Thus, the believer feels that he is a good soldier of our Lord Jesus 
(2 Tim. 2:3) and that he has joined the ranks of the heavenly powers. 
This is the happiness of the believer and his continual joy  on a daily, weekly, monthly, 
and annual basis. 
1080. What is the annual Church cycle? 
This cycle, in fact, subsumes all the days of the year. We celebrate the major and minor 
feasts of the Lord, the feasts of the Theotokos, the feasts of saints, the commemoration s of 
the consecration of churches, and the annual fasts. Through all of  this, we repeat in our 
depths the words  St. Athanasius  records in one of his Paschal letters: “‘Our Passover, 
Christ, is sacrificed’ (1 Cor. 5:7). Henceforth the feast of the Passover is ours.”618 
1081. What are the major feasts of our Lord? 
The feasts that celebrate important events in the life of our Lord can be categorized as 
major or minor, depending on their role in the salvation offered by the Lord Christ. The 
major feasts of the Lord  are below. Three have set dates in the Coptic calendar whi le the 
other four have moveable dates that change each year. 
a. Annunciation ( 29th Paremhotep / 7 th April). The evangelist repeat s the word 
“virgin” to affirm her virginity and declare that the Lord Christ was not born of the 
seed of man. This the prophet Ezekiel also declares (Ezek. 44:2–3). St. Mary heard 
the angel say to her , “The Lord is with you,” an expression with a unique meaning 
when applied to her. She tasted God’s presence on a unique level, for she carried the 
Word of God in her womb and offered Him her body and blood!  
 
618 St. Athanasius of Alexandria, Festal Letters 19.1 (NPNF II/4:544).

records.question: Who was St. George the Cappadocian?
records.answer: St. George the Cappadocian was born in Cappadocia in Asia Minor to pious, wealthy parents of noble origin. His father was Anastasius, the governor of Melitene in Cappadocia, and his mother was Theobesta (Theognosta), the daughter of the governor of Lydda in Palestine. His father was a faithful Christian who was beheaded for his faith when George was only fourteen years old. After his father's martyrdom, his mother took George and his siblings to her homeland Diospolis in Palestine. George was made a cavalryman by a God-fearing prince named Justus, who loved the Lord Jesus Christ. George excelled in his military career, becoming a leader of 1,000 warriors and later a leader of 5,000 warriors, earning the title "Prince George the Roman" from the emperor. He was known for his noble character, prudence, and courage in battle. George sold all his inheritance to help the poor, released his slaves, publicly tore up the emperor's decree against Christians, and prepared joyfully for martyrdom. He was tortured for seven years for his faith, during which God supported him with miracles and heavenly visions. He died a martyr's death by beheading during the reign of Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD) [2][8][1].

With His Uncle Armenius's Daughter: 
After the death of his parents, his uncle Armenius, the governor of 
Alexandria, took him under his care . The uncle had a kind -hearted daughter, 
she happened to go for a picnic with some of her girlfriends, and they passed 
by a monastery outside Alexandria. She was very impressed to hear the monks 
praising God with sweet hymns. On coming back home, she inquired from her 
cousin George about what she heard, and he told her that it was Divine 
Christian praises sung by monks, who forsook the world to practice angelic 
lives. The young man then talked to her about the faith in the Lord Jesus Christ, 
eternal life, and the e ndless suffering. She was so impressed with what she 
heard that she accepted belief in the Lord Jesus. 
Getting to know about what happened to his daughter, her father governor 
Armenius attempted first to lure her into changing her mind, and she did not, 
then he threatened her . Yet, she, in complete love for her Lord Jesus Christ, 
was ready to deliver her own life as a sacrifice to God. So, her cruel father cut 
her head off, and she gained the crown of martyrdom.  
His Martyrdom: 
When the governor knew that it was his nephew George, the one who 
convinced his daughter to receive her new faith, he put him under arrest. Then, 
he tortured him fiercely and sent him to Arianus, the governor of Ansena, who 
tortured him more and finally had his head cut off, and he too gained the crown 
of martyrdom during the reign of Emperor Diocletian (284 -305 AD) . A 
deacon, by the name of Samuel, took his holy body, shrouded him with great 
respect, and took it Manuf in the province of Giza . On hearing about it, his 
uncle's wife took the body and buried it in Alexandria next to that of her 
martyred daughter. His relics now are in St. Mark's church in the city of Rashid.

GEORGE, THE CAPADUCIAN (The martyr) 
Time of His Martyrdom: 
Saint George was most probably considered as the Prince of Martyrs in the 
time of Emperor Diocletian (284 -305 AD). He led a revolt in the province of 
Cappadocia against the persecution de cree of the Christians . However, the 
majority of the Coptic manuscripts did refer to this saint as a martyr who lived 
in an era before Diocletian time. He lived during the reign of a pagan king of 
Persia called Dadianus, whom the province of Cappadocia was  under his

control. This version would be in agreement with what was documented in the 
biography of the martyr George of Alexandria, where he was born after his 
father attended the feast of the consecration of the church of St. George , the 
Cappadocian in the city of Lydda in Palestine. Some of the Coptic manuscripts 
did not assign his era, but only mentioned that its events happened “in the old,” 
probably meaning before the time of Diocletian. 
His Upbringing: 
This saint was born in Cappadocia in Asia Minor, to pious, wealthy parents 
of noble origin . His father was Anastasius, the governor of Melitene in 
Cappadocia, and his mother was Theobesta (Theognosta), the daughter of the 
governor of Lydda in Palestine. His father was said to be a pious man, faithful 
to God and the king, that he was so loved by the king to make him one of his 
entourage who accompan ied him wherever he would go , but when he 
discovered that Anastasius believed in the Lord  Jesus Christ, he gave the 
command to cut off his head. This happened when his son St. George was only 
fourteen years of age. Anyhow, St. George came as a fruit of a holy seed, buried 
in a holy land, to provide to the church, as well as to the celestials, what brought 
pleasure to their hearts. The martyrdom of his father gov ernor Anastasius did 
not break the souls of his family but inflamed the heart of his blessed son 
George with the fire of the Divine Love to make him a martyr for the Lord, as 
well. After the martyrdom of her husband, governor Anastasi us, Theobesta 
took her  children: George, Casset , and Madrona, and she set forth to her 
homeland Diospolis in Palestine.  
Prince George the Roman 
After the martyrdom of governor Anastasius , a prince named Justus 
replaced him. He was a God-fearing man who loved the Lord  Jesus Christ. 
Hence, he did well to the household of Anastasius , the martyr, and made the 
young man George a cavalryman to prepare him for a military career . George 
surpassed all his peers on every aspect and showed rare courage that he soon 
became a hero whose fam e spread all over Palestine and was promoted to a 
leader of 1,000 warriors. The prince sent him to the emperor with a message 
that revealed his achievements and sought from the emperor to grant him the 
rank of a prince. There, the emperor was very impressed by him and gave him 
the title: Prince George the Roman. He made him a leader of 5,000 warriors 
and gave him a blonde horse of the rarest kind to show how he was pleased 
with him. All loved George, and his noble characters, prudence, and his stature 
that would project his courage in battle qualified him to become the highest 
commander in the army. He was still twenty years of age at that time, and his 
mother also reposed in the Lord shortly after.

It was said that on the feast of the Pentecost when it was time for the Divine 
Liturgy, they realized that they were out of the wine . When St. Fronto prayed 
to God about it , a white dove came holding by her beak a bottle of wine and 
delivered it to the saint . This bottle is kept in the church of Neuilly as a holy 
treasure. 
The history of this saint is full of a multitude of miracles performed by God 
on his hands. Those miracles were the cause of converting so many to the true 
faith and as a testimony to the Evangelic work . It was also said about these 
miracles that on his return to the city of Perigueux, a woman was planning to 
give a bath to her suckling and it was the custom in that city that the infant 
would be placed in a basin of water over a low fire until the water would 
become mildly warm. The mother would remove the fire from under the basin 
and bathe the baby. That woman put her infant in the water basin over the fire, 
and hearing the reception procession of St. Fronto, she forgot all about her 
baby and rushed to watch it . After about half an hour, she came back to find 
the water boiling in the basin and the suckling sitting up and cry, unconcerned 
with his scalding bath. It was also said that the saint, in a vision, saw the two 
saints Peter and Paul at the time of their martyrdom . There, he built a church 
in their names. The relics of St. Fronto are kept in the Cathedral of Perigueux.  
           [Baring-Gould: Lives of the Saints, October 25] 
 
GEORGE OF ALEXANDRIA (The martyr) 
His Upbringing: 
St. George (Gawargios) was born to wealthy pagan parents. His father was 
a merchant in the city of Alexandria , and the family had no children . Then, 
once he traveled to the city of Lydda in Palestine, where it happened that the 
people there were celebrating the feast of the consecration of the church of the 
martyr St. George the Cappadocian. He was quite impressed and moved by the 
awesome celebration and with the church hymns, and when he listened to the 
biography of the martyr, he so loved the Christian faith that his soul was happy, 
and he sought to be baptized. The saint's father prayed to God that through the 
intercession of the great martyr, he would be granted a son. On returning home 
to Alexandria, he narrated to his wife what he encountered , and she believed 
as well and got baptized. God received their supplications and granted them a 
boy whom they called George . The child was raised in a pious atmosphere, 
loved the chu rch, and had compassion on the poor and the needy . When he 
reached the age of twenty-five years, his parents departed to heaven.

towards the Celestials. The saint preached her about Salvation and explained 
to her the exalted Evangelical life. 
The emperor 's men came to the prison to take the woman back to the 
emperor. They found her indecent clothing and actin g in a chase manner. She 
declared to them her belief in the Lord  Jesus Christ, her Savior. The emperor 
and his men were shocked to realize what happened , and the command was 
issued to cut the woman's head off by the sword. When she was led to the arena 
of death, she prostrated herself, exultantly prayed to her Savior, our Lord Jesus 
Christ, to receive her soul, and to grant her the grace of martyrdom. 
In the Royal Palace: 
After such a multitude of Divine miracles performed by God through the 
saint, the emperor felt so ashamed, he took the young man George to his palace, 
in a final round of seduction. There, the empress heard him praying and sought 
from him to explain his faith to her, and God opened her heart up, and the Spirit 
of God led her to f aith. The empress started to admonish her husband , the 
emperor, saying: “I told you not to go against those of Galilees, for their God 
is strong!” Perceiving that she was seduced by the saint to faith in the Lord, 
the emperor gave the order to comb her body wit h an iron comb, then to cut 
her head off. 
On her way to the place of execution, the empress asked the saint, how she 
would go to death without being baptized. The saint told her not to worry, for 
shedding her blood for the faith in Christ would be a Holy B aptism in itself, 
which would open the gates of Paradise before her. On hearing those words, 
the empress exultantly approached her martyrdom, saying: “O Lord, as I left 
the gates of my palace wide open, I pray to You not to close the gate of Your 
Paradise before my face, but open it the way You did for the right -hand thief 
on the Cross .” The empress had her head cut off , and her s oul set forth to 
Paradise to enjoy the company of Jesus Christ, her Savior. 
The Martyrdom of St. George: 
The emperor finally gave the order to cut the head of St. George off because 
of his fear that a possible public revolt against him would erupt due to all God's 
works through His saint . This took place on the 23 rd of the Coptic month of 
Baramhat. 
About the Icon of St. George the Roman: 
It carries the following symbolic meanings: 
 The young girl in the icon refers to the church that looks at her martyred 
children with joy and appreciation. 
 The dragon refers to Satan, who moves the evil world against faith.

THEODORE, BISHOP OF CAPPADOCIA 
This St. Theodore (Tadros), a pparently was a shepherd before he was 
ordained as a bishop on Cappadocia. Even though he was freshly ordained and 
just got acquainted w ith St. Gregory of Nazianzus (329-390 AD), he was 
assigned to urge St. Gregory to shepherd the Orthodox congregation in 
Constantinople. St. Gregory wrote him in response  [Letter# 222], to tell him 
about what he did . He told him also about the insults that came on him from 
the bishops of that region . He also apologized about what happened to him, 
being new in his bishopric. 
 [Smith and Wace, Vol. 4, p. 932] 
 
THEODORE, BISHOP OF CONSTANTIA 
This St. Theodore (Tadros)  was the bishop of Constantia in Cyprus . He 
attended the Council of Ephesus in the year 431 AD due to the persistence of 
the bishops of Cyprus. However, he was ill -treated by the clergy of Antioch, 
because he refused to let the Church of Cyprus submit to the Church of 
Antioch. 
 
THEODORE, BISHOP OF CORINTH (The martyr) 
This St. Theodore (Tadros) was a bishop of Corinth. Some people reported 
him to the two princes Lucius and Difnanyous , as being a Christian bishop . 
The ruling pagan princes called St. Theodore and asked him about his faith , 
and he proclaimed clearly that he was a Christian . The saint was beaten, 
reviled, and drawn on the ground . Then, they dragged him to the temple to 
offer incense to the idols . There, he kicked the table on which the idols were 
placed. At that point, the two princes got angry and ordered to cut his flesh by 
the sword and to have cloth rags soaked with vinegar and salt stuffed into his 
wounds; while the saint kept joyfully testifying to his Christ. The princes gave 
the command to cut his tongue off . A woman who happened to be standing 
nearby picked it up off the ground and delivered it to him in prison . He put it 
back in his mouth, and by the grace of God, it functioned back as normal. 
Again, the bishop was called up from prison to resume his trial, and he kept 
on testifying to the Lord Christ . Suddenly, a white dove and a peacock 
appeared before the two princes and all those present . Prince Lucius believed 
in the words of the bishop. However, prince Difnanyous got angry and ordered

PHOTINUS 
Photinus grew up in Ancyra in Galatia. He was a disciple of Marcellus, the 
bishop of Ancyra. He was ordained as a deacon, then as a priest. He moved to 
Sirmium in Pannonia Secunda (nowadays Serbia) , probably when his bishop 
Marcellus was expelled f rom his diocese in the year 336 AD, and Photinus 
kept wondering between Rome and Constantinople. 
Photinus did not hide the teachings he received from his teacher but 
managed to find listeners.  He was attacked by the Eusebians in Antioch, 
counting him as a follower of his mentor; and was also attacked in Milan, 
then in the capital.  He became a bishop on Sirmium (344 -351 AD), then he 
was also expelled from his bishopric and was exiled because of his views 
concerning the Person of the Lord Christ (he denied th e Incarnation of 
Christ). Finally, he died in 376 AD. Having left no written documents behind, 
it was difficult to make an elaborate decision concerning his views , and his 
errors remained vague. Quite often, his personality was tied up to that of 
Sabillius, who denied the existence of the Holy Trinity, counting the three 
Divine Hypostasis as just three forms or names, through which God 
manifested Himself. 
He was highly educated, an eloquent orator , knowledgeable in Greek and 
Latin. He wrote against the heretics and the pagans , and his influence 
remained after his exile and even after his death.  He was condemned in the 
Council of Constantinople in 381 and 428 by Emperor Theodosius II (402 -
450 AD). 
[Socrates: Ecc. Hist. 2:18,19,30; Sozomen: E.H. 4:6; Epiphanius; Panarion, 71]  
 
PHOCAS, THE GARDNER (The martyr) 
The biography of St. Phocas (Fucas) , the martyr, got to be known through 
what was told about him by St. Asterius bishop of Amasea and St. John 
Chrysostom. St. Phocas lived near Sinope on the Black Sea. He had a garden, 
and he planted it by himself, imitating the early Holy Fathers and our first 
parents on earth in the Garden of Eden. 
This saint used to mix his work with prayer, to turn his garden i nto his 
mentor, and the source of his contemplations in the Divine Creator. He also 
opened his house to strangers and travelers to provide them with hospitality. 
Once the fruit of his love and service to the poor was consummated, God 
found him worthy to deliver his life for the sake of the Lord Christ.

The Love of the Governor for Him: 
Justus planned to select George to be wed to his only daughter , the little 
pure princess who feared God . He revealed his intention to Theobesta, the 
mother of George, before she died, and she was immensely exultant to hear it. 
He also appointed George as his deputy on all his possessions. However, Justus 
had to postpone the wedding because of the young age of his girl, unaware that 
God prepared something more significant for the young man. 
The Zeal of Prince George: 
When George heard that the emperor had gathered an assembly of seventy 
of his governors and proclaimed his intention to wipe out Christianity from the 
face of the earth, he readied himself to confront the persecution. He planned to 
make his religion known to the emperor and sold all that he inherited from his 
father, including his clothes and his house furniture , and gave the entire 
proceeds to the poor . Then he released all his slaves , and when the emperor 
issued his decree, George took it and tore it off in public before multitudes of 
people, and he prepared himself for martyrdom with joy. 
Before the Emperor: 
Then, they led him before the emperor, who started by talking to him nicely, 
promising him with extraordinary gifts . However, the young man utterly 
disregarded all these promises. On failing to seduce him, the emperor tortured 
the saint for an extended period. He kept torturing him for a whole seven years 
period. During that time, God 's hand supported him and made him a tool to 
bring a multitude of souls to the true faith . During being tortured, St. George 
died three times, and God kept raising him to be glorified in him, and amid his 
suffering, He made him enjoy heavenly visions to support him. 
More durable than Magic or Poison: 
Among the tortures that St. George was expo sed to was that the emperor 
brought a famous magician named Athanasius, who prepared a highly deadly 
poison and gave it to the saint to drink . By faith, the saint drank it , and it did 
him no harm . Right away, the magician declared his faith in the Lord  Jesus 
Christ. The angry emperor gave the order to squeeze the saint by a press  with 
sharp iron teeth until he gave his last breath , but the Lord Jesus Christ raised 
him from death, and a multitude of those who watched him tortured, died and 
getting raised from the dead, declared their faith in the Lord  Jesus Christ and 
their readiness to be martyred for His sake.  
With the emperor, there were several governors among the spectators . 
Those governors sought to test the saint, so they asked him to make their

         [Butler: May 31] 
 
CAPITOLINA, ST. 
(The martyr) 
This lady martyr was from ‘Cappadocia.’ She confessed before the governor 
that her dwelling place was the heavenly Jerusalem; and that her fathers were 
the teachers of Christianity, among them was bishop ‘Firmilian’ (232-269 AD). 
She was arrested and put in prison, where her maidservant ‘Eroteis’ visited 
her and kept kissing the chains of her mistress. 
It was said that St. ‘Capitolina’ was beheaded on the 27th of October, 
followed by her maidservant ‘Eroteis’ on the next day. Their martyrdom took 
place in the days of the Emperor ‘Valerian’ (253-260 AD). 
    [A Dictionary of Christian Biography, Vol. I, p. 399] 
 
CAPITON, ST. 
The Repentant Thief: 
This saint was living on the edge of Mount ‘Thebes.’ He was formerly a 
thief, but he repented . Afterward, he lived inside a cavity in the rocks for 15 
years. He never left that cavity, not even to go to the bank of the Nile. He used 
to say: “How can I get together with those people who made me sin? ” He 
meant: How could he return to where he sinned? 
         [The Paradise of Saints; p. 50] 
 
CAPRASIUS, THE BISHOP, ST. 
The Bishop of Agen: 
St. ‘Caprasius’ lived in the 3rd century AD, and he was the first bishop of 
the city of ‘Agen’ (in France). When ‘Dacian,’ the governor of ‘Agen’ started 
persecuting the Christians there,1 most of them escaped from the city with their 
bishop ‘Caprasius,’ who kept taking care of them. However, while he was still 
hiding, he had a chance to observe the torture of St. ‘Faith,’ and he witnessed 
the great miracles that God performed with her . So, the bishop came down

GEORGE, THE DEACON 
He was a contemporary of the 42nd Pope of Alexandria, St. Simeon I (692-
700 AD). After the departure of that pope to heaven, he was sought by some to 
be worthy of sitting on the Seat of Alexandria, although because he was not in 
the rank of priesthood, he was not selected for the papal seat. This did not 
bother him, and he continued to serve diligently and faithfully in his church, 
and eventually, he got the priestly rank . While dedicating all his energy to 
ministry, he managed to document the biographies of the popes of Alexandria. 
When he was residing in the monastery of Prince Tadros in Ablag, he started 
to write the journal of the 24 th Pope St. Cyril I, the Pillar of Faith (412-444 
AD). Then, he followed it by his successors, until he reached the biography of 
the 43rd Pope St. Al exandros II (704-729 AD), who was leading the Coptic 
Church at that time. This pope at that period was residing in the monastery of 
Abba Macarius the Great in the Scetis. Fr. George gave a good account of the 
political events through which Egypt was passin g, as well as the civil rulers 
who governed the land. He covered almost four centuries, from the 4th to the 
8th century, during which twenty Alexandrian popes sat on the throne of St. 
Mark. 
   [Iris Habib El-Masry: The Story of the Coptic Church – Bk 2, p. 328] 
 
GERASIMUS, THEODOTUS AND BISHOP ATHANASIUS 
(The martyrs)

records.question: Who was St. Mina the Wonder-Maker?
records.answer:
St. Mina the Wonder-Maker was an Egyptian martyr born around the year 285 AD in the town of Nikiu (Nakiyos) in the district of Menuf in El-Monufyia governorate on the Nile delta. His father, Eudoxius, was the governor of the city, and his grandfather Plondionus was also a governor before him. St. Mina was raised with a strong Christian upbringing, loving the Holy Bible and church teachings. After his parents died when he was young, he inherited significant wealth and spiritual blessings. He was appointed an officer in the army in ancient Africa (Algeria) but abandoned military service to dedicate himself to God, distributing his wealth to the poor and entering monastic life in the wilderness [1][7].

He desired martyrdom and was eventually arrested during the persecution under Emperors Diocletian and Maximian. Despite torture, including scourging and attempts to saw him with a sharp iron saw that melted like wax, he remained steadfast in faith. He was beheaded around the year 309 AD at the age of twenty-four. His body was miraculously preserved from burning and was buried with honor. His relics were later moved to Marriott, where many miracles and wonders occurred through his prayers [7][8].

St. Mina's tomb became a pilgrimage site where many were healed, including a lame boy and the daughter of the Emperor of Constantinople, who was cured of leprosy after following the saint's instructions in a dream. Churches were built in his honor, including one by St. Athanasius the Apostolic and later expansions supported by Emperor Arcadius. His monastery in Marriott flourished and became a center of monastic life and evangelism, with monks from there preaching to Ireland and building the first church in St. Mina's name there [3][4].

His spiritual influence continues to this day, with many people worldwide receiving healing and blessings through his intercession. His relics have been distributed to many countries, and his iconography is found in museums such as the Louvre. St. Mina is remembered for his love for God and his ongoing support for the Church and its members, even centuries after his martyrdom [3][4][6].

In summary, St. Mina the Wonder-Maker was a young soldier turned monk and martyr whose life and prayers have been associated with numerous miracles and healing, making him one of the most famous Egyptian saints [1][3][4][7][8].

he moved to El -Ashmonein, where he stayed in a monastery for sixteen 
years, during which he never left the monastery. When the Arabs ruled the 
country (after 640 AD), he heard that they denied that God has a Son from 
His nature and essence, and equal with Him in Eternity. This denial of faith 
was painful to the saint, so he took permission from the Abbot of the 
monastery and went to El-Ashmonein.  
He came before the commander of the Arab camp and asked him: “Is it 
true that you say that God has no Son from His Nature and Essence? ” The 
commander replied, saying: “We deny that saying about God and reject it. ” 
The saint told the Arab commander that it should only be rejected if His Son 
was born through parental procreation, b ut we believe that the Lord Jesus 
Christ is God from God and Light from Light. The commander replied: “In 
our faith, this is blasphemy. ” The saint told him that the Bible says: "He who 
believes in the Son has everlasting life , and he who does not believe in the 
Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God abides on him. " (John 3:36)  
The commander became enraged at this and ordered his soldiers to cut the 
saint into pieces and to throw him into the river. The believers gathered the 
parts of his body, shrouded it, and buried it. They arranged a commemoration 
to celebrate the martyrdom of St. Mina the Monk on the 17th of Amshir.  
 [The Synaxarion: 17 Amshir] 
 
MINA, THE WONDER-MAKER (The martyr) 
This St. Mina is the most famous of the Egyptian martyrs. He bec ame so 
well-known in and outside of Egypt, because of the so many wonders, 
performed by God through his prayers, up to this very day.  
St. Mina was born around the year 285 AD in the town of Nikiu (Nakiyos) 
in the district of Menuf in El -Monufyia governorate on the Nile delta. His 
father, Eudoxius was the governor of the city, and his grandfather Plondionus 
was also governor before him. Because Eudoxius had an excellent reputation 
and was loved by everybody around him due to his piety and virtues, his 
brother Anatolius was envious of him. He brought charges against him before 
Caesar Carinus (283-285 AD). However, the Caesar wanted to gain the favor 
of both men, so he sent Hypatus the leader of his army, with an order to 
appoint Eudoxius as a governor on anci ent Africa (Algeria), in place of its 
governor who passed away, and he asked Hypatus to accompany Eudoxius 
and his family on the trip and make sure that everything was for them in their 
new residence. The people of Nikiu were unfortunate to lose Eudoxius, while 
his brother Anatolius showed remorse on what he has done.

MINA, THE RELEASE DEACON, ST. 
This St. Mina is celebrated by the church on the 15th of Bashons.   
 
MINA, THE ASCETIC, ST. 
This St. Mina lived for fifty-nine years in a monastery near Alexandria. He 
reached a high level of asceticism that he forgot all about himself. Also, in his 
honor to his monastery's Abbot, he used to bow low in front of him whenever 
he would enter his cell until the Abbot would give him his blessing. Such a 
practice of piety was used by the Abbot of the monastery to teach a lesson to 
the new monks entering the monastery. Some of those monks used to ridicule 
such practices of giving honor to the elderly monks. So, it happened once that 
Mina entered the cell of the Abbot and prostrated himself before him to the 
ground as he used to do while saying: “Bless me, father.” The Abbot chose to 
disregard his presence and left him bowing for hours until it was time for 
prayer. Then, he gave him the blessing, and only then, Mina stood upright. A 
young monk said to him: “By so doing, you have wasted your precious time 
while doing nothing.” The saint answered him: “No, I did not waste my time, 
because I did use that chance to recite the whole book of Psalms.” 
God chose to honor this ascetic worshipper after his departure. So, while 
they were praying on him during his funeral, the church was filled with sweet 
fragrance as a testimony of the virtues by which he was adorned.  
 [The Faithful Synaxarion: 26 Baba] 
 
MINA, THE BISHOP (The martyr) 
This St. Mina lived in the 8 th century AD and became the bishop of Tamai 
el-Amdid in Sinbellawein. His father was from Samannud. He was the only 
son of God -fearing parents, who were known to practice a monastic style of 
prayers and fasting, which made them famous all around the area. His parents 
forced him to get married, but he got his bride's consent to keep their 
virginity. They practiced so many worships like those performed by the 
monks, they put on sackcloth and spent most of their nights in prayers and in 
reading the Bible.  
His Monastic Life: 
St. Mina longed for monastic life, so he said to his wife: “It is not befitting

morning, when the worried parents of the lame boy found him, they kept 
screaming at his face. However, they were amazed to see him jump and run 
away from them. The healed boy told the people in the village about what he 
saw. People came to the tomb, and they saw the splendid light coming out of 
it. Multitudes of people came to the saint's tomb to enjoy many wonders that 
God performed through the prayers of St. Mina.  
Healing of the Emperor's Daughter: 
Sometime later, a shepherd who was attending to his flock outside of the 
city had a sheep inflicted with skin disease. Then, it happened that the 
inflicted sheep went down into a nearby swamp, then came out and rolled 
over into the dirt , and it was instantly healed. Incredibly amazed, the 
shepherd brought over all the inflicted sheep into the swamp, then let them 
roll over in the dirt to be repaired in the same fashion. Soon enough, the news 
spread around and reached the emperor 1 of Con stantinople, whose only 
daughter was inflicted with leprosy. He sent her with a large entourage to 
Egypt to be healed in that fantastic location. In that spot, the saint appeared to 
her in a dream, instructed her to have that location dug few meters deep t o 
find his relics. So, she did, and she was instantly healed. Her father built a 
small church on that spot in the name of St. Mina, which was consecrated on 
the 15th of Paona.  
In (363-373 AD), the 20th pope of Alexandria St. Athanasius, the Apostolic 
(328-373 AD), built a church in that location, and he placed the holy relics of 
St. Mina in a special chamber beneath the Altar. Then, the 23 rd Pope St.  
Theophilus (385-412 AD) wrote to Emperor Arcadius (E: 383 -408 AD), the 
son of Emperor Theodosius the Great (379-395 AD), to ask for his help 
because St. Mina's church became too small to accommodate the multitudes 
of visitors. The emperor responded and helped him in building a sizeable 
beautiful church, in the form of an eastern extension to the church previous ly 
built by St. Athanasius the Apostolic.  
Then, in the days of the 82 nd Pope Benjamin II (1327 -1339 AD), the holy 
body of St. Mina was moved to the church of St. Mina in Fum el -Khalij on 
the outskirts of Cairo. In the days of the 116 th Pope St. Kyrillos VI (1959 -
1971), a part of his relics was moved back to its original location and was 
placed in the new monastery of St. Mina in Marriott.  
His Spiritual Effect: 
St. Mina has been martyred over 1,700 years ago when he was twenty -
four year s old, but his fragrant life and prayers still have their miraculous

effect on so many. At the beginning of the 5 th century, the hearts of many 
young men flared with God's love, sold all their possessions, and set forth to 
St. Mina's holy tomb to practice the monastic life and establish his monastery 
in Marriott.  
The history testifies that seven monks of the St. Mina Monastery preached 
the Gospel to Ireland and built the first church there in the name of St. Mina. 
The Irish Church still keeps in its prayer s up to this very day, a litany for the 
Coptic fathers who carried to them the torch of faith. According to the 
historical accounts 1 of that area, the great city of St. Mina went through 
several stages of ups and downs, flourishing and looting. During the  papacy 
of the 52 nd Pope Yusab I (831-849 AD), St. Mina's cathedral was ransacked, 
and most of its marble columns were stolen. However, its monastery came to 
flourish again in the era of the 55th Pope St. Shenouda I (859-880 AD).  
It is believed that the e ventual demise of the first great city of St. Mina 
took place around the end of the 13th century AD. Then, in the era of Pope St. 
Kyrillos VI (1959 -1971), the new monastery of Mar Mina was built, and 
another wave of monastic renaissance started anew in Marriott.  
Monuments of the era of St. Mina: 
In the German city of Frankfurt, there is a museum that is wholly 
dedicated to St. Mina. The reason behind that was the German scholar bishop 
Carl Maria Kaufmann (1872 -1951), who discovered the location of St. 
Mina's ancient city in Marriott in the year 1906/1907, managed to take back 
with him to Germany about 100 large size boxes full of beautiful artifacts, 
crowns of marble columns, etc. After that discovery, the museums of the 
whole world moved to take some of St . Mina's monuments, but Kaufman got 
the best of it. Some German researchers kept working on the location until 
2013 through an assignment by the German Museum of antiquities in 
collaboration with the Coptic Museum of Cairo, to carry out new and 
elaborate excavations.  
The departed Coptic scholar Banoub Ĥabashy moved a lot of St. Mina's 
antiquities to a section of the Graeco -Roman Museum in Alexandria, and he 
called that section: [The Coptic Museum in the era of St. Mina.]  
An Ecumenical Love:  
The heart of St. Mina was full of love for God, and he kept working, even 
after his martyrdom. Many sick people from all over the world came to get 
the blessing of his prayers and to get healed from their sicknesses. They went

of us to practice a monastic life while being in the world.” On having her 
approval, he set forth to the monastery of Abba Anthony in the eastern desert, 
to be as far as he could from his parents. They diligently searched for him for 
a while, an d then they stopped. From there, he went to the monastery of St. 
Macarius, in the wilderness of the Scetis accompanied by Abba Khael (who 
eventually became the 46 th Pope on the See of Alexandria: (743 -767 AD). 
There, they both started their monastic life, in the days of the two shining 
stars St. Abram and St. Gawargi. St. Mina became a disciple of these two 
saints and had the benefit of their vast knowledge, imitated their worship, and 
grew in the angelical work, more than many other fathers. Satan envied h im 
for his strife, and he severely struck him in his legs, that he was left bed -
ridden on the ground for two months. Then, he was healed by the power of 
the Lord Jesus Christ.  
Ordained as a Bishop: 
Then, St. Mina was called for the rank of a bishop by mes sengers sent by 
the pope. He cried for forsaking the wilderness, but after being told by the 
fathers that it was a call from God, he obeyed and went along with the pope's 
messengers, and the pope ordained him as a bishop on Tamai el-Amdid.  
God granted him  the grace of healing the sick and that of knowing the 
hidden matters in the minds of people. The other bishops all around used to 
visit him and seek his counsel. The multitudes from everywhere would come 
to him to hear his teachings. He was a contemporary  to four of the popes of 
Alexandria, and he laid his hand upon some of them during their ordinations: 
Abba Alexandros II (704 -729 AD), Abba Cosmas I (729 -730 AD), Abba 
Theodore I (730-742 AD), and Abba Khael I (743-767 AD).  
When the Lord Jesus Christ wish ed him to depart from this world, He 
informed him about it. So he called up the people of his diocese, urged them 
to abide in the upright faith, and to keep the Divine commandments. Then, he 
committed them to their True Shepherd Jesus Christ and departed t o His 
Savior, who loved him. He was so mourned by his people, who buried him in 
a place he assigned to them ahead of time.  
 [The Synaxarion: 7 Hator] 
 
MINA, THE MONK (The martyr) 
This saint was born in a village around Akhmim to Christian parents who 
lived on farming. Since his youth, his heart longed toward asceticism. He 
became a monk in one of the monasteries of Akhmim, where he dwelt, 
fasting every two days and practicing ascet icism in his food and drink. Then,

back home with holy water in small clay fl asks (ampoules) on which his 
name and picture were engraved. These ampoules are still found in many 
countries far apart, like Colon and Heidelberg in Germany, Marseille in 
France, Dalmata in Yugoslavia, Milan in Italy, Dengela in Sudan, Jerusalem 
and parts of England.  
The Icon of St. Mina: 
In the Louvre Museum in Paris, there is a Coptic icon from the 5th century, 
in which we see the Lord Jesus Christ puts His blessed hand on St. Mina's 
shoulder in exalted amiability. Such an icon reveals how the church views the 
saints, through whom we get to recognize the elevated compassion of God 
and His longing toward the believer to set with Him a covenant of love and 
friendship on an everlasting level.  
An Unceasing Action: 
My dear friend (Ĥ. Y .), who was also a frie nd of Pope St. Kyrillos VI, 
since he was a monk in Old Cairo, told me the following story:  
“One evening in the monastery of St. Mina in Marriott, when the only 
persons attending the church with the pope were just two or three people, 
during the vesper I n oticed that the pope was laughing while he was alone in 
the sanctuary. At the end of the prayer, I hastened toward the pope and told 
him: ‘I never saw you laughing in the sanctuary. Would you please tell me 
what you have seen.’ After much reluctance, he to ld me: ‘You know the 
intense tribulation we are living through these days. 1 I was complaining to 
God that, because of such bitter anguish, I am not able to resolve any 
problems for His children, but right away, St. Mina appeared to me and 
pocked my belly with his finger, saying: ‘You think that you are alone!? We 
are all working together with you. Do not despair. ’ For that reason, I 
laughed!” After more than seventeen centuries since his martyrdom and 
departure from this world, St. Mina's heart, full of love, still works for the 
kingdom of heaven, to support so many: patriarchs, b ishops, priests and the 
members of the congregation. Indeed: "Love never fails" (1 Cor 13: 8). 
[The Church of St. ‘Mina’ in Fleming: Mar Mina, the Wonder-Maker, 1963] 
[The Church of St. George in Sporting: The Egyptian Martyr Mina, 1974]

The Son of the Promise: 
St. Mina's mother, Euphemia, had no children, and one day, she went to 
the church on one of the feasts of the Virgin St. Mary, the Mother of God, at 
Atrib on the 21 st of Toba. She saw the children in the church wearing their 
beautiful clothes with their parents. She heaved a sigh and wept before the 
icon of our Lady St. Mary, imploring her to intercede for her before her 
beloved Son, so that He would give her a son. A v oice came from the icon 
saying, Amen. She rejoiced in what she had heard and realized that the Lord 
had heard her prayers. When she returned to her home and told her husband 
about it, he replied: “May God's Will be done.”  
Euphemia conceived and gave birth  to the son of her prayers, promised to 
her by the Lord Jesus, whom she called Mina, meaning ‘Amen.’ The whole 
city rejoiced for his birth, and his father Eudoxius, the governor, released 
many prisoners and gave away many donations in celebration.  
His Upbringing: 
His father cared to educate him with an Evangelic spirit about all the 
church teachings. He planted in him the love of the Holy Bible and the right 
knowledge, with the mood of worship and the pious behavior. Then, his 
father passed away when Mina was only eleven years old, followed by his 
mother when he was fourteen years old. The saint inherite d from them a 
significant wealth and much spiritual blessings and honor.  
A year after the repose of his mother, when he was fifteen years old, he 
was appointed an officer in the army in the regiment of ancient Africa 
(Algeria), for the high regard they had for his departed father.  
Becoming a Monk: 
In the year 303 AD, when a decree was issued by the two evil Emperors 
Diocletian and Maximian (284 -305 AD) ordering everyone to worship and 
offer sacrifices to the idols, the officer Mina distributed his wealth on Jesus' 
little brethren and decided to dedicate all his time and energy to the kingdom 
of God. He abandoned the military service after three years and set forth to 
the wilderness to worship God, which he was longing to do for some time.  
Then, it happened that after five years in his monastic life, Mina saw while 
praying the martyrs were being crowned by the angels and carried by them to 
Paradise, with their shiny countenance more splendid than the sun. Desiring 
to become a martyr, he heard a voice from h eaven, saying: “Blessed you are 
Abba Mina, for you are called for piety since your childhood. You will get 
three immortal crowns: one for your virginity, one for your monastic life, and 
the third for your martyrdom. Your name will be famous among the marty rs,

The Saint's Martyrdom: 
On the next day, the governor brought him up before the court of justice; 
started to treat him tenderly to bring him to his side, then when he failed, he 
threatened him with death. The governor ordered his men to scourge the saint 
with oxtails. Then, they tried to sow him with a sharp iron saw, but the saw 
melted like wax. Finally, the governor ordered to cut his head off by the 
sword. In the arena of martyrdom, the saint knelt, and after raising his hands 
in prayer toward heaven, the swordsman struck him with the sword. St. Mina 
was ma rtyred on the 15 th of Hator, around the year 309 AD , when he was 
twenty-four years old. The soldiers ignited a fire to burn his body. However, 
it remained three days and three nights in flames without being burned. Some 
believers came, took his body, shrou ded it with precious fabrics, and buried 
him with honor.  
The Body of St. Mina: 
After a few years from St. Mina's martyrdom, some of the Barbarians 
came from Eastern Libya and attacked the city of Marriott. Athanasius, the 
army commander, was asked to take his troops and defend that area. He used 
to be a very close friend of St. Mina when they were together in the army. So, 
he decided to take the body of the saint along with him. The soldiers 
uncovered St. Mina's tomb, a great light came out, before which t hey fell on 
the ground worshipping the God of St. Mina. While sailing with the body on 
a boat toward Alexandria in their way to Marriott, fierce marine beasts 
attacked them, but fire came out of the body and scared them away.  
After arriving at Alexandria with the body loaded on a camel, they 
marched to Marriott, and they defeated the Barbarians, and on their way 
back, the camel refused to get up to go with them, despite striking it very 
hard. They loaded the saint's body on another more robust camel, but i t 
refrained from moving, as well. When this was repeated, the prefect 
Athanasius perceived that it was the will of the Lord for the body to stay in 
Marriott.  
The Lord Jesus Christ Reveals the Location of the Body: 
Around the period (320-325 AD), according to the 48th Pope of Alexandria 
St. John IV 1 (777-799 AD), a lame boy who was living in a village near the 
place where the body of the saint was buried, happened to crawl out of his 
village, and when he saw a brightly lit lamp at a distance, he kept crawl ing 
toward it, when he got there, he fell asleep, from exhaustion. The next

‘Yoannes XIX’ (1928-1942) accompanied by an American author who was 
planning on writing a book about the monastic life, and the general director of 
the Ministry of Antiquities ‘Dr. Ĥassan Fouad.’ After a while, he dwelt in a 
windmill, by approval of the same director of the Ministry of Antiquities. In 
that windmill, which had no roof or door, he was accompanied by a wolf, 
which used to come  to him every evening and leave the next morning. Later 
on, with the help of those who loved him, he built a roof and a second floor for 
the windmill to have a room for a church. The Lord sent him a deacon to 
minister the Holy Liturgy every day with him. 
Abbot of the Monastery of Abba Samuel the Confessor: 
By the counsel of Abba ‘Yusab’ who was made a deputy -pope after the 
repose of Abba ‘Yoannes XIX,’ Fr. ‘Mina the Recluse ’ was installed as the 
Abbot of the monastery of Abba ‘Samuel el-Qalamony.’ Fr. ‘Mina’ started right 
away, reconstructing its empty buildings and its St. Mary church. Then, the 
church was consecrated by Abba ‘Athanasius,’ who made him a Hegumen on 
it. In this way, life returned to the monastery on the hands of that simple hermit.  
The building of Mar Mina Church in Old Cairo: 
After failing to reconstruct the monastery of Mar Mina in ‘Marriott,’ Fr. 
‘Mina the Recluse’ requested the purchase of a plot of land in old Cairo. There, 
he built a church in the name of ‘Mar Mina.’ He dwelt on its ro of and made 
some other rooms for ministry, teaching the young men new professions and 
for the dwelling of an out -of-towner, college students; among them were the 
first generation of the college graduates young monks.  
In Old Cairo, he resumed producing the  magazine of ‘The Harbor of 
Salvation.’  
Father ‘Tadros Malaty’ told this story: 
“On my visit to one of the hospitalized Sunday school teachers after being 
admitted to the University Hospital in Alexandria, he introduced me to a fellow 
patient in the same hospital, saying: ‘This is a professor in the university and 
a close friend of the departed Pope ‘Cyril VI. ’ Seeing that I was a little 
astonished in how such a young man would be a friend of the aged pope, the 
professor explained: ‘Along with a number of friends, we (as Moslem and 
Christian children) used to get together and go to visit Fr. ‘Mina the Hermit,’ 
with whom we had a really close friendship. The parents of this friend of mine 
– non-Christians – used to say to me: “This man is not of this world. ”’ Such 
was the testimony of even the non -Christians; that he carried features which 
befit those in heaven.”  
Although Fr. ‘Mina the Recluse’ was engulfed in his silence, prayers, and 
fasting; God granted him the gift of discernment, healing the sick and dr iving

wedding ceremony. Then, when he joined his wife in seclusion, he preached 
to her the virtues of chastity and living a godly life, which she accepted. After 
they had lived together for three days, without any physical contact, she 
allowed him to withdraw to the wilderness silently. There, he became a 
disciple of one of the saintly old mo nks, to whom he revealed his situation 
and his chastity in the seclusion of his cell. His family, thinking that he has 
died, set over him great mourning. In the monastery, his virtues of asceticism, 
humility, gifts, broad knowledge, and simplicity became well known.  
Then, when his spiritual father recommended him for the patriarchate, 
they took him by force to Alexandria, where he was ordained in December 
956 AD. His papacy lasted for seventeen years and eleven months (956 -974 
AD).  
His Pastoral Activities: 
The new pope started his mission by making a pastoral tour with his 
bishops to meet his congregation in the different dioceses in the country, and 
when he got to his village of Sandala, one of the natives divulged to the 
bishops that pope Mina II was a m arried man. St. Mina acknowledged the 
marriage and told them to call on his wife to hear from her. Her public 
revelation of their nominal marital relationship and their purity appeased the 
bishops. Pope Mina II began one of the essential patriarchal reigns, during 
which momentous events in the history of Egypt took place.  
Also, it happened that the level of the Nile flood continued to below for 
three consecutive years, during which famines and plagues spread around 
Egypt until God lifted them because of the prayers raised by the church.  
During the reign of the Abbasid caliph Al -Mutiå Lillah (946 -974 AD) in 
Baghdad, this revered pope was contemporary of Egypt's acting governor 
(Amir) Abu al-Misk Kafur (966-968 AD) who was an Abyssinian eunuch and 
became the guardian over the underage children of the deceased governor Al-
Ikhshid ibn Tughj. Kafur was known for his justice and leniency. Under these 
circumstances, the Copts and the patriarchate had a breathing space and a 
period of relative peace and security, providing that they rendered the Kharaj 
(Tax) to the ruler. During his rule, the Coptic feasts were publicly celebrated.  
The pope focused his efforts on building and mending the churches, and 
establishing preschools and regular schools for the children. He consecrated 
the Holy Myron in th e church he built in the name of St. Mark at Maĥalet 
Daniel, instead of the well -established custom of consecrating it in the 
monasteries. While he was in that town, he departed to the heavenly glories 
on the 13 th of November 974 AD. His body was then move d to be buried in 
the tombs of the Patriarchs in Alexandria.

records.question: Who was St. Shenouda the Archimandrite?
records.answer:
St. Shenouda the Archimandrite was a prominent monastic leader in Egypt during the 4th and 5th centuries, known for representing Coenobitic Monasticism after St. Pachomius. He was the Abbot of The White Monastery near Sohag in the desert of Thebes for more than 56 years, supervising about 2,200 monks and 1,800 nuns [1][2]. He was given the title "Archimandrite," meaning the head of the anchorites, because he practiced a life of seclusion periodically and encouraged monks to retreat to the wilderness after practicing communal monastic life [1].

He was born to pious Christian parents and raised with strong Christian principles. As a child, he was dedicated to prayer and fasting, and was placed under the care of his maternal uncle, Abba Pigol, the abbot of the Red Monastery, who blessed him to become a spiritual father to many [3]. Shenouda was girded with the Holy Eskeem (monastic belt) by his uncle after a divine vision [3].

St. Shenouda developed a monastic system with certain unique plans for joining the monastery, emphasizing both communal life and preparation for seclusion [1][3]. He was deeply involved in social and political matters, defending the oppressed, feeding the hungry, and awakening patriotic feelings among Egyptians against Byzantine occupation and Chalcedonian imposition [8]. He used the Upper Egyptian dialect of Coptic in his writings and sermons, and did not allow foreigners to join his monastic congregation, which was exclusively Coptic [1][8].

He also cared for nuns, writing letters to guide and teach them, and maintained his seclusion annually despite his large responsibilities [2]. During a barbarian attack on Upper Egypt, he bravely negotiated the release of captives and opened his monastery to shelter thousands for three months, providing medical care and sustenance [2]. He lived to the age of 118, with 66 years as abbot, and handed over leadership to his disciple St. Wissa [2][9].

In 431 AD, he accompanied Pope Cyril the Great to the third Ecumenical Council in Ephesus [1]. His life combined spiritual leadership, social reform, and patriotic activism, making him a key figure in the history of Egyptian monasticism and the Coptic Church [1][8].

SHENOUDA, THE ARCHMANDRITE, ABBA 
St. Shenouda is considered the most prominent personality representing the 
Coenobitic Monasticism in Egypt after St. Pachomius. Therefore, he was given 
the title of Archimandrite, meaning (the head of the anchorites), on account 
that he used to practice the life of seclusion now and then. He also encouraged 
some of his monks to retreat to the w ilderness after they practice the life of 
fellowship for a few years, yet without completely losing their relationship 
with the monastery. While St. Pachom saw in the Fellowship the climax of the 
monastic exaltation, St. Shenouda saw it as a transition sta ge that would 
prepare the soul for the more elevated monastic life of seclusion. 
St. Shenouda the Archimandrite was the Abbot of The White Monastery in 
Attrib near Sohag in the desert of Thebes in the 4 th and 5th centuries for more 
than 56 years. According  to his disciple, who succeeded him, he supervised 
about 2,200 monks and 1,800 nuns during that time. 
In the year 431 AD, he accompanied the 24 th pope of Alexandria St. Cyril 
the Great (412-444 AD) to attend the third Ecumenical Council in Ephesus. 
St. Shenouda never allowed a foreigner to join his monastic congregation, 
but all his monks were of Coptic descent. That is why many European scholars 
avoided mentioning his name when they spoke about the Fathers of the 
wilderness. For many centuries, they did not try to translate any of his works. 
His Youth: 
Shenouda is the Upper Egyptian Coptic (Sahidic) version of the saint's 
name. He used only the Upper Egyptian dialect in his writings, sermons, and 
daily talks. The Lower Egyptian (Bohairic) version of his nam e is Shenoute,

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Volume 4, p. 137

137 
 
and the thousands of his monks did not try to isolate themselves from Egyptian 
society. As an example, when the Barbarians attacked Upper Egypt and looted 
all the possessions and took thousands of citizens as prisoners, St . Shenouda 
dared to face the invaders and convince them to take the spoils, but to let the 
captives go free. He then opened his monastery before the thousands of 
captives to dwell there for three months, during which the monks dedicated 
their time to serve them, including seven physicians among the monks, to nurse 
their wounds. During that period, 94 persons died and were buried in the 
monastery, 52 babies were born, and 8,500 bushels of wheat and vast amounts 
of lentil and beans were consumed. From this ex ample, we can imagine the 
number of guests who were served in the monasteries within that extended 
period; and how the monks got to believe in the practical love, as more critical 
virtue than any monastic law or system. 
His Care for the Nuns: 
Abba Shenouda was a Father and Mentor, not only to thousands of monks 
but to 1,800 nuns as well. For them, he wrote multi -purpose letters to teach, 
guide, and hold them fast to the Upright Faith. But despite being a Father over 
such a vast number of monks and nuns, yet  he kept on practicing his life of 
seclusion. So, he earned the title of Archimandrite. Every year, he used to 
spend some time in seclusion, during which no one dared to approach him. 
He lived to reach 118 years of age, of which 66 years as the Abbot of several 
monasteries, some for monks and others for nuns. However, during those long 
years, until he reached that advanced age, God granted him health and strength 
to keep all his life working hard, from the time he received the leadership of 
the Red Monaster y after the repose of his uncle Pistol. And through his 
persistent strife, he managed to establish the order of his monasteries; until he 
handed the flame shining to his disciple Wisa. He also managed to wake up in 
his fellow citizens their patriotic emotions toward their country. 
 [Fr. Tadros Yacob Malaty; The Coptic Church is a Church of Monasticism]  
 [The Coptic Encyclopedia: Shenute Saint, by K. H. Kuhn; pp. 2131 -3] 
 
SHENOUDA (The martyr) 
He lived during the 2 nd half of the 7 th century when the Arab invasion to 
Egypt has just begun. This saint was raised in a truly Christian way. He 
observed a lifestyle within God's commandments and guidelines. He did not 
stop at fasting, prayers and attending masses, but he was also a generous giver 
to the poor, and always visiting the sick and imprisoned. Some evil people 
were annoyed by his piety, so they went to the Arab governor, claiming that 
the saint was mocking their religion. So, they brought him over for

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Volume 4, p. 134

134 
 
meaning (The servant of God or the one dedicated to God). 
Shenouda was born to pious Christian parents, who raised their son on the 
ideal Christian principles. His father had a field where he and his farmers 
worked; he also had herds of sheep, which he trained his ten years old son 
Shenouda to shepherd. The little boy used to be all day long with the other 
shepherds, to whom he gave his food and kept fasting the rest of the day, and 
instead of going directly back to his parents, he used to stand beside a well and 
pray until late at night. 
With his Uncle Pigol: 
When his father became aware of his son's behavior, he took him to his 
maternal uncle, the well -known Abbot Abba Pigol, and sought from him to 
bless his young son. Abba Pigol took th e boy's hand and laid it on his head, 
saying: “You bless me, my child, for you will be a Father for so many peoples.” 
On hearing this, Shenouda's father was immensely rejoiced and left his little 
son in the monastery in the care of his uncle. So, he learne d all the Christian 
virtues. He kept striving for spiritual perfection through fasting, praying, 
perseverance, and humility. Watching him with great interest, his uncle 
rejoiced in his rapid and persistent growth in knowledge and virtue. And, his 
joy was concluded by a night vision in which an angel of the Lord told him: 
“Put the Holy Eskeem on the young man Shenouda.” In the very early morning, 
Pigol woke up, prayed the prayer of the Eskeem, and girded the young 
Shenouda with it. 
Through the following year s, Shenouda lived in the “Red Monastery,” 
where his uncle Pigol was the Abbot of the monks. Since he got the honor of 
the Eskeem, he doubled his efforts in studying the Divine books, not only for 
his benefit but also of the monks and the visitors who came to the monastery, 
whom he gathered around him and taught them the Upright Faith. 
The Archimandrite: 
One day, the elderly monks heard a voice, saying: “Shenouda became an 
Archimandrite.” (Meaning head of the anchorites). The enflamed zealously of 
Shenouda, his exalted holiness, and the many Divine proclamations granted to 
him by the heavenly Father; drew multitudes of people to live under his 
guidance to learn the Christian virtues. And when Abba Pigol departed to the 
Church of the firstborn, they chose Shenouda to replace him. 
His Monastic System: 
Even though Abba Shenouda followed the monastic system that was 
prevailing in Egypt, yet he set up a plan for his monks to adopt. In that plan, 
there were certain differences concerning the way to apply for joining  the

125 
 
archons, in particular Ibn Bakr, the pope issued a decree that all the possessions 
of the bishops should be inherited by the patriarchate after their death. The new 
system first applied to the bishop of Shenan, and then it continued to be applied 
until our present era; until pope Shenouda III (1971 -2012), canceled it and 
decided to keep the diocese possessions of a reposed bishop for the one who 
would follow him. As a result of the e rroneous behavior of that pope and his 
persistent seeking for wealth, the Church’s clergy wanted to deliver the affairs 
of the Church to a particular Council. However, the pope rejected their request. 
So, the whole congregation turned to prayers, asking Go d to protect His 
Church. The patriarch was inflicted by a problematic disease that caused him 
to shake violently, and all the physician’s attempt to cure it ended with failure; 
until he departed from this world in the year 1047 AD. 
 [Revealing the Secrets in the History of the Patriarchs, vol. 2, p. 11] 
 [Fr. Menasseh Yohanna: The History of the Coptic Church] 
 [The Coptic Encyclopedia: Shenute II, by Subhi Y. Labib; p. 2135] 
 
SHENOUDA III, The 117th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA 
On the 17 th of March 2012, the long trip of pain which his holiness Pope 
Shenouda III has lived had ended and began the journey of the glories hidden 
from the human eyes. During those days when Egypt was living through his 
departure to Paradise, his funeral gathered all Egyptian categories; it included 
Muslims and Christians from all the denominations, leaders, and ordinary 
people. He had been a messenger of peace struggling in a difficult time and a 
man of peace, even in his departure from this world. 
They all expressed their heart-felt deep grief, which shared by a lot of the 
presidents and institutions of the world uniquely and beautifully. His 
marvelous love for the leading figures in the Arab world; made some of them 
say: "He isn't the Pope for the Christians only , but he is the Pope for all the 
Arab countries." For his funeral, the people got crowded in such a compact 
fashion that three people died in the process, and six ambulances carried those 
who couldn't handle the unbelievable crowding. One of the broadcasters said: 
"I am not surprised to see some people here preferring to die in this crowded 
procession, just to have the blessings from his corpse! " The unique way that 
the people were expressing their grief of him after his departure was a natural 
fruit for the fertile seeds of love which he planted within them during his life. 
Pope Shenouda III (1971-2012) was the 117th pope of Alexandria and the 
patriarch of the See of St. Mark. His episcopate lasted over 40 years from the 
14th of November 1971 until his deat h on the 17 th of March 2012. He was a 
conservative figure within the Church and was also highly respected within the 
Muslim community.

the governor that they saw him sound with no wounds, he said that he was a 
sorcerer. Then, he ordered to hang him upside down and ignite fire underneath 
him. When it caused him no harm, he ordered pressing him in the Henbazin;

SHENOUDA I, The 55th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA 
Pope Shenouda I (Shenute/Sanutios: 859-880) was a native of the village of 
El-Batanun in Menufyya governorate. He became a monk in the monastery of 
St. Macarius. There, he progressed in virtue,  and he was ordained a hegomen 
on the church of the monastery. His fame extended beyond the wall of his 
monastery, for when his predecessor, the 54th Pope Cosmas II (851-858), died. 
the bishops, the clergy, and the leading Coptic archons unanimously though t 
of him as a worthy successor to the throne of St. Mark. At a meeting in Al -
Fustat/Cairo, they decided to hasten to his monastery to bring him to the valley 
for his ordination. But one archon, Abraham, knowing that he would be 
unwilling to accept their call, suggested that he should go and ask Shenouda to 
come only to help them in finding the right candidate for that dignity. Once he 
was present, the council forced him to go to Alexandria with them for 
consecration, even against his will. And that happened. Ultimately the bishops 
laid their hands on him on the 13th of Toba 576 AM (8 January 859 AD) in the 
church of Abu-Serga during the reign of caliph El-Mutawakkil (847-861), and 
he had to face the heavy responsibilities of his office. 
Many Great Tribulations: 
At the beginning of his papacy, there was a period of peace over the Church; 
for the governor, Ăbdel Waĥed ibn Yeĥya was a just man who treated all 
Egyptians fairly. But after four years, new Turkish governors were appointed 
by the Ăbbasid caliphate, and they brought upon the pope and the people 
severe persecutions. 
In the year 861, when Yazid åbd -Allah became a governor on Egypt, he 
ordered the pope to pay him 5,000 dinars every year., Not able to pay such an 
enormous sum of money, the pope  fled to a faraway monastery. When the 
governor attacked the churches and robbed the priests and the people, the pope 
gave himself up to the governor, who cast him in prison and demanded from

questioning. St. Shenouda declared that he believed in Christ, who commanded 
his followers to love everybody. He explained to the governor that he was just 
doing that, and he never made fun of any religion. The governor did not accept 
his reasoning and ordered him to deny his Christ and  join Islam. The saint 
refused to proclaim his pride in being a Christian. The governor put him 
through so many tortures, which he accepted gladly. 
Finally, they beheaded him, and he received the crown of martyrdom. 
    [The Synaxarion: 13 Abib] 
 [Iris El-Masry: The Story of the Coptic Church, vol. 2, p. 85] 
 
SHENOUDA, THE MONK, ST. 
This saint was a hearing-impaired elder monk who lived during the Fatimid 
era (909-1171 AD), in a cell near the town of Nousa, the province of Aga in 
the Daqahlyia governorate. The biography of this saint was written in the great 
work The History of the Patriarchs , which was started by Severus ibn al -
Muqaffaå (died 987 AD) and was completed by others to cover the period 
ending in 1167 AD. One of the authors of this book sent the saint a message 
asking for his prayers on his behalf and the behalf of his brother Fahd, for both 
were put in prison through an order made by Badr el-Gamaly (~1070 AD) the 
commander of the army of the caliph Al-Mustansir bi-Allah (1035-1094 AD). 
The saint answered him, saying: “Today, the Lord Jesus Christ will set you 
both free.” On the same day, they were released. 
 [The Patriotism of the Coptic Church and its History, p. 130] 
 
SHENOUSI, THE YOUNG MAN (The martyr) 
Saint Shenousi's name was also mentioned under the name (Sanusi) and 
(Sinosius) in the Synaxarion of the 4 th of Paona. This saint was 12 years old, 
an innocent boy from the town of Balkim in the province of El -Santa 
nowadays. While he was shepherding the sheep, an angel of the Lord appeared 
to advise him on martyrdom and encouraged him that he would be with him. 
He bid his mother farewell without telling her where he was going, prayed, and 
went his way to the town of Towwa. And, when he found out that the governor 
left to Saresanah, then to Daku, he looked for someplace to spend the night. 
He was led to the house of a saintly woman called Mariam, dedicated to 
providing hospitality to strangers. 
The next day, he went along with Mariam to the governor and confessed the 
Name of Christ before him. The governor ordered to place him in the press, 
which got split into two once they put him there. Assuming that he was a

the “Sunday-School” Monthly Magazine. In 1950, Nazir resigned from secular 
employment to take up a full-time lecturing position at the seminary.  
In 1952 he was elected as a member of t he Egyptian Journal Syndicate. In 
1953, he was appointed a lecturer at the Monastic College in Helwan, offering 
courses in Theology there. In the same year, he began his dialogue with 
“Jehovahs Witnesses,” writing articles about their beliefs in the Sunday-School 
Magazine. Nazir, with others, labored for several years to establish a strong 
Sunday-School and youth group at St. Anthony’s Church in Shubra. His 
ministry produced many devoted servants, who began developing youth 
groups in neighboring parishes. 
An avid reader, he was a keen student of languages and a man of vast 
ecumenical insights. Besides the Arabic, he spoke fluent English and French, 
read Greek and Latin, and also mastered the Amharic language. 
His Monastic Life and Educational Service: 
On the 18 th of July 1954, Nazir joined the monastic life at the Syrian 
Monastery of the Virgin Mary the Theotokos in Scetis in the Natron Valley in 
the Western desert of Egypt. He was given the name of Fr. Antonius el-Suriani 
(Anthony the Syrian. From 1956 to 1962, he lived as a hermit in a cave about 
7 miles away from the monastery, dedicating his time to meditation, prayer and 
asceticism. His austerity was known to be exceptional, even by monastic 
standards. On the 31 st of August 1958, he was ord ained as a priest by bishop 
Theophilus, the Abbot of the Syrian Monastery.  
Fr. Antonius el-Suriani was among the candidates nominated for the papal 
throne in 1959. But, at that time, Fr. Mina the Anchorite was chosen by an 
“Altar Lot” for the post to become Pope Cyril VI (1959-1971). 
Ordained as a Bishop of Education: 
On the 30 th of September 1962, Pope Cyril VI appointed him to the 
bishopric of Christian Education and as Dean of the Coptic Orthodox 
Theological Seminary. He renamed him Bishop Shenouda in honor of the most 
renowned scholar and writer in Coptic, St. Shenouda the Archimandrite (348-
466). Under the leadership of Bishop Shenouda, the number of students at the 
Coptic Orthodox Theological Seminary tripled. Bishop Shenouda used to have 
weekly lectures in Cairo for the general public, which was attended by a vast 
number of believers.  
Ordained as a Pope: 
Bishop Shenouda was enthroned as Pope Shenouda III, the 117th Pope of 
Alexandria and patriarch of the See of St. Mark on the 14th of November 1971 
by an “Altar Lot,”  nearly nine months after the death of Pope Cyril VI of

the Egyptians stood up as one entity against the Chalcedonian intruders and 
rejected them, even when they took the religious form. 
Ecclesiastical Political Leader (Against Byzantine Occupation): 
Even though Abba Shenouda led a life of seclusion since his childhood, yet 
he was observing the world in which he lived. He attentively watched the 
events and the political disturbances taking place in the outside world. He 
perceived that the faithful disciple of Jesus Christ is the one who delivers His 
message to other men. On looking around, he noticed how his fellow citizens 
were burdened by the bitter servitude of worries and fears induced by 
paganism. He also realized that the Byzantine rulers were sucking the blood of 
the striving people and robbing the fruits of their labor. So, he dedicated 
himself to set them free; first from their fears, by confirming to them that the 
Divine care would protect them from any harm. He combined his teaching with 
action, by feeding the hungry, clothing the naked, treating the ill, and giving 
hospitality to the stranger. Above all that, he accompanied the oppressed to the 
court of justice to defend them; and when he failed to bring justice to them, he 
would bring their complaint up to the emperor. And, he would not have peace 
until the oppressed had judgment. 
Once, in a public assembly, he stirred up the multitudes by saying: “The 
hearts of the rulers are filled with evil, deception, injustice , and greed. They 
have only one goal, to gather money at the expense of the poor . Who could 
count the troubles endured by our people from those rulers? I  know some 
people who lack the necessary food for themselves and their cattle . I am sure 
they have the intention to turn the Egyptians to slaves and put the yoke on their 
shoulders.” 
He used what God granted him of the gift of eloquence and writing to stir 
up the patriotic spirit in the people, addressing them only with the Coptic 
language in its Upper Egyptian dialect. By such pure Egyptian tongue, he 
managed to inflame their hearts with zeal, to wake up their spirit, and to make 
them perceive the honor of being Egyptians. That fire ignited in them by Abba 
Shenouda came to be the driving force, which enabled the Egyptians t o stand 
firm before their occupation rulers. This was expressed in their firm stand 
against the hateful Chalcedonian Council when they refused to bow their heads 
before Emperor Mercian (450-457 AD), when he thought that he would be able 
to force them to ad opt his Chalcedonian belief; contrary to the Orthodox 
doctrine which they inherited from their Fathers. 
A Spiritual and Social Reformer; 
Abba Shenouda felt that worship was bound to the social life, and religion 
was both an applied love as well as a spirit ual love. Therefore, St. Shenouda

WISSA, ST. 
St. Wis sa (Bessa) was the closest disciple to Abba Shenouda the 
Archimandrite (348-465), and he was the one who wrote the biography of the 
archimandrite. Although we do not know much about his life , we see a lot 
about his thoughts, views , and spiritual tendencies. His written works still in 
existence, the most important of which is the biography of his great mentor, 
Archimandrite. St. Wissa wrote, as well, many letters, essays , and mymers, 
which were included in a collection of manuscripts in the Saåidic dialect of the 
Coptic language, now kept in the Museum of Napoli in Italy. There is also 
another collection, known as ‘The Collection of Carzon,’ kept in the British 
Museum, which consists of 11 complete and three incomplete letters; all of 
which are addressed from ‘ Wissa’ to his monks and nuns.  Even th ough 
‘Carzon’ said that he purchased those documents from the monasteries of the 
Natron Valley, yet it is evident that their source was ‘The White Monastery’ in 
Upper Egypt. Those letters gave a shining portrait of the monasteries 
established by Abba Shenouda and were taken care of by St. Wissa after him. 
They are, as well, shining evidence of the excellent care ‘Wissa’ was giving to 
the monks and nuns under his supervision. 
The researcher might find one day the biography of St. Wissa, and they 
might not. Still, either way, it is enough for us to know that he consummated 
his mission and proved his worthiness to succeed his most prominent mentor 
Abba Shenouda the Archimandrite. 
 [The Story of the Coptic Church, Bk 1, p. 481]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Volume 4, p. 124
passages.text:
124 
 
death of the Godhead. The pope debated with them and explained to them the 
upright faith, based on the Holy Bible and the Sayings of the Fathers, until they 
returned to the mother church and offered obedience towards their bishops. 
That pope cared so much for the church's affairs and its various institutions. 
And, whatever remained in the patriarchates funds, he distributed among the 
poor. When he completed his unique struggle, he reposed in peace on the 14th 
of Baramhat 597 AM (869 AD), after he sat for about 21 years on St. Mark 
Seat. 
 [Fr. Menasseh Yohanna: History of the Coptic Church] 
 [The Coptic Encyclopedia: Shenute I, by Subhi Y. Labib; pp. 2133 -5] 
 
SHENOUDA II, The 65th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA 
After the repose of the 64 th Pope Zecharias (1004 -1032), the bishops and 
the archons recommended the monk Shenouda of the monastery of St. 
Macarius to sit on the papal seat. A night vision confirmed their choice to one 
of the bishops. He was  ordained by the name of Pope Shenouda II (Sanutios: 
1032-1046) in the year 1032; in the days of the Fatimid caliphate (909-1171). 
The Tolerance of the Caliph: 
At that time, it was the custom that the caliph would be paid by the Copts 
6,000 dinars to get h is approval on the appointment of their new patriarch. 
However, there was among the Copts a man of high status called Ibn Bakr. He 
managed to convince the caliph to issue an order to waive such a fee. 
Out of the graces of God on the Copts during the time of this patriarch, the 
caliph Al-Zahir bi-Allah (1021-1036) followed the lead of his earlier ancestor 
the great caliph Al -Ăziz bi -Allah (975 -996) in his tolerance with the non -
Muslims, which resulted in a vast growth in the creative and artistic 
achievements in the country The caliph’s tolerance went so far to allow 
anybody converted to Islam to go back to his Christianity if that was his wish. 
He also allowed for building so many new churches. 
The Patriarchs Preoccupation with Wealth: 
During the ordination process, the clergy of Alexandria made it a condition 
on the papal candidate to promise that he would spend 500 dinars on their 
churches every year. Also, the archons made his pledge to refrain from 
receiving any bribes (simony) from those seeking clergy positions. Despite his 
promise to reject the Simonism in ordaining the clergy, yet he took a bribe to 
ordain a bishop for Assiut without even conferring with the people. That made
